docs.title: Computational Neuroscience
docs.text:
A free, self-paced course in computational neuroscience, built around Dayan & Abbott's Theoretical Neuroscience (MIT Press, 2001) and the exercise sets the authors publish alongside it. No enrollment, no instructor. 28 lessons, about 135 hours.

Eleven foundation lessons work through the textbook chapter by chapter: spike trains and firing rates, receptive fields, neural decoding, information theory, membrane biophysics, integrate-and-fire neurons, cable theory, network models, synaptic plasticity, reinforcement learning, and representational learning. A synthesis checkpoint closes the track. Sixteen advanced lessons follow, in three tracks: spiking network dynamics, biology for modellers, and predictive coding.

Each lesson pairs a lecture with a spec of acceptance criteria and four pieces of coursework: guided reading, a pen-and-paper derivation, a simulation under 100 lines, and a written explanation. Where the textbook authors publish their own exercises for a chapter, those take precedence over the course's own. Every simulation in the foundation track was run before its answers were written — the numbers in the lectures are measured, not plausible.

Needs linear algebra, calculus, probability, and the ability to write a simulation. No neuroscience background assumed.

docs.title: Figures and attribution
docs.text:
The diagrams throughout these lessons are reproduced from Dayan & Abbott, Theoretical Neuroscience (MIT Press, 2001), from the figure sets the authors publish for teaching at gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~dayan/book. They are the authors' work, not this course's, and are used here with attribution in a free non-commercial guide intended to send readers to the book rather than replace it.

The same site offers the exercise sets, data, errata and chapter 7 in full, all free. If you are reading this course, buy or borrow the textbook — the lessons are a guide through it, not a substitute for it.

Rights holders who would prefer a figure removed need only ask, and it will be.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Everything this course needs, and where to get it. One required purchase; everything else is free.

docs.title: The textbook
docs.text:
Dayan, P. & Abbott, L.F. — Theoretical Neuroscience: Computational and Mathematical Modeling of Neural Systems. MIT Press, 2001.

  • Publisher: https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262041997/theoretical-neuroscience/
  • Paperback ISBN 978-0-262-54185-5 · Hardcover ISBN 978-0-262-04199-7
  • Authors' companion site: https://www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~dayan/book/ — table of contents, figures, errata, teaching support

The whole foundation track (F1–F11) is this book, chapter by chapter, and it carries five of the advanced lessons outright. There is no substitute in the course as written.

Check a university library before buying: most institutions with a neuroscience or machine-learning programme hold it, often with electronic access.

./fetch_book_materials.sh

docs.title: The exercise sets
docs.text:
https://www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~dayan/book/exercises.html

Dayan & Abbott publish problem sets for all ten chapters, with MATLAB code and data files. These are assigned in every foundation lesson and take precedence over this course's own exercises where the two overlap — they are the authors' problems.

Chapter 1's set includes c1p8.mat: twenty minutes of real recordings from a fly H1 neuron responding to white-noise visual motion, collected by Rob de Ruyter van Steveninck, sampled at 500 Hz. Several problems build on it.

fetch_book_materials.sh pulls these along with everything else. The files are the authors', so they are gitignored rather than committed.

docs.title: Python
docs.text: Python 3 with numpy. matplotlib for the plotting exercises, scipy for a few, torch only if you prefer it — every simulation in the course runs on numpy alone. The exercise sets are written for MATLAB; translating them is part of the work.

docs.title: Supporting papers
docs.text:
Twenty-eight papers are cited across the advanced tracks. Ten are openly available and fetch automatically:

python3 fetch_papers.py

That script doubles as the bibliography — every entry carries a DOI resolved against Europe PMC. It lands files in papers/ (gitignored).

Of the twenty-eight, twenty-one can be had for nothing and seven need a library. The split is not the one a publisher page suggests, so it is worth stating precisely.

Downloaded by script (12). fetch_papers.py gets these: Izhikevich 2006 · Hertäg & Sprekeler 2020 · Ólafsdóttir, Bush & Barry 2018 · Bogacz 2017 · Millidge, Seth & Buckley 2021 · Feldman & Friston 2010 · Salvatori et al. 2022 · Friston, Daunizeau & Kiebel 2009 · Song et al. 2020 · Whittington & Bogacz 2017. Then fetch_closed_papers.py adds two more from author-hosted copies: McClelland, McNaughton & O'Reilly 1995 (Stanford) and Rao & Ballard 1999 (UT Austin) — both of which the open-access indexes wrongly list as closed.

Free, but you have to click (9). These are genuinely open access — OpenAlex confirms it — but PubMed Central, SAGE and Cell all refuse automated downloads, so no script will get them. Open each in a browser and save it:

Paper Lesson Link Hopfield 1982 A2 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/346238 Tsodyks & Markram 1997 A4 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/19580 Wang 2010 A3 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/2923921 Attwell & Laughlin 2001 A5 https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001 Yu & Dayan 2005 B1 http://www.cell.com/article/S0896627305003624/pdf Bastos et al. 2012 B2 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2012.10.038 Poirazi, Brannon & Mel 2003 B3 http://www.cell.com/article/S0896627303001491/pdf Schafer et al. 2012 B4 http://www.cell.com/article/S0896627312003340/pdf Hensch 2005 B4 via OpenAlex: https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1038/nrn1787 → best_oa_location

Save them into papers/ using the filenames in fetch_closed_papers.py and the scripts will stop asking for them. That closes B2, which was the lesson most damaged by a missing source — Bastos is the canonical-microcircuit paper the Step 5 layout depends on.

Genuinely needs institutional access (7). Fries 2005 · Roy, Jaiswal & Panda 2019 · Schultz, Dayan & Montague 1997 · Larkum 2013 · London & Häusser 2005 · Huttenlocher & Dabholkar 1997 · Foster & Wilson 2006. a university library will cover these; the lessons that use them name a substitute.

DOIs for all twenty-eight are in fetch_papers.py, each resolved against Europe PMC.

docs.title: NotebookLM — free
docs.text:
https://notebooklm.google.com

The packs in notebooklm/ generate an audio overview for a lesson, which is the first step of the running order. A free Google account is enough. Each pack folder holds the sources to upload and the prompts to paste; the Drive mirror is convenient on a phone.

docs.title: Further reading, where the book stops
docs.text:
• Gerstner, Kistler, Naud & Paninski — Neuronal Dynamics. Free online at https://neuronaldynamics.epfl.ch/. Modern, spiking-focused, good where Dayan & Abbott is thin (synaptic delays, adaptive exponential models).
  • Buzsáki — Rhythms of the Brain. Breadth on oscillations for A3.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text: No copy of the textbook is distributed with this repo, and none will be. Buy it, borrow it, or use a library copy.

docs.title: Plan and progress
docs.text: The map over the whole course. foundations.md and lessons.md hold the lesson specs; this page is the order they go in and a place to track what is done.

docs.title: The two halves
docs.text:
Foundations (F1–F11) work through Dayan & Abbott end to end, assuming no neuroscience. Advanced (A, B, C) go past the textbook into the literature, and depend on the foundations being in place. Between them sits the Bridge, a synthesis checkpoint.

Roughly 135 hours: ~60 for foundations, ~75 for advanced.

docs.title: The ordering rule
docs.text:
Foundations first, in order. F1 before F2 before F3, and so on. The dependency graph:

F1 ──┬── F2 ── F3 ── F4
     └── F5 ──┬── F6 ── F8 ── F9 ──┬── F10
               └── F7                └── F11 (also needs F3)

Then the Bridge, which gates entry to the advanced half.

In the advanced half: track A is sequential and finishes before track C starts. Track C is sequential too. Track B runs alongside either and gates nothing, with three dependencies — B4 assumes B2, B2 assumes B3's E/I material, and B5 assumes A2.

The reason A precedes C: spiking dynamics and predictive coding are separate bodies of theory, and the lessons that combine them only make sense once each stands on its own.

docs.title: Questions the course leaves open
docs.text:
These are live research questions, not gaps in the material. Each is raised by the lesson named.

  • Whether enforcing Dale's principle — that a neuron is excitatory or inhibitory, never both — matters for a model that is not trying to be a brain (B2).
  • Whether a model that grows its own structure should add units or add capacity inside existing ones (B3).
  • Whether an error-driven growth signal and an activity-driven homeostatic signal should be separate variables (B4).
  • Whether a network learning online from a correlated stream needs a replay mechanism, and what the cheapest version looks like (B5).
  • Whether the equivalence between predictive coding and backpropagation survives arbitrary topologies, spiking nonlinearities and structural change (C6). It does not, and C6 is about why that matters.

docs.title: How to use the coursework
docs.text:
Each lesson has a lecture, a spec with five acceptance criteria, and four pieces of coursework, plus the textbook authors' own exercises for that chapter. Work them in the published order: read, derive, build, explain.

The acceptance criteria are criteria for the lesson. If you cannot reason your way to them afterwards, the lesson did not do its job — go back to the section rather than grinding at the question.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
Sixteen lessons in three tracks, past the textbook and into the literature. Gated behind the Bridge checkpoint. About 75 hours.

Track A is sequential and must finish before track C begins. Track C is sequential, starting after track A. Track B runs alongside the other two; B4 needs B2, B5 needs A2.

docs.title: A1 · Synaptic delays and temporal structure
docs.text:
At a glance

Length — one to two sittings · about ~3.5 hours across one to two sittings (Piece 1: 60 min, Piece 2: 50 min, Piece 3: 50 min, Piece 4: 45 min) Before this — the Bridge checkpoint; F1 (spike trains), F6 (integrate-and-fire), F9 (STDP) Reading — Thin in D&A — ch. 5 Synaptic Conductances and ch. 6 The Cable Equation give transmission and propagation, but not delay as a computational resource. Primary: Izhikevich 2006, Polychronization: Computation with Spikes. Supporting: Gerstner et al., Neuronal Dynamics (free online) on transmission delays.

  • A1 · Synaptic delays and temporal structure
    • Lesson spec
    • Coursework
    • Verified against the source
    • Completion bar

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: Replace the instantaneous weight-matrix picture — spike in, weighted sum out, same tick — with one where when a spike arrives matters as much as how strong it is. Topology plus delays is a computation over time, not just space. Walks away able to distinguish delay-based mechanisms (coincidence detection, delay lines) from weight-based ones.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • Real figures: axonal conduction delay (~0.5–10 ms depending on myelination and distance) vs synaptic transmission delay (~0.3–3 ms), and where these numbers come from physically
  • How delay converts a static weight matrix into a temporal computation: coincidence detection and delay lines
  • Delay as a third learnable or evolvable parameter alongside weight and connectivity — what it means for a virtual-memristor synapse to store a delay as well as a weight
  • Polychronous groups (Izhikevich 2006): memory that lives in the delay structure, requiring no weight change
  • Not covered: network-wide rhythms and synchrony (A3), attractor dynamics (A2)

You should be able to answer: 1. Give typical ms ranges for axonal conduction delay vs synaptic transmission delay, and name one anatomical factor that shortens each. 2. Describe a concrete 2-input circuit where a delay difference — not a weight difference — is what makes a downstream neuron fire. 3. If two synapses feeding the same neuron have delays of 3 ms and 7 ms, under a ±20 ms STDP window, does that 4 ms gap meaningfully change which side of the STDP curve a near-simultaneous pre/post pairing lands on? 4. What does a polychronous group store — weights, delays, or both — and why can one fixed network support many more such groups than it has neurons? 5. Name one way delay could be treated as a plastic parameter like a weight, and one way it is more naturally treated as fixed structural wiring.

Project tie-in: Feeds Step 3 directly — whether the virtual-memristor synapse carries a delay field alongside its weight, and whether the prediction→error neuron link inside a neuron pair should account for transmission lag.

Done when: You can sketch a coincidence-detection circuit with explicit delay values and state why polychronous-group memory needs no weight update.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine:

audio overview → guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written defence (Piece 4)

Pieces are numbered by type, not by sequence. The reading front-loads the concepts, the derivation makes them exact, the simulation is where they stick and get refined, and the defence is where you find out whether they did.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1 — Coincidence and the STDP curve derivation 2 (primary), 3 (primary) 2 — Delay-only coincidence detector simulation 1 (delay values realistic), 2 (primary, computational confirmation of Piece 1A) 3 — Reading Izhikevich 2006 guided reading 1 (primary), 4 (primary), 5 (primary) 4 — Should the neuron-pair link learn a delay? written defence 3 (reinforced), 4 (reinforced), 5 (primary) Piece 1 — Coincidence and the STDP curvePiece 2 — Delay-only coincidence detector (simulation)Piece 3 — Reading Izhikevich 2006 (guided reading)Piece 4 — Should the neuron-pair link learn a delay? (written defence)

Type: derivation · Time: 60 min

Learning goals - Compute EPSP arrival times from source spike time + transmission delay, and show algebraically that a downstream neuron's firing outcome can flip when only a delay changes, weights held fixed. - Place a delay difference on the STDP timing curve and judge whether it changes which side of the curve (potentiation vs. depression) a pairing lands on, versus merely changing magnitude.

Task

Part A — delay flips the outcome, weight does not. Two presynaptic neurons, A and B, both synapse onto neuron C with identical weight w = 0.6 (dimensionless, same units as threshold) and identical EPSP shape: an alpha function EPSP(s) = w · (s/τ) · exp(1 − s/τ) for s ≥ 0, and 0 for s < 0, where s is time since the EPSP's arrival at C and τ = 2 ms. (This alpha function peaks at value w when s = τ — check that you get EPSP(τ) = w before going further.) C fires if the summed potential V(t) = EPSP_A(t − t_arr,A) + EPSP_B(t − t_arr,B) reaches threshold θ = 1.0 at any t. Ignore membrane leak and reset for this derivation — you are only checking whether the sum of two EPSP curves clears the bar.

A fires at t = 0 ms; total transmission delay (axon + synapse) A→C is 5 ms, so its EPSP arrives at t = 5 ms. B fires at t = 3 ms. Consider two scenarios for B's transmission delay only — A's delay and both weights are unchanged throughout: - Scenario 1: delay B→C = 2 ms → EPSP arrives at t = 5 ms (coincident with A's). - Scenario 2: delay B→C = 6 ms → EPSP arrives at t = 9 ms (4 ms after A's).

For each scenario, write V(t) as the explicit sum of the two shifted alpha functions, find its maximum value analytically or by evaluating at ≥ 6 well-chosen t values spanning the region where both EPSPs have non-negligible amplitude, and state whether C fires.

Part B — does a 4 ms delay gap matter to STDP? Now treat A→C (only) as a plastic synapse under a standard exponential STDP rule with a ±20 ms window: Δw = A₊ · exp(−Δt/τ₊) if Δt > 0 (pre-before-post, potentiation), Δw = −A₋ · exp(Δt/τ₋) if Δt < 0 (post-before-pre, depression), with τ₊ = τ₋ = 20 ms and A₊ = A₋ = 1 (normalized units), Δt = t_post − t_pre,arrival.

A single presynaptic spike at t = 0 reaches C via two candidate synapses with transmission delays 3 ms and 7 ms respectively (so arrivals at t = 3 ms and t = 7 ms). C fires once, at t_post = 10 ms. Compute Δt and Δw for each of the two arrival times. State in one sentence: does the 4 ms delay gap change which side of the STDP curve (potentiation vs. depression) the pairing lands on, or only its magnitude — and by roughly what percentage?

Deliverable Handwritten or typed: (A) V(t) expressions and evaluated maxima for both scenarios with a fire/no-fire verdict for each; (B) Δt, Δw for both delays and the one-sentence verdict with the percentage.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Part A: correct V(t) construction, correctly locates near-peak by evaluation or calculus, gets both fire/no-fire verdicts right, explicitly states weight was held fixed. Part B: correct Δt and Δw for both delays, correctly identifies both land on the potentiation side, gives a percentage difference within ~5 points of the correct ~22%. Adequate Gets both fire/no-fire verdicts right in Part A by evaluation even if the peak-finding is approximate; Part B gets Δt right and correctly says "same side, different magnitude" without an accurate percentage. Not yet Flips a fire/no-fire verdict in Part A, or claims in Part B that the 4 ms gap flips potentiation to depression (or vice versa), or conflates the two parts' delay values.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation · Time: 50 min

Learning goals - Build a minimal leaky-integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron receiving two synaptic inputs and confirm computationally that varying delay alone — weights and everything else fixed — flips the firing outcome. - Connect the discrete-time simulation result back to the closed-form alpha-function argument in Piece 1 Part A, and be able to say why the two models don't have to agree numerically to agree qualitatively.

Task Write a self-contained Python script (numpy or PyTorch, your choice; under 100 lines) implementing: - Postsynaptic neuron C, membrane equation dV/dt = −V/τ_m + I(t), τ_m = 10 ms, V(0) = 0, Euler integration with dt = 0.1 ms over T = 20 ms. - Two synaptic input currents, each an exponential PSC I_syn(t) = w · exp(−(t − t_arr)/τ_syn) for t ≥ t_arr (0 otherwise), τ_syn = 1 ms, w = 0.65 for both synapses, held fixed across every run. - Synapse A: arrival always at t_arr,A = 5 ms. - Synapse B: run the simulation twice, changing only the arrival time: (i) t_arr,B = 5 ms ("coincident" — matches the total delay used in Piece 1 Scenario 1), (ii) t_arr,B = 9 ms ("offset" — matches Piece 1 Scenario 2). - Firing threshold V_th = 1.0 (no reset needed — just detect whether V(t) ever reaches V_th and report the peak value and, if fired, the first-crossing time).

Print, for both runs: peak V, the time of the peak, whether the neuron fired, and (if fired) the crossing time. Your script must produce one run that fires and one that does not, using only the two arrival times above and no other parameter changes between runs.

Deliverable The script, plus a 3–5 line written note: (a) the two printed results, (b) whether the outcome matches the fire/no-fire pattern from Piece 1 Part A, (c) one sentence on why the numeric peak values differ between the alpha-function derivation and this LIF simulation even though the qualitative pattern matches.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Script runs, uses exactly the specified parameters, correctly reproduces fires=True for the coincident case and fires=False for the offset case, note correctly explains the qualitative match and correctly attributes the numeric mismatch to the different PSP/EPSP model (exponential PSC + leaky integration vs. alpha function), not to a bug. Adequate Script runs and gets the right fire/no-fire pattern but the note is thin (just restates the numbers without explaining the model-mismatch point), or minor parameter drift (e.g. dt=1ms) that doesn't change the qualitative result. Not yet Script does not reproduce a clean fire/no-fire split (e.g. both fire, or neither fires) without you noticing/investigating, or weights differ between the two runs, or delay values used don't match the two scenarios specified.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: guided reading · Time: 50 min

Source: Izhikevich, E.M. (2006), Polychronization: Computation with Spikes, papers/A1_izhikevich_2006_polychronization.pdf.

Learning goals - Extract the paper's own numeric range and construction method for conduction delays, and identify one anatomical/positional factor the paper ties to delay magnitude. - State precisely, in the paper's own terms, what a polychronous group is defined by (weights, delays, or both) and why a fixed network supports far more such groups than it has neurons. - Determine whether the paper treats delays as plastic (co-evolving with STDP) or fixed for the simulation's duration.

Task — answer these five questions, citing section/figure/table where you found each answer: 1. What integer-millisecond range does the paper assign to synaptic conduction delays in its simulated network, and how is each synapse's specific delay value chosen (fixed at construction? drawn randomly? structured by some spatial/anatomical rule)? 2. In the paper's own words or your close paraphrase, what does it mean for a group of neurons to fire polychronously, as distinct from firing synchronously? Give the distinguishing feature. 3. According to the paper, what is fixed to define a given polychronous group — the set of synaptic weights, the set of delays, or both? Quote or closely paraphrase the specific passage that answers this. 4. The paper argues a fixed network of N neurons can support far more than N coexisting polychronous groups. What mechanism does it give for this (what combinatorial structure is being exploited), and what approximate number of coexisting groups does it report for its example network — and how does that compare to the neuron count used? 5. Does the paper hold conduction delays fixed for the duration of a simulation, or does it let delays change (e.g. via a delay-analogue of STDP) alongside weight changes from STDP? Quote the passage that settles this.

Deliverable — five short answers (2–5 sentences each), each with a section/figure/table citation from the paper.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All five answers correct with a specific citation each; Q3 and Q4 correctly identify delays (not weights) as the defining/fixed structure of a PNG and correctly state the combinatorial argument (many distinct delay-compatible subsets exist within one fixed network) rather than just asserting "there are more groups than neurons" without the mechanism. Adequate Four of five correct with citations; Q4's reported group-count is in the right order of magnitude even if not exact; Q3 correctly says "delays" without fully articulating why weights alone aren't sufficient to define a group. Not yet Q3 or Q5 answered backwards (e.g. claims delays are learned via STDP, or that weights alone define a PNG), or no citations given, or Q4 answer just repeats "many more groups than neurons" with no mechanism.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: written defence · Time: 45 min

Learning goals - Synthesize criteria 3, 4, and 5 into a single argued design decision applicable to Step 3 of the project. - Take an explicit, falsifiable position and defend it against the strongest counterargument, rather than listing pros and cons neutrally.

Task Write a 300–600 word position paper answering: Should the prediction→error neuron link within a neuron pair (Step 3 of this project) carry a learnable delay parameter, in the same way it carries a learnable weight?

Take an explicit position — learnable delay, fixed delay set at construction, or some third option (e.g., delay fixed but weight-dependent at construction time, never updated afterward) — and defend it using all three of the following, each addressed explicitly: (a) Where the intra-pair link sits on the axonal (~0.5–10 ms) vs. synaptic (~0.3–3 ms) delay spectrum, and what that implies about the physical/computational role this delay would play if the architecture is meant to be neuromorphic-hardware-compatible. (b) The polychronous-group argument (Piece 3, Izhikevich 2006) for why fixed delays are computationally valuable on their own, without any weight plasticity — and whether that argument transfers to a two-neuron pair, or specifically needs the combinatorics of a larger network to do any work. (c) Whether a local STDP-style rule operating within a ±20 ms window (Piece 1 Part B) is even fine-grained enough to distinguish and act on delay differences of the size relevant to a neuron pair (a few ms) — i.e., could a purely local plasticity rule meaningfully learn a delay at all, given what Piece 1 found about a 4 ms gap only producing a ~22% magnitude change, not a sign flip.

You must address the strongest counterargument to your own position, not just state your view.

Deliverable — 300–600 words, plain prose (no bullet-point dumping of (a)/(b)/(c) as a checklist — they should be woven into a single argument).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Takes an explicit, specific position; correctly uses the fact that Izhikevich's PNG argument depends on network-scale combinatorics of many delay-compatible subsets, and explicitly reasons about whether/how that scales down to (or fails to apply to) a single neuron pair; correctly uses Piece 1B's finding (4ms gap → sign-preserving, ~22% magnitude change) to argue about the feasibility of local delay-learning at pair-relevant delay scales; engages a real counterargument and rebuts or concedes it explicitly; stays in the 300–600 word band. Adequate Takes a position and uses at least two of (a)/(b)/(c) correctly and specifically (not just gesturing at them); counterargument is present but thin (stated, not really engaged); word count close to the band. Not yet No explicit position taken (lists pros/cons and stops), or misuses the PNG argument (e.g. claims it directly implies pair-level delays must be fixed, without addressing the scale mismatch), or ignores Piece 1B's quantitative finding entirely, or no counterargument addressed.

The paper's claim is stronger than "more groups than neurons": with five neurons the example network has 14 polychronous groups, and "adding a sixth neuron triples the number of groups so that there are more groups than synapses in the network". It also states the self-organisation into groups "is a robust phenomenon that occurs despite the experimentalist's efforts to prevent it", and that changing model parameters twofold changes how many groups are supported without eliminating them. Grade the synapse comparison as the correct answer; neurons is the weaker version.

docs.text:
At a glance

Length — two to three sittings — includes running the diagnostic against the saved model · about ~7-8 hours across 2-3 sittings Before this — A1; LIF dynamics, graph topology with reciprocal connections, homeostasis Reading — D&A ch. 7 Recurrent Networks (selective amplification, continuous line attractors, bump/ring attractors) and Stochastic Networks (energy functions, Hopfield/Boltzmann) — the core text for this lesson. Supporting: Hopfield 1982 (PNAS) for the original.

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: Describe network state as a point moving on an energy landscape, explain why a trained recurrent network settles to discrete fixed points instead of drifting, and separate state (fast, per-trial) from weights (slow, cross-trial) as two memory timescales. Closes the gap exposed by your own CartPole attractor test: they can observe distinct settled states but have no principled way to decide whether those are real basins or an artifact of stopping too early.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • Energy/Lyapunov framing: fixed points as local minima, basins of attraction, why symmetric recurrent weights guarantee convergence
  • Hopfield network as the worked example: patterns as attractors, capacity limits, spurious attractors
  • State as short-term memory vs weights as long-term memory — why the same weights give different committed outputs from different starting states
  • Diagnosing genuine multi-basin structure vs unconverged slow modes: convergence-rate check (geometric decay vs plateau), perturbation test, Jacobian/eigenvalue check near the fixed point
  • Attractors in spiking networks: bump attractors, persistent activity
  • Not covered: limit cycles and rhythmic dynamics (A3), the PC energy function itself (C1)

You should be able to answer: 1. In a Hopfield network, why does a symmetric weight matrix guarantee the energy never increases as the state updates? 2. Give a concrete perturbation-test protocol for the saved 256-neuron CartPole network that distinguishes "20 genuine basins" from "20 slow-converging trajectories" — what do you perturb, what do you measure, and what result rules out which hypothesis? 3. In your attractor test, pairwise L2 distance dropped from ~2.1 (100 iters) to ~1.7 (10000 iters) — ~19% over a 100× increase in iterations. Is that consistent with geometric convergence to fixed points, or with a slow mode still relaxing? What further datapoint settles it? 4. What stays fixed and what changes when you compare "the network learns" to "the network settles to an answer for one input"? 5. What is a bump attractor, and how does persistent spiking activity implement a fixed point when individual neurons cannot hold a static real-valued output?

Project tie-in: Resolves the open interpretation question left by the 2026-04-15 attractor test in comp_neuro_notes.md, and explains why state persists across CartPole timesteps in network.py / online_rollout.py independently of weight updates.

Done when: You designs and describes, unprompted, the diagnostic in question 2 and runs it against the saved model — evidence, not intuition.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine:

audio overview → guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written defence (Piece 4)

Pieces are numbered by type, not by sequence. The reading front-loads the concepts, the derivation makes them exact, the simulation is where they stick and get refined, and the defence is where you find out whether they did.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1 — Hopfield energy monotonicity derivation 1 2 — Hopfield capacity/spurious attractor + CartPole diagnostic simulation 1, 2, 3 3 — D&A ch. 7 guided reading guided reading 4, 5 4 — State vs weights, and judging the diagnostic written defence 2, 3, 4 Piece 1 — Energy monotonicity in a symmetric Hopfield networkPiece 2 — Hopfield capacity/spurious attractor, then the real CartPole diagnosticPiece 3 — Guided reading: D&A ch. 7Piece 4 — Written defence: state vs weights, and judging the diagnostic

Type: derivation · Time: 45-60 min

Learning goals - Derive, from the Hopfield energy function, the exact algebraic identity that links one asynchronous neuron update to the resulting energy change. - Show numerically that the identity forces ΔE ≤ 0 under the standard update rule when weights are symmetric. - Show numerically that the guarantee breaks when weights are asymmetric — i.e. show the counterexample, not just assert the theorem.

Task

Binary Hopfield network, N=4 units, states s_i ∈ {−1,+1}, energy

E(s) = −½ Σ_i Σ_j w_ij s_i s_j (i ≠ j, w_ii = 0)

Asynchronous update rule for unit i: s_i ← sign(h_i), h_i = Σ_j w_ij s_j (j≠i, sign(0) = keep current value).

Part A (general identity). Show that if w_ij = w_ji for all i,j, then E(s) = −s_i h_i + C, where C does not depend on s_i. Use this to derive ΔE = −(s_i' − s_i)·h_i = −Δs_i·h_i for a single-unit update, and show this quantity is always ≤ 0 given the update rule s_i' = sign(h_i). State the two conditions on W your derivation used.

Part B (concrete numbers). Use

      j=1  j=2  j=3  j=4
i=1 [  0    1   -1    1 ]
i=2 [  1    0    1   -1 ]
i=3 [ -1    1    0    1 ]
i=4 [  1   -1    1    0 ]

Initial state s⁽⁰⁾ = (+1, −1, +1, −1).

  1. Compute E(s⁽⁰⁾) directly from the energy formula (sum over the 6 pairs i<j).
  2. Compute h_1 under s⁽⁰⁾, apply the update to unit 1 only, get s⁽¹⁾. Compute ΔE two ways: (i) via the shortcut −Δs_1·h_1, (ii) by recomputing E(s⁽¹⁾) directly. They must agree.
  3. Repeat for unit 3, updating from s⁽¹⁾ to s⁽²⁾. Report E(s⁽⁰⁾), E(s⁽¹⁾), E(s⁽²⁾) and both ΔE's.

Part C (why symmetry, concretely). Using the same energy formula but the asymmetric matrix w₁₂ = 1, w₂₁ = −5 (others 0), and the row-based update rule h_i = Σ_j w_ij s_j, start from s⁽⁰⁾ = (+1, −1). Update unit 1 only, and show E increases. Report the before/after energy and ΔE. State in one sentence which step of your Part A derivation fails when w_ij ≠ w_ji.

Deliverable: A written derivation (Part A), the three numeric energy values and two ΔE checks (Part B), and the asymmetric counterexample with its ΔE (Part C). Plain text/LaTeX, no code required (arithmetic only).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Part A derivation is algebraically correct and identifies both conditions (symmetry, zero self-weight) explicitly; Part B numbers match the grader key exactly with both ΔE methods agreeing; Part C shows a genuine energy increase and correctly diagnoses which line of the Part A derivation breaks. Adequate Part A reaches the ΔE = −Δs_i h_i identity but is vague about why symmetry is required; Part B numbers are correct or have one arithmetic slip caught by the two-method cross-check; Part C shows an increase but the explanation of why is hand-wavy ("weights aren't equal") rather than tied to the derivation step. Not yet Part A skipped or asserts the theorem without deriving it; Part B numbers wrong and not cross-checked; Part C either doesn't show an increase (arithmetic error) or is missing.

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation (two parts) · Time: 3-4.5 hours (the centerpiece of this lesson)

Learning goals - Reproduce, with a self-contained script, the classic Hopfield capacity curve and a spurious attractor, so "basin," "capacity," and "spurious minimum" are concrete before applying them to a real network. - Design and run a perturbation-test protocol on the actual saved CartPole network that could, in principle, distinguish genuine multi-basin structure from an unconverged slow mode. - Practise stating a decision rule before seeing the result, and reporting an honest "inconclusive" when the data doesn't cleanly resolve it.

Type: guided reading · Time: 1.5-2 hours

Learning goals - Connect the eigenvalue/eigenvector treatment of linear recurrent networks to the energy argument derived by hand in Piece 1. - Articulate concretely how a continuous attractor (bump/ring) differs from an isolated point attractor, and how a population of spiking neurons can implement either. - Locate, in the text, exactly where a weight variable and a state variable each appear, to ground the state-vs-weights distinction before writing about it in Piece 4.

Task. Read D&A ch. 7, the Recurrent Networks sections covering selective amplification, linear/nonlinear recurrent dynamics, and continuous line / bump / ring attractors, plus the Stochastic Networks section on energy functions and the Hopfield network. Answer, in writing:

  1. In a bump/ring attractor, what continuous variable does the bump's position encode, and why does the network have a whole continuous family of fixed points along that variable rather than one isolated fixed point? Describe the geometric picture (valley vs single-point minimum).
  2. A single LIF neuron cannot rest at an arbitrary constant real-valued output — it either spikes or is silent. What quantity is actually held fixed at a "fixed point" of persistent activity, if not any one neuron's voltage trace? Name the coding variable and how it's constructed from spikes.
  3. D&A analyse linear recurrent networks via the eigenvectors/eigenvalues of the (symmetric) weight matrix. Connect this to Piece 1: what role do eigenvalues play in whether a mode gets amplified into persistent activity vs decays, and why does W's symmetry (guaranteeing real eigenvalues) matter for getting monotone convergence rather than oscillation?
  4. D&A state the same "energy never increases under asynchronous update" result you derived by hand in Piece 1. Check: do their stated conditions match yours exactly (symmetric weights, zero self-weight)? Name any condition they add that you didn't need to state explicitly in Piece 1 (hint: synchronous vs asynchronous update).
  5. Find one equation in the recurrent-network sections containing both a weight term and a state/activity term. State which of the two is being held fixed while the other evolves during (a) the settling/dynamics phase and (b) the learning phase.

Deliverable: written answers, roughly half a page each, citing the specific mechanism (not just "the book says so").

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Every answer names the correct mechanism with correct terminology (continuum of degenerate minima / zero eigenvalue along the ring direction; population rate as the persistent variable; eigenvalue-driven amplification tied explicitly back to Piece 1's ΔE argument; correctly flags the synchronous/asynchronous condition; correctly identifies which variable is frozen in which phase). Adequate Answers are directionally correct but stay at the level of restating the text without connecting to Piece 1's derivation or the CartPole project (e.g. answers Q3 without mentioning eigenvalues, or Q2 without naming a rate/population variable). Not yet Confuses a bump attractor with a single isolated point attractor, or claims persistent activity requires every neuron to fire at literally the same instant/rate as every other, or misses the synchronous/asynchronous distinction in Q4 entirely.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: written defence · Time: 1-1.5 hours

Learning goals - Articulate, precisely, the state/weight timescale separation and its exception in this project's own online-learning setting. - Take a defensible, falsifiable position on the multi-basin vs slow-mode question grounded in your own Piece 2(b) data, not intuition. - Reason about whether a specific observed fact (the action sign crossing zero) is actually evidence for either hypothesis, or a red herring.

Task. Write 300-600 words addressing all three:

(a) What stays fixed and what changes between "the network learns" and "the network settles to an answer for one input"? Ground this in both the Hopfield formalism (Piece 1: which symbol is w_ij, which is s_i, in the update rule vs the storage rule) and the CartPole network. Explicitly address the wrinkle in this project's own online-learning setting (campaign 02), where weights do update during a rollout — does the clean state/weight separation still hold there, and if not, what replaces it?

(b) State your current best judgment on the multi-basin vs slow-mode question from Piece 2(b), using your own decision rule and your own numbers. If your data was ambiguous, say "inconclusive" and say why. Either way, state one concrete, checkable observation that would change your mind.

(c) The settled ACTION value ranged from −0.69 to +0.67 across different initial states, for the identical clamped observation. Is the fact that it crosses zero itself informative about which hypothesis (basins vs slow mode) is more likely — or is it uninformative, and the sign alone should be ignored? Justify your position.

Deliverable: 300-600 words, prose (not bullet points for the main argument; a short table is fine as support).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong (a) correctly states weights=slow/cross-trial, state=fast/per-settle, AND correctly identifies that online learning blurs this by letting weights move within a single rollout at a much slower rate than the settling dynamics but on the same trial — some remaining separation of timescales, not a clean binary. (b) States a position consistent with their own Piece 2(b) numbers and decision rule, with one concrete falsifying observation named. (c) Correctly argues the sign crossing alone is not informative — either hypothesis could plausibly place the settled action on either side of an arbitrary zero threshold; what would be informative is repeatability of sign given the same reference point, not the specific value. Adequate (a) states the basic weights/state distinction correctly but doesn't engage with the online-learning wrinkle. (b) takes a position but it doesn't clearly trace back to their own Piece 2(b) numbers, or no falsifying condition is given. (c) takes a defensible position but the justification is thin (asserts rather than reasons through what each hypothesis would predict). Not yet (a) confuses which variable is "learning" and which is "settling," or ignores the online-learning case entirely when asked. (b) asserts certainty with no numbers or falsification condition — or contradicts their own Piece 2(b) findings. (c) treats the zero-crossing as proof of two genuine attractors (or proof of one), without considering that a slow-mode account could produce the same crossing.

docs.title: Part (a) — Hopfield capacity and a spurious attractor
docs.text:
Task. Self-contained numpy script (no torch, no downloads), exact parameters:

  • N = 100 units, s_i ∈ {−1,+1}.
  • Generate a pool of 30 random ±1 patterns: rng = np.random.default_rng(0), pool = rng.choice([-1, 1], size=(30, 100)).
  • Storage: for a given P, patterns = pool[:P], weights W = (patterns.T @ patterns) / N, then zero the diagonal.
  • Async settle: repeatedly sweep units in a random order (np.random.default_rng(order_seed).permutation(N) per sweep), for each unit set s_i = sign(h_i) with h_i = row i of W dotted with current s (keep s_i unchanged if h_i == 0), stop when a full sweep makes zero changes, cap at 20 sweeps.
  • Corruption for a stored pattern p (index idx): flip each bit independently with probability 0.2 using np.random.default_rng(2000+idx).
  • Capacity curve: for P in {5, 8, 10, 13, 15, 18, 20, 25, 30}: store pool[:P]; for each of the P patterns, corrupt it (seed 2000+idx), settle (order seed 3000+idx), compute overlap m = (s_final · p)/N; count "recalled" if m ≥ 0.95; report recall fraction and mean overlap vs P.
  • Spurious attractor: store only pool[:3]. Build the mixture state mix = sign(pattern1+pattern2+pattern3) (ties → +1). Settle starting from mix (order seed 11). Report the overlap of the settled state with each of the 3 stored patterns. Then run one more verification sweep (order seed 555) from the settled state and report how many units change — a true fixed point changes zero.

Deliverable: the script, a printed table (P, recall_fraction, mean_overlap), and the spurious-attractor overlaps + verification-sweep change count, plus 2-3 sentences: does the recall curve show a sharp knee, and roughly where relative to the textbook capacity α_c·N ≈ 0.138·100 ≈ 13.8? Is the mixture state a genuine, stable, non-recalled fixed point by the 0.95 threshold?

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Recall curve matches the grader key within noise (mean overlap trend included, not just the pass/fail fraction); correctly locates the knee near P≈13-18 and connects it to 0.138N; spurious attractor confirmed stable (0 changes) with all three overlaps correctly reported and correctly identified as below the recall threshold. Adequate Curve shape is right (recall degrades with P) but exact numbers are off because a spec detail was changed (different seed, different sweep cap) without acknowledging it; spurious attractor demonstrated but the stability check is skipped or misinterpreted. Not yet No knee / recall doesn't degrade (bug in settle or overlap sign convention); "spurious attractor" reported is actually one of the 3 stored patterns (overlap ≈1.0 with one of them) — i.e. didn't check against all three.

docs.title: A3 · Oscillations and synchrony
docs.text:
At a glance

Length — one to two sittings · about ~3.5–4.5 hours, split across 1–2 sittings Before this — A1, A2; E-I balance, lateral inhibition / WTA, Dale's principle Reading — D&A ch. 7 Excitatory-Inhibitory Networks — D&A derives oscillation onset from E-I dynamics directly, which is exactly the PING mechanism. Not in D&A: communication-through-coherence and phase coding — Fries 2005; Wang 2010 (Physiol Rev) for a rhythms review; Buzsáki, Rhythms of the Brain, for breadth.

  • A3 · Oscillations and synchrony
    • Lesson spec
    • Coursework
    • Completion bar

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: Understand how an E-I feedback loop plus conduction delays produces a population rhythm, why different frequencies map to different circuit time constants and functions, and that relative phase — not just rate — can carry information and gate which inputs get through. Closes the gap between "oscillations are a side effect of recurrent circuits" and "oscillations are a functional routing mechanism", with both positions statable.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • PING vs ING: how the E→I→E loop and its time constants set cycle period; why inhibition, not excitation, paces the rhythm
  • Bands with real numbers: theta ~4–8 Hz (long loop, navigation and sequence memory) vs gamma ~30–80 Hz (short local loop, feature binding and attention)
  • Communication-through-coherence: spikes arriving inside vs outside a receiving neuron's excitability window
  • The binding problem and phase alignment across assemblies
  • Phase-of-firing as an information channel additional to rate
  • Not covered: replay and sharp-wave ripples (B5), attractor fixed points (A2)

You should be able to answer: 1. Given excitatory decay ~5 ms, inhibitory decay ~10 ms and a 2 ms loop delay, estimate whether the rhythm lands in gamma or theta, and why. 2. Why does a short local E-I loop produce gamma while a longer loop produces theta — what specifically about loop delay changes? 3. In a 25 ms gamma cycle with a 5 ms postsynaptic excitability window, work out whether two inputs 12 ms apart in phase both get through, and what determines the answer. 4. Give a concrete example of information carried in phase-of-firing that could not be recovered from rate alone. 5. State the strongest evidence that oscillations are causally functional, and the strongest evidence they are epiphenomenal — one piece each.

Project tie-in: Bears on Step 3 — whether coordination across graph nodes needs an explicit phase/synchrony mechanism, or whether the purely-local constraint (no global clock) can achieve equivalent routing without a shared oscillatory reference.

Done when: You sketches the PING loop timing diagram unprompted, places theta and gamma with their functions, and gives one concrete piece of evidence for each side of the functional-vs-epiphenomenal debate.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine:

audio overview → guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written defence (Piece 4)

Pieces are numbered by type, not by sequence. The reading front-loads the concepts, the derivation makes them exact, the simulation is where they stick and get refined, and the defence is where you find out whether they did.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1 — PING loop timing and the coherence window derivation AC1, AC2, AC3 2 — E-I rate-model rhythm and its onset simulation AC1, AC2 (validation) 3 — D&A ch.7 guided reading guided reading AC2 (primary-source grounding), background for AC5 4 — Functional or epiphenomenal? written defence AC4, AC5 Piece 1 — PING loop timing and the coherence windowPiece 2 — E-I rate-model rhythm and its onsetPiece 3 — D&A ch.7 guided readingPiece 4 — Functional or epiphenomenal?

Type: derivation · Time: 60–75 min

Learning goals - Derive an E-I loop's oscillation period from its inhibitory decay and loop delay, and show excitatory decay does not enter. - Explain mechanistically why inhibition, not excitation, paces a PING rhythm. - Compute whether two phase-separated inputs both fall inside a receiving neuron's excitability window, and identify what that outcome depends on.

Task

Part A — period from decay + delay. Model: an excitatory population E and inhibitory population I in a feedback loop. E fires a volley; after one-way conduction delay d it reaches I; I fires and releases inhibition that decays with time constant tau_I; once that inhibition has decayed, and after a further one-way delay d for the inhibitory signal to reach E, E is free to fire the next volley. Use the approximation

T ≈ tau_I + 2d
f = 1000 / T      (T in ms, f in Hz)

(the 2d is the round-trip conduction delay: once E→I, once I→E; tau_I is the time inhibition takes to decay enough for E to escape).

Given parameters: - tau_E = 5 ms (excitatory synaptic/membrane decay) - tau_I = 10 ms (inhibitory decay) - d = 2 ms (one-way loop delay)

  1. Compute T and f from the formula. State whether the rhythm lands in theta (~4–8 Hz) or gamma (~30–80 Hz).
  2. tau_E = 5 ms was given but does not appear in the formula. Explain in 2–3 sentences, in terms of the PING mechanism, why the excitatory decay constant does not set the inter-volley interval, while the inhibitory decay constant does.
  3. Recompute T and f for a "long loop": tau_I = 100 ms, d = 15 ms. State the resulting band.
  4. Sketch (ASCII is fine) a timing diagram of one full cycle of the case in (1): a time axis in ms from 0 to T, with marks for "E fires," "signal reaches I," "I fires / inhibits," "inhibition reaches E and starts decaying," and "E free to fire again." Every mark must have a real ms value from your computation, not a placeholder.

Part B — the coherence window. A gamma rhythm has a 25 ms cycle. The receiving neuron has a 5 ms window of postsynaptic excitability once per cycle (the period right after inhibition bottoms out, when the membrane is close enough to threshold for an incoming EPSP to trigger a spike). Two excitatory inputs, A and B, are phase-locked to two different upstream assemblies; B arrives 12 ms later in phase than A on every cycle.

  1. If A arrives inside the excitability window, work out whether B also arrives inside a window (same cycle or a neighbouring one). Show the arithmetic (12 ms vs. window width 5 ms vs. cycle length 25 ms).
  2. State explicitly what determined your answer to (5) — is it the number of spikes, the firing rate of A and B, or something else?

Deliverable: one page (typed or scanned handwriting) with: Part A steps 1–4 (including the diagram), Part B steps 5–6, one line of computed numbers per step — no unexplained final answers.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Both Part A cases correctly classified (gamma, theta) with correct T/f arithmetic; explanation of why tau_E drops out is mechanistic (references the loop's "brake" being inhibition, not "E is ready to fire" hand-waving); timing diagram has all four marked events with correct ms values; Part B correctly concludes B is filtered out with reasoning tied to phase modulo cycle length, not rate. Adequate Correct band classification in both Part A cases but the "why tau_E drops out" explanation is vague or only restates the formula; diagram present but missing one mark or one value; Part B has the right numeric conclusion but the "what determines the answer" line is hand-wavy or conflates phase with rate. Not yet Either Part A case misclassified (e.g. calls the 5/10/2 case theta or the 100/15 case gamma); no mechanistic account of why tau_E is irrelevant; Part B concludes "both get through" or "neither gets through" without correct 12 vs. 5 vs. 25 arithmetic.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation · Time: 75–100 min

Learning goals - Build a minimal delayed-feedback E-I rate model and measure its emergent oscillation frequency numerically, without assuming the answer. - Empirically confirm the direction of the tau_I → frequency relationship predicted in Piece 1. - Observe that oscillation is not guaranteed for every parameter setting — there is an onset/offset boundary (ties to D&A ch.7's treatment of when the E-I system transitions from a stable fixed point to a sustained rhythm).

Task

Implement, in Python (numpy or PyTorch, no autograd needed), a two-population rate model with an explicit conduction delay, Euler-integrated:

dE/dt = ( -E + sigmoid( gain * (w_EE*E   - w_EI*I_delayed + I_ext - theta_E) ) ) / tau_E
dI/dt = ( -I + sigmoid( gain * (w_IE*E_delayed - w_II*I           - theta_I) ) ) / tau_I
where E_delayed(t) = E(t - d), I_delayed(t) = I(t - d) (implement the delay with a ring buffer / array indexing, not an approximation), sigmoid(x) = 1/(1+exp(-x)).

Exact fixed parameters (do not change these): tau_E = 5 ms, d = 2 ms, w_EE = 2.0, w_EI = 2.0, w_IE = 2.0, w_II = 0.0, I_ext = 1.0, theta_E = 1.0, theta_I = 1.0, gain = 10.0, dt = 0.1 ms, T_total = 1000 ms, initial condition E[0..d] = 0.3, I[0..d] = 0.1.

Sweep: run the model once per value of tau_I ∈ {5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 65, 70} ms, all other parameters fixed as above.

Measurement: discard the first 400 ms as transient. On the remaining E(t) trace, count rising zero-crossings of E(t) - mean(E(t)) and compute the mean inter-crossing interval as the period; frequency = 1000/period (Hz). If fewer than 3 crossings are found in the retained window, report "no sustained oscillation" for that tau_I rather than a spurious frequency.

Deliverable: 1. The script (under ~100 lines). 2. A table or plot of frequency (Hz) vs. tau_I (ms) for all 7 sweep values. 3. 3–5 sentences: (a) does frequency increase or decrease with tau_I, matching or contradicting Piece 1's prediction that longer tau_I → lower frequency? (b) what happens at the high end of the sweep, and why is that a real result and not a bug? (c) explicitly note that the exact Hz values will NOT match Piece 1's T ≈ tau_I + 2d formula number-for-number — explain in one sentence why not (different model: saturating/nonlinear feedback vs. the linear round-trip approximation), while the direction of the trend should still agree.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Correct delay-buffer implementation (verified by delay ≠ 0 having an effect); frequency strictly decreases as tau_I increases across the range where oscillation exists; correctly reports "no sustained oscillation" at tau_I = 70ms (or wherever it empirically stops in their run) rather than reporting a fabricated near-zero frequency; the three explanatory sentences are all present and (b) correctly frames the disappearance as a stability transition (fixed point becomes stable / Hopf-type boundary), not a numerical artifact. Adequate Correct qualitative trend and correct script, but the write-up conflates "no oscillation" with "very low frequency," or the explanation in (c) is missing or superficial ("numbers are different because it's a different model" with no reason why). Not yet Frequency trend is flat, increasing, or noisy/non-monotonic (implementation bug — likely delay not applied, or measurement window too short); no acknowledgment that oscillation can disappear; script silently reports frequency = 0 or NaN without comment.

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: guided reading · Time: 45–60 min

Learning goals - Ground Piece 1's period formula in D&A's own coupled excitatory-inhibitory rate equations. - Locate, in a primary source, the actual condition D&A gives for an E-I network to transition from a stable fixed point to sustained oscillation. - Identify explicitly what D&A does and does not cover about phase/timing, so you knows the boundary of the source material before Piece 4.

Task

Read D&A, Chapter 7, the section(s) on excitatory-inhibitory network dynamics (the part that sets up coupled rate equations for an E and an I population and analyzes their stability). Answer:

  1. Write down D&A's coupled rate equations for the E and I populations (their notation, not Piece 1's). Map each of D&A's coupling terms onto Piece 1's w_EE, w_EI, w_IE, w_II.
  2. Find the condition D&A states for the coupled system to move from a stable fixed point to a sustained oscillation. Write it in your own words. Does it talk about eigenvalues, a trace/determinant condition, or something else?
  3. In Piece 1 Part A, w_II = 0 yet the loop still oscillated because of the E↔I cross-coupling. Does D&A's stability condition depend on self-inhibition (w_II), or purely on the cross terms (w_EI, w_IE) and the time constants? State which, citing the relevant equation/expression.
  4. D&A's basic E-I model has no explicit axonal conduction delay term (unlike Piece 1's d). Note one place where D&A comes close to discussing timing/delay between populations, or explicitly note "no such discussion found in this section" if that's the case — do not invent one.
  5. Find one place where D&A connects the E-I network's dynamics to a concrete phenomenon (e.g., response to a step or ramp input, contrast-invariant tuning, or similar). State it in one sentence.

Deliverable: half a page, five numbered short answers, each citing the specific equation number or a clear paraphrase location (e.g. "the paragraph introducing the linearized Jacobian of the coupled rate equations") since page numbers vary by printing.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Equations transcribed correctly with correct term-by-term mapping to Piece 1's notation; stability condition stated correctly in terms of the linearized system's eigenvalues/trace-determinant (or D&A's equivalent framing) and correctly identifies that cross-coupling, not self-inhibition, is what produces the complex (oscillatory) eigenvalues; answer to (4) is honest about what is/isn't there rather than invented; (5) gives one accurate concrete example. Adequate Equations correct but mapping to Piece 1 terms is loose or partially wrong; stability condition described qualitatively correct but without the eigenvalue/trace-determinant machinery; (4) and (5) present but vague. Not yet Equations missing or wrong; stability condition is guessed rather than found in the text; (4) invents a delay discussion that isn't in the cited material; (5) is generic ("oscillations are important in the brain") rather than the specific example D&A gives.

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: written defence · Time: 45–60 min · 300–600 words

Learning goals - State a concrete example of phase-carried information that rate alone cannot recover. - Marshal one piece of evidence each for "oscillations are functionally causal" and "oscillations are an epiphenomenon of recurrent E-I dynamics." - Take an explicit, falsifiable position on whether Step 3's purely-local, no-global-clock constraint can substitute for an oscillatory phase reference — and say what evidence would change you's mind.

Task

Write 300–600 words that do all of the following:

  1. Give one concrete, specific example of information that is carried in the phase of firing relative to a population rhythm and that could not be recovered from firing rate alone (rate = spike count in a window, with phase information discarded). Use a real quantity (e.g. a phase value in degrees or ms relative to cycle, mapped to something it encodes) — not just "phase carries information."
  2. State the single strongest piece of evidence you can identify (from D&A ch.7, your Piece 1 derivation, your Piece 2 simulation, or the available papers list — C1–C6, B2, B5) that oscillations are causally functional (the rhythm itself is used downstream, not just a byproduct).
  3. State the single strongest piece of evidence, from the same source pool, that oscillations can be epiphenomenal (a byproduct of E-I feedback dynamics with no computational role attributed to the rhythm itself). Your own Piece 2 simulation — a toy E-I loop that oscillates purely as a consequence of feedback and delay, without any "use" being defined for the rhythm — is a legitimate example here if you argue it correctly.
  4. Take a position on the project tie-in: does Step 3's hard constraint (all learning purely local — pre-synaptic activity, post-synaptic activity, local error signal; no global loss; no global clock) rule out relying on an emergent oscillatory phase reference for coordinating graph nodes, make it necessary, or leave it irrelevant? Argue for one of these three, using your Piece 1/2 results as evidence (e.g., is a shared phase reference something that could emerge locally from many small E-I loops without a global clock, or does synchrony of that kind require exactly the kind of global timing signal the constraint forbids?).
  5. State one specific observation or result that would change your mind on point 4 — not "more evidence" in general, but a stated, checkable thing (e.g. "if two unconnected local E-I loops in a graph topology spontaneously phase-lock without any shared input or connection between them, that would suggest synchrony is achievable without a global clock").

Deliverable: 300–600 words, five clearly labeled parts matching 1–5 above (a numbered list or headers is fine — flowing prose is not required to hit all five points explicitly).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong (1) is a specific, correctly-reasoned example where rate provably loses information that phase retains; (2) and (3) each cite one specific, correctly-described piece of evidence (not a vague appeal); (4) takes one clear position with an argument that actually uses Piece 1/2 results; (5) is concrete and falsifiable, not "more data." Adequate All five points addressed but (2)/(3) are generic ("oscillations seem important" / "the sim just did it automatically") rather than a specific named source or result; (4) states a position but doesn't connect to the derivation/sim; (5) is vague ("if I saw more evidence"). Not yet Missing one or more of the five points; (1) restates "phase carries information" without a concrete example; (4) refuses to take a position ("it depends" with no argument); (5) is unfalsifiable or absent.
