docs.title: A4 · Short-term plasticity, refractory period, reset modes
docs.text:
At a glance

Length — one sitting · about ~3.5 hours (one sitting) Before this — A1; STDP, LIF dynamics, eligibility traces and three-factor rules Reading — D&A ch. 5 Synaptic Conductances (release probability, short-term depression and facilitation) and Integrate-and-Fire Models (refractoriness, reset) — both knobs in one chapter. Supporting: Tsodyks & Markram 1997 (PNAS) for the canonical STP model. Trace-stacking is an implementation choice, not in either.

  • A4 · Short-term plasticity, refractory period, reset modes
    • Lesson spec
    • Coursework
    • Completion bar

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: Split short-term plasticity off from the single "synaptic change over time" bucket: STP is a separate, self-reversing mechanism that scales transmission without touching the stored weight. Then pin down two implementation knobs — reset mode and trace-stacking rule — that decide what a neuron carries forward tick to tick.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • Short-term facilitation (residual calcium) and depression (vesicle depletion): what variable changes — a resource/utilization term, not w — its ~100s-of-ms decay, and why it undoes itself with no input
  • STP vs STDP: the variable each modifies, timescale, permanence
  • Absolute vs relative refractory period and the firing-rate ceiling each imposes
  • Reset-to-zero vs subtract-threshold: the fate of overshoot voltage and its effect on next-spike timing
  • Eligibility-trace stacking on repeated spikes: additive vs saturating accumulation
  • Not covered: neuromodulator dynamics (B1), long-term plasticity rules (already known)

You should be able to answer: 1. A neuron has an absolute refractory period of 2 ms. What is its maximum possible firing rate in Hz? 2. In a Tsodyks-Markram-style facilitation model with baseline U = 0.2, each spike updating U ← U + 0.2(1 − U), and three spikes 10 ms apart (decay negligible) — what is U just after the third spike? 3. A neuron's membrane hits 1.2× threshold at spike time. Under reset-to-zero, what happens to the 0.2× overshoot? Under subtract-threshold, what happens to it, and how does that change next-spike timing? 4. Three spikes land within an eligibility trace's decay window. Under additive stacking, what happens to the peak trace value? Under saturating stacking, what caps it? Why does this matter for the size of a weight update triggered by a delayed reward signal? 5. Does short-term depression modify the weight w or a separate resource variable? If the synapse then receives no input for 500 ms, what happens to that variable?

Project tie-in: The virtual-memristor synapse currently models one persistent weight; STP needs an additional transient resource variable decaying independently of w — a Step 3 design question, and distinct from the persisted weights in online_rollout.py.

Done when: You computes a firing-rate ceiling from a refractory period and explains, without conflating them, how STP, reset mode and trace stacking each separately affect what a neuron carries forward.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine:

audio overview → guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written defence (Piece 4)

Pieces are numbered by type, not by sequence. The reading front-loads the concepts, the derivation makes them exact, the simulation is where they stick and get refined, and the defence is where you find out whether they did.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1 — Refractory ceiling and facilitation arithmetic derivation Q1 (refractory ceiling), Q2 (facilitation arithmetic), Q3 (reset-mode overshoot, symbolic) 2 — LIF under eight knob combinations simulation Q3 (reset-mode overshoot, empirical), Q4 (trace stacking) 3 — D&A ch. 5 guided reading guided reading Q5 (STD: resource variable vs w, recovery with no input), reinforces Q1–Q3 4 — Written defence: does the memristor synapse need a second variable written defence Project tie-in (STP as a second transient variable alongside persistent w) Piece 1 — Refractory ceiling and facilitation arithmeticPiece 2 — LIF under eight knob combinationsPiece 3 — D&A ch. 5 guided readingPiece 4 — Written defence: does the memristor synapse need a second variable?

Type: derivation · Time: 40 min

Learning goals - Derive a firing-rate ceiling directly from an absolute refractory period. - Hand-compute a recursive facilitation update (Tsodyks–Markram-style utilization variable) across several spikes. - State symbolically what happens to threshold-crossing overshoot under two reset conventions, and how it shifts next-spike timing.

Task

Work all three parts by hand (or in a text file), showing every intermediate number — no skipped steps.

  1. Refractory ceiling. A neuron has an absolute refractory period of 2 ms: for 2 ms after every spike it cannot fire again no matter how much input arrives. What is the maximum possible firing rate, in Hz? Then, in 2–3 sentences: a relative refractory period (elevated threshold that decays back to baseline, rather than a hard block) doesn't give a single ceiling number — explain what it gives instead and why you can't answer "what's the max rate" with one number the way you could in the absolute case.

  2. Facilitation arithmetic. A synapse's utilization variable starts at baseline U₀ = 0.2. Each presynaptic spike updates it as u ← u + 0.2·(1 − u) Three spikes arrive 10 ms apart. Treat decay back toward baseline between spikes as negligible (you'll test that assumption's cost in Piece 2). Compute u immediately after spike 1, after spike 2, and after spike 3. Show the arithmetic for each step — don't just state the final number. Then compute the ratio u_after_3 / U₀ — this is roughly how much more transmitter this synapse releases per spike after 3 spikes than it did on the very first one.

  3. Reset and overshoot (symbolic). A neuron's membrane reaches 1.2× threshold at the instant of a spike (threshold normalized to 1.0, so overshoot = 0.2). Under reset-to-zero, what happens to that 0.2 of overshoot? Under subtract-threshold (V ← V − V_th), what happens to it instead? If, after the reset, the membrane were then driven toward threshold at some constant rate R (units: threshold-fraction per ms), write the expression for how much sooner (in ms) the next spike occurs under subtract-threshold compared to reset-to-zero, in terms of the retained overshoot and R.

Deliverable

A single page (markdown, plain text, or a photo of handwritten work) with three clearly labeled sections (1, 2, 3), each showing the arithmetic, not just the final answer.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All three parts correct with arithmetic shown; part 1's relative-refractory explanation correctly identifies that it's a time-varying threshold, not a fixed ceiling; part 3 gives the correct symbolic expression for the timing shift (overshoot / R) with correct reasoning about which direction it goes. Adequate Parts 1 and 2 numerically correct; part 3 correctly identifies that subtract-threshold retains overshoot and reset-to-zero discards it, even if the symbolic timing expression is missing or off. Not yet Part 1 or Part 2's arithmetic is wrong, or part 3 has reset-to-zero and subtract-threshold's effects reversed or conflated.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation · Time: 75 min

Learning goals - Implement short-term plasticity as a transient resource variable that modulates transmission without touching a stored weight. - Observe, empirically, how reset mode changes next-spike timing when overshoot is non-negligible. - Observe how additive vs. saturating trace-stacking diverge under repeated spikes, and connect that to the size of a delayed three-factor weight update.

Task

Build a single-file simulation (PyTorch or numpy, no dataset downloads, under ~100 lines) of one LIF neuron driven by one synapse carrying a fixed presynaptic spike train. Use exactly these parameters (deviating changes what you're testing):

dt        = 1.0 ms       T = 200 ms        (200 steps)
tau_m     = 20 ms        V_th = 1.0        V starts at 0
tau_syn   = 5 ms         PSC amplitude scale A = 6.0
w         = 4.0          (fixed synaptic weight, the "memristor" value)
t_ref     = 2 ms absolute refractory (matches Piece 1 Q1's 500 Hz ceiling)

presynaptic spike train: t = 10, 20, 30, ..., 190 ms  (19 spikes, regular)

STP (Tsodyks-Markram style), used only when STP is "on":
  U = 0.2, tau_facil = 200 ms, tau_rec = 300 ms
  baseline before first spike: u = U = 0.2, x = 1.0
  at each presynaptic spike i, after decaying u toward U (tau_facil) and
  x toward 1.0 (tau_rec) over the elapsed inter-spike interval:
      u_new = u_pre + U*(1 - u_pre)          # facilitation jump
      efficacy_i = u_new * x_pre             # what actually reaches the neuron
      x_new = x_pre - u_new * x_pre          # depletion
  When STP is "off": efficacy_i = 1.0 for every spike (no dynamics at all).

Each presynaptic spike injects a current pulse of size A * w * efficacy_i
into an exponentially-decaying PSC (tau_syn), which drives the LIF membrane:
    V += dt * (-V + PSC) / tau_m
During the 2 ms refractory window after a spike, V does not integrate
(holds at its post-reset value); integration resumes the following step.

Part A — reset × STP (4 conditions). For each of {reset-to-zero, subtract-threshold} × {STP off, STP on}, run the simulation and record: total output spike count, and the first three output spike times.

Part B — trace stacking (applied to Part A's 4 spike trains, 8 rows total). For each of the 4 output spike trains from Part A, compute the peak value of an eligibility trace e(t) over the 200 ms window under two stacking rules, sampled every dt = 1 ms with decay time constant tau_e = 50 ms: - Additive: each output spike does e += 1.0 (after that step's decay is applied). - Saturating: each output spike does e = e + (1.0 − e) * 0.5 (a saturating jump toward ceiling 1.0 — the same "move a fraction of the remaining distance to a target" form as Piece 1 Q2's facilitation update).

Report peak e for both rules, for all 4 spike trains (8 numbers).

Deliverable

The script, plus a results table: 4 rows (reset mode × STP) × columns {spike count, first 3 spike times, peak_e_additive, peak_e_saturating}. Plus 3–4 sentences: (a) what STP on vs off does to spike count and why, (b) whether reset mode changed spike timing, spike count, or both, in your run, (c) whether additive stacking's peak ever looks unbounded-ish across a busier condition vs. a sparser one, and what that implies for a three-factor update that fires on whichever step the trace happens to be sampled.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All 8 numbers present and consistent with the run; STP on shows markedly fewer output spikes than STP off (mechanism correctly implemented, not just parameter-matched); explanation correctly separates "reset mode changed timing" from "STP changed count" without conflating the two knobs; notes that additive peak scales with spike count while saturating peak is bounded near 1.0 regardless of count. Adequate Simulation runs and produces a plausible 4-condition table (STP on has fewer spikes than STP off); trace-stacking part computed for at least 2 of the 4 conditions; explanation present but conflates reset-mode and STP effects somewhat. Not yet STP on/off produce near-identical spike counts (STP not actually implemented as a depleting/recovering resource), or trace stacking not attempted, or no results table.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: guided reading · Time: 45 min

Learning goals - Ground the STP resource-variable formalism used in Pieces 1–2 in D&A's own treatment of release probability and short-term depression/facilitation. - Locate D&A's account of refractoriness and reset convention in the integrate-and-fire section, and identify which convention D&A treats as the default.

Task

Read D&A ch. 5, the Synaptic Conductances section (release probability, short-term depression and facilitation) and the Integrate-and-Fire Models section (refractoriness, reset). Answer in writing:

  1. D&A models short-term plasticity with variables for available/depleted resources and utilization (however they're notated in your edition). Write the correspondence explicitly: which of D&A's variables plays the role of this coursework's x (depletable resource), and which plays the role of u (utilization/facilitation)?
  2. According to D&A, what determines whether a given synapse's spike train looks net-facilitating or net-depressing overall — what's the role of the baseline release probability in that outcome?
  3. Does short-term depression, in D&A's account, modify the synaptic weight itself, or a separate resource variable? If that synapse then receives no presynaptic input for 500 ms, what happens to the resource variable — name the relevant recovery time constant and describe the direction it moves (toward what value)?
  4. What refractory mechanisms does D&A describe for integrate-and-fire neurons, and how does D&A implement reset after a spike? Which reset convention does D&A treat as the default case, and does it discard or retain overshoot above threshold?
  5. In 2–3 sentences: why is "what happens to overshoot at reset" a free modeling choice for an integrate-and-fire neuron, in a way it wouldn't be for a conductance-based model (e.g. Hodgkin–Huxley) where the spike shape and downswing are generated by the membrane dynamics themselves rather than imposed by a reset rule?

Deliverable

Five short written answers (2–5 sentences each), with a page/section reference into D&A for each.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All 5 answered with correct D&A page/section references; Q3 correctly states depression modifies a resource variable (not w) and correctly names the recovery time constant and its direction (recovers toward full/baseline availability); Q5 correctly identifies the reset rule as an approximation imposed on top of a simplified (non-conductance-based) spike mechanism. Adequate 4 of 5 answered correctly with references; Q3's core distinction (resource variable, not w) is present even if the time constant is mis-cited. Not yet Q3 says depression changes w, or fewer than 3 of 5 questions answered with a text reference.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: written defence · Time: 45 min

Learning goals - Apply the STP-vs-w distinction from Pieces 1–3 to a concrete architectural decision in your own project. - Argue a position with reference to specific downstream consequences (step 02b's persisted per-synapse weights, step 04's stress/pruning), not in the abstract.

Task

Write 300–600 words answering: Should the project's virtual-memristor synapse — which currently models one persistent weight w per synapse, updated only by local learning rules — be extended with a second, transient resource variable (an x/u-style pair, decaying independently of w over ~100s-of-ms) to implement short-term plasticity? Or should STP be left out of the design, keeping the synapse single-weight?

Address, specifically: - What would the second variable have to persist across (a single tick, an episode, forever) versus what w persists across in the current design — and whether the existing per-synapse persistence machinery (built for step 02b's online learning) generalizes to a variable with a much shorter, self-resetting timescale. - What happens if STP is not modeled and its effect is left to be absorbed into w by the existing local learning rule instead — is that a loss of a real distinct mechanism, or a harmless simplification, and what specific behavior (if any) would the network fail to reproduce as a result? - Step 04's stress/pruning mechanism prunes connections with "near-zero weights for sustained periods." If a synapse's transmission is being suppressed by short-term depression (a transient x near 0) while its stored weight w is fine, does pruning need to be able to tell those two apart? What breaks if it can't?

Deliverable

A single markdown or text file, 300–600 words, taking and defending one position (not a both-sides summary).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Takes an explicit position; correctly distinguishes what persists across a tick/episode/lifetime for w vs. a hypothetical STP variable; engages concretely with the step 04 pruning conflict (transient depression vs. genuinely near-zero w) and states what breaks if the two aren't distinguished; within 300–600 words. Adequate Takes a position and addresses at least 2 of the 3 bullet points concretely (not just restating them); some hand-waving on the pruning interaction is acceptable. Not yet No clear position taken, or the answer never engages with step 04's pruning rule at all, or it's a generic "STP is biologically realistic so it should be included" essay with no reference to this project's specific mechanisms.

docs.title: A5 · State of the field: why SNNs, where they stand vs ANNs
docs.text:
At a glance

Length — one to two sittings · about ~4-5 hours (two sittings) Before this — A1–A4. Closing lesson of track A; passing it opens track C. Reading — Not in D&A — the book predates the neuromorphic hardware era. Attwell & Laughlin 2001 for the cortical energy budget; Roy, Jaiswal & Panda 2019 (Nature) on spike-based machine intelligence; current vendor documentation at teaching time — see the perishability note in Scope.

  • A5 · State of the field: why SNNs, where they stand vs ANNs
    • Lesson spec
    • Track B — biology for design
    • Coursework
    • Completion bar

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: State the brain's energy budget with real numbers and use it to make — or refute — the energy argument for SNNs; classify the major neuromorphic chips by what they actually support; give an honest account of the accuracy and tooling gap. Turns "SNNs are efficient" from a slogan into a claim defensible with figures in front of an examiner.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • Brain energy budget: ~20 W, ~86B neurons, ~10¹⁴–10¹⁵ synapses, sparse mean firing rates (~1–5 Hz), and what that implies per synaptic event versus a GPU's per-MAC energy
  • Event-driven vs clocked computation: why "no spike, no computation" changes the equation, and the dense/high-rate regime where it stops applying
  • Real hardware as illustration: Loihi 2, SpiNNaker 2, IBM TrueNorth/NorthPole, memristor crossbars — and the recurring axes they differ on (digital vs analog, on-chip learning or inference-only, topology freedom, weight precision)
  • The honest gap: accuracy on MNIST / CIFAR-10 / ImageNet-scale, tooling maturity (PyTorch vs snnTorch/Norse/vendor SDKs), and the ANN-to-SNN conversion criticism
  • Where SNNs genuinely win: event cameras, always-on sensing, low-latency control — with numbers
  • Not covered: PC-specific efficiency and locality claims (track C), biological energy detail beyond the headline budget
  • Perishable: specific chip capabilities and benchmark numbers date fast. Check them when the lesson is taught. What should survive is the shape of the argument, not the table.

You should be able to answer: 1. From ~20 W across ~10¹⁵ synapses firing at a few Hz, derive the rough energy per synaptic event — and say what has to be true of a workload before that figure is the right thing to compare against a GPU's per-MAC energy. 2. What are the recurring axes on which neuromorphic chips differ, and which of them actually constrain this project's design? Use two current chips as illustrations rather than as the answer. 3. What is the ANN-to-SNN conversion criticism, and what does a conversion-based accuracy number hide about the cost of getting it? 4. How would you establish the current accuracy gap between natively trained SNNs and ANNs — and what would a large gap tell you about where the difficulty sits: the neuron model, the learning rule, or the tooling? 5. What property must a task have for event-driven hardware to win on latency or power? Name one task that has it and one that plainly does not.

Project tie-in: Grounds why the project insists on purely local learning and virtual-memristor synapses — that choice targets the hardware surveyed here, not accuracy parity with backprop-trained ANNs on the Step 1–2 benchmarks.

Done when: You can derive the per-event energy figure rather than recall it, argue the efficiency case to a skeptic without leaning on a memorized table, and explain why the Step 1–2 benchmark numbers are not an apples-to-apples accuracy contest.

docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine:

audio overview → guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written defence (Piece 4)

Pieces are numbered by type, not by sequence. The reading front-loads the concepts, the derivation makes them exact, the simulation is where they stick and get refined, and the defence is where you find out whether they did.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1 — Energy budget derivation derivation AC1 (derive per-event energy; state the workload conditions for a fair GPU comparison) 2 — Sparsity/energy simulator simulation AC1 (applies the cost model), AC5 (shows numerically what sparsity a task needs for spiking to win) 3 — Neuromorphic hardware source hunt guided reading AC2 (recurring axes, two chips as illustration), AC3 (conversion criticism), AC4 (accuracy-gap methodology) 4 — Written defence written defence AC1, AC3, AC4, AC5 (synthesises all four into one argument for a skeptic) Piece 1 — The brain's energy-per-synaptic-event budgetPiece 2 — Sparsity/event-count simulator with an energy cost modelPiece 3 — Neuromorphic hardware: find your own source, then interrogate itPiece 4 — Written defence: make (or refuse) the efficiency case

Type: derivation · Time: 45-60 min

Learning goals - Turn population-level numbers (total power, synapse count, mean firing rate) into a per-event energy figure using nothing but unit arithmetic. - Identify which of those inputs is doing the real work in the estimate and which is a loose bound. - State, precisely, the conditions under which "energy per synaptic event" is the right unit to put next to a GPU's "energy per MAC" — and when it silently compares two different things.

Task

Using these inputs — brain power draw ≈ 20 W, synapse count ≈ 10^14–10^15, mean firing rate ≈ 1–5 Hz — do the following on paper (typed or scanned, show every step):

  1. Estimate total synaptic events per second across the whole brain. State the assumption you're making about how "firing rate" (a per-neuron quantity) turns into "events per second at a synapse" (hint: what do you need to know about fan-out per neuron, and does it cancel out if you work in total synapses rather than per-neuron?).
  2. Divide power by events/second to get energy per synaptic event, in joules. Convert to femtojoules (fJ) or picojoules (pJ), whichever is the more natural unit for the result.
  3. Redo steps 1-2 at both ends of the synapse-count range (10^14 and 10^15) and both ends of the firing-rate range (1 Hz and 5 Hz). Report the resulting range, not a single number.
  4. Find (do not just assert) a modern digital MAC's energy cost. Distinguish compute-only cost (the multiply-add itself, on-chip) from memory-inclusive cost (fetching the operands from SRAM vs. DRAM/HBM). Cite where each number came from — a datasheet, a paper, a vendor claim — and note which one is closest in spirit to "one synaptic event."
  5. State explicitly: what has to be true of an artificial workload before your per-event brain figure is a fair number to set against a GPU's per-MAC figure? Cover at least: (a) whether the ANN workload is itself sparse/event-driven or dense, (b) whether the hardware running it actually skips work for inactive units or evaluates everything every cycle regardless, (c) whether you're comparing compute-only or memory-inclusive energy on the artificial side.

Deliverable

A worked derivation (1-2 pages, real arithmetic shown, not just final numbers) ending in: a stated energy-per-synaptic-event range, a stated GPU per-MAC range with its source, the ratio between them, and a paragraph answering point 5.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Correct order-of-magnitude range from real arithmetic (steps shown); correctly identifies that fan-out cancels when working in total synapse count rather than per-neuron; cites a real, checkable source for the GPU MAC figure and correctly separates compute-only from memory-inclusive; the "what has to be true" paragraph names sparsity of the workload and skip-on-inactivity of the hardware as separate, both-required conditions. Adequate Correct order of magnitude reached, arithmetic shown, but one of: the fan-out/cancellation reasoning is hand-waved, the GPU figure is asserted without a checkable source, or the "what has to be true" answer names only one of the two required conditions. ns Not yet Final number given without shown arithmetic; range collapsed to a single point without acknowledging the two input ranges; GPU comparison number invented with no source; no engagement with when the comparison is unfair.

Type: simulation · Time: 60-90 min

Learning goals - Build a minimal, self-contained comparison between "dense synchronous evaluation" and "sparse event-driven evaluation" of the same computation. - Apply an explicit, stated energy cost model (not a black box) to both regimes and read off where the crossover is. - Connect the result numerically to acceptance criterion 5: what property a workload needs before event-driven wins.

Task

Write a single Python file (PyTorch or plain numpy, no dataset downloads — synthetic data only), under ~100 lines, that:

  1. Defines a small feedforward network (e.g. 784→128→10 sized, weights random-initialized — this is about counting operations, not training).
  2. Generates a batch of synthetic input patterns without downloading anything — e.g. torch.rand thresholded into a sparse binary image, or a hand-built pattern (a few "on" pixels), so you control the input sparsity directly.
  3. Runs the network in two modes on the same inputs:
  4. Dense mode: one ordinary forward pass; count total MACs (sum of in_features × out_features per layer, independent of input values).
  5. Event mode: encode each input unit as a Poisson spike train over T timesteps at a rate proportional to its activation (cap the max rate, e.g. 50-100 Hz equivalent); at each timestep, only units that spike contribute — count total synaptic events actually delivered (spikes × fan-out reached), not just spikes.
  6. Applies a stated cost model: energy_dense = MACs × E_mac, energy_event = synaptic_events × E_event, using constants you justify with a one-line comment citing where they came from (can reuse the ranges from Piece 1, or state your own — just be explicit).
  7. Sweeps one variable — input sparsity (fraction of "on" pixels) or T (timesteps) — over a small range and prints/plots total energy for both modes side by side, so the crossover point (if any, within the swept range) is visible in the output.

Deliverable

The script, plus a 5-10 line written note: at what sparsity level (or T) does event mode stop being cheaper than dense mode, given your chosen constants, and does that threshold move if you change E_event/E_mac by 10x?

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Script runs standalone with no downloads, under ~100 lines; dense MAC count is input-independent (correctly reflects that dense hardware pays regardless of value); event count correctly scales with both spike count and fan-out (not just spike count); cost-model constants are stated and justified, not silently hardcoded; sweep clearly shows a crossover or explains why none exists in range; written note correctly reasons about the sensitivity to the E_event:E_mac ratio. Adequate Script works and produces a sensible energy comparison, but one of: event count conflates "spikes" with "synaptic events" (misses the fan-out multiplication), cost constants are unexplained magic numbers, or the sweep doesn't clearly locate/discuss a crossover. Not yet Script requires a downloaded dataset or external data file; dense/event energy computed without a stated cost model (e.g. just spike count reported as "energy"); no sweep, single-point comparison only; script exceeds scope significantly (full training loop, etc. — this is a counting exercise, not a training exercise).

Type: guided reading · Time: 75-90 min

Learning goals - Locate a credible, openly-available current source (survey or vendor technical document) on neuromorphic hardware without institutional-access papers. - Extract the recurring axes hardware differs on from primary/vendor material rather than from a memorized list. - Identify what a vendor or survey claim does not tell you — sparsity assumptions behind an energy number, benchmark methodology, what's on-chip vs. off-chip.

Task

This lesson has no assigned reading — Dayan & Abbott predates this hardware entirely, and the two natural papers (Attwell & Laughlin 2001; Roy, Jaiswal & Panda 2019) need institutional access you don't have. Find your own source.

  1. Find one current, openly-available source that is either (a) a survey/review paper on neuromorphic computing (arXiv is fine — search terms like "neuromorphic computing survey," "spiking neural network hardware review"), or (b) a vendor technical brief/whitepaper for a specific chip (Intel Loihi 2, SpiNNaker2, IBM NorthPole, a memristor-crossbar research group's paper). Note the publication/last-update date — prefer 2022 or later given how fast this field moves.
  2. Read enough of it to answer the questions below. You do not need to read it cover to cover.
  3. Answer, using your source and citing where in it (section/page/figure) each answer comes from: a. What are the recurring axes this source uses (explicitly or implicitly) to differentiate neuromorphic hardware — at minimum, check for: digital vs. analog, on-chip learning vs. inference-only, fixed topology vs. flexible/reconfigurable, and weight/activation precision. b. Pick two chips or architectures your source discusses (or that you look up briefly alongside it) and fill in those same axes for each, side by side. c. Of the axes you found, which ones actually constrain this project's design (purely local learning rules, virtual-memristor synapses, graph topology rather than fixed layers)? Which are irrelevant to this project even though they matter for other use cases? d. Find where your source states or implies an energy-per-operation number. What sparsity or activity-rate assumption is that number conditioned on — is it stated, or do you have to infer it's a best case? If your source reports a benchmark accuracy or throughput number, what methodology detail (dataset, task, whether it's simulated vs. measured on real silicon, whether comparison hardware is contemporaneous) would you need to check before trusting it?
  4. State your source's title, authors/vendor, and URL or DOI at the top of your answer.

Deliverable

A written answer (½-1 page) to 3a-3d, with the source cited at the top, and inline pointers (section/page/figure) for each claim you pull from it.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Source is genuinely openly accessible (grader can reach it with the given link, no paywall) and reasonably current; all four axes correctly identified and correctly attributed to specific chips with source pointers; correctly separates "matters for this project" from "matters in general" with a concrete reason tied to the project's local-learning/memristor/graph-topology constraints; explicitly identifies what the energy or benchmark number is silent about (sparsity assumption, dataset, simulated-vs-measured) rather than repeating it uncritically. Adequate Source is accessible and used, axes mostly identified correctly, but the project-relevance filter (3c) is superficial (e.g. "all of these matter") or the critique of the energy/benchmark number (3d) restates the number without probing its conditions. Not yet Source is paywalled/inaccessible to the grader, is not actually about neuromorphic hardware, or answers are given without any source pointers (i.e., recalled from general knowledge rather than extracted from the found source) — this defeats the point of the exercise, which is the search-and-extract skill, not the facts.

Type: written defence · Time: 45-60 min

Learning goals - Synthesize the derivation, simulation, and reading into a single argument addressed to a specific skeptical audience. - State the honest accuracy/tooling gap without it undermining the parts of the efficiency argument that do hold. - Distinguish "SNNs are efficient" (unsupported slogan) from the narrower, defensible claim this lesson supports.

Task

Write 300-600 words addressed to a skeptical examiner who opens with: "Every efficiency number for spiking hardware I've seen assumes the workload is sparse and the comparison hardware is a GPU running dense FP32 at low utilization. Isn't this just a favorable-conditions argument dressed up as a hardware argument? And even if the energy case holds, your accuracy is worse and your tooling is years behind PyTorch — why should anyone care?"

Your answer must: 1. State the energy claim you can actually defend (using your Piece 1 figures) and the conditions it depends on — not the unconditional "spikes are efficient" slogan. 2. Concede the accuracy and tooling gap honestly (from Piece 3), including what the ANN-to-SNN conversion criticism is and why a conversion-based accuracy number is a weaker claim than it looks. 3. Give at least one concrete example (with a number or a stated order of magnitude, from your simulation or reading) of a task where event-driven hardware plausibly wins on latency or power, and one where it plainly does not — using acceptance criterion 5's property (what the task needs to have) explicitly. 4. Explain, briefly, why this project chooses purely local learning and virtual-memristor synapses anyway — targeting hardware compatibility, not accuracy parity with backprop-trained ANNs on the Step 1-2 benchmarks (MNIST/FashionMNIST/CIFAR-10).

Deliverable

300-600 words of prose (not bullet points — this is a defence, it should read as an argument), addressed directly to the examiner's challenge.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong States a conditional, defensible energy claim (references real figures from Piece 1) rather than a slogan; explicitly names the conditions (workload sparsity, hardware's ability to exploit it) as the examiner demanded; honestly states the accuracy/tooling gap and correctly explains why conversion-based accuracy hides training cost/native-training difficulty; gives a concrete win-case and lose-case tied to the sparsity/latency property, not generic examples; ties the project's design choices to hardware-targeting rather than claiming an accuracy or efficiency win the project hasn't earned. All within 300-600 words. Adequate Covers most of the four required elements but at least one is asserted rather than argued (e.g. states the gap exists without explaining the conversion criticism; gives a win-case example with no number or order of magnitude attached). Not yet Restates "SNNs are efficient" as an unconditional claim; ignores the accuracy/tooling gap or handwaves past it; no concrete win/lose task example; doesn't connect back to why this project specifically makes its design choices; well outside the word count in either direction.

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: Replace "a success/error chemical is misted over the whole network, each synapse scales by how brightly it is glowing" with what the modulators actually do: distinct signals (reward prediction error vs uncertainty vs gain), released with real spatial and temporal structure, read out with a sign that depends on local receptor type.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • Dopamine as reward-prediction-error: Schultz's recordings at cue, at reward, and at omission
  • ACh and noradrenaline per Yu & Dayan: expected vs unexpected uncertainty, plus gain control on cortical responsiveness
  • Volume transmission: real diffusion radius (tens to hundreds of microns) and timescale (hundreds of ms to seconds) vs synaptic transmission, and vs the instantaneous global broadcast a three-factor rule assumes
  • Where the abstraction holds (slow, spatially broad, gates plasticity) and where it breaks (multiple co-active modulators, receptor-dependent sign such as D1 vs D2, target-specific innervation density)
  • Not covered: astrocytic modulation (already written up), specific interneuron types (B2)

You should be able to answer: 1. In Schultz's paradigm, what does a dopamine neuron do at cue, at reward, and at omission of an expected reward — and why is the omission response the strongest evidence against "reward = fixed brightness signal"? 2. Give rough numbers: diffusion radius and timescale of volume transmission vs a synaptic release event. 3. A cue's meaning shifts unpredictably. Which modulator dominates, ACh or NE, and why? 4. Why can the same dopamine concentration increase plasticity at a D1-expressing synapse and decrease it at a D2-expressing one — and what does that break in the "one chemical, one direction" model? 5. State one concrete, specific way your "misted chemical" model is factually wrong about real biology.

Project tie-in: Any three-factor-style rule in Steps 3–4, and the stress variable itself, currently assumes a single scalar broadcast. This is the check on whether that is a defensible simplification or needs separate reward-like and uncertainty-like channels before it gates growth and pruning.

Done when: Question 5 is answered with a specific correct mechanism — not a restatement of the goal — without further prompting.

docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine:

audio overview → guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written defence (Piece 4)

Pieces are numbered by type, not by sequence. The reading front-loads the concepts, the derivation makes them exact, the simulation is where they stick and get refined, and the defence is where you find out whether they did.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1. TD prediction error by hand derivation AC1 (cue/reward/omission dynamics, why omission is the strongest counter-evidence) 2. Dopamine signatures from a TD agent simulation AC1 (same three signatures, seen emerging from a rule you wrote) 3. Guided reading — D&A ch. 9 guided reading AC1 (grounds the derivation/simulation in the primary account: Rescorla-Wagner → TD → dopamine correspondence) 4. Written defence — one or two channels? written defence AC2, AC3, AC4, AC5 + project tie-in decision

Note on sourcing: AC2 (diffusion/timescale numbers), AC3 (ACh vs NE under unpredictable uncertainty) and AC4 (D1/D2 opposite sign) are not covered by D&A ch. 9, which is a TD/dopamine chapter, not a neuromodulator-anatomy chapter. The paper that would normally carry AC3 (Yu & Dayan 2005, expected vs. unexpected uncertainty) is explicitly unavailable. Piece 4 therefore hands you the minimum factual scaffolding for AC2-AC4 directly in the task text and grades their reasoning from it, rather than pretending a citation exists. This is called out again in Piece 4.

Piece 1 — TD prediction error by handPiece 2 — Dopamine signatures from a TD agentPiece 3 — Guided reading: D&A ch. 9, Classical Conditioning and Reinforcement LearningPiece 4 — Written defence: does the stress variable need more than one channel?

Type: derivation · Time: 60 min

Learning goals - Compute TD(0) prediction errors and value updates by hand across trials, not just write the equation - See the value signal shift backward in time (reward → cue) as learning proceeds - Derive, from the update rule itself, why omitting an expected reward produces a negative error rather than merely "no signal" - Connect the arithmetic to Schultz's dopamine recordings via D&A ch. 9's account

Task

Two states per trial: cue state C, then reward state R, then trial ends (terminal value 0). TD(0) rule, with \(\gamma=1\), \(\alpha=0.5\):

\[\delta(C) = 0 + \gamma V(R) - V(C) \qquad \delta(R) = r_R + \gamma \cdot 0 - V(R)\] \[V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha\,\delta(s)\]

\(V(C) = V(R) = 0\) initially. Every trial, \(r_R = 1\) (reward always delivered) — until trial 6, where \(r_R = 0\) (reward omitted, but the cue still fires normally).

Compute, trial by trial for trials 1-6, in this order each trial: \(\delta(C)\), then \(\delta(R)\), then update both \(V(C)\) and \(V(R)\). Show your working for at least trials 1, 2, and 6 in full; a table is fine for 3-5.

  1. What happens to \(\delta(C)\) across trials 1-5? What happens to \(\delta(R)\)? State the pattern in one sentence and connect it to "the dopamine response migrates from reward to the earliest reliable predictor."
  2. Compute \(\delta(R)\) on trial 6 (omission) using the \(V(R)\) value carried in from trial 5. Compare its sign and magnitude to \(\delta(R)\) on trial 1.
  3. In one or two sentences: why is the omission result harder to explain under "reward = fixed-brightness success chemical" than the cue and reward results are? (A fixed-brightness model can still shrug off "no glow" at omission — what can't it explain?)

Deliverable A table with columns [Trial, V(C) before, V(R) before, δ(C), δ(R), V(C) after, V(R) after] for trials 1-6, plus written answers to sub-questions 1-3 (a paragraph total, not an essay).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All 6 rows arithmetically correct; correctly identifies δ(C) rising toward 1 and δ(R) falling toward 0 as the backward-shift signature; correctly computes δ(R) on trial 6 as strongly negative (not just "smaller than trial 1"); answer to Q3 names the specific gap (a magnitude-only signal has no mechanism to go below its resting/no-event level, so it cannot represent "worse than expected," only "how much"). Adequate Arithmetic correct for at least trials 1-3 and 6 (minor slips elsewhere tolerated); gets the backward-shift direction right but describes it vaguely; gets the omission sign right but the Q3 explanation just restates "it's negative" without saying what that breaks in the fixed-brightness model. Not yet Arithmetic errors in trial 1 or 2 (wrong sign or wrong update target); reports δ(R) on trial 6 as zero, small-positive, or "no response"; Q3 answer only repeats the lesson's framing back without a mechanism.

Type: simulation · Time: 105 min · This is the centrepiece of the lesson.

Learning goals - Implement TD(0) over a within-trial timeline (not just two lumped states) and watch the value function reshape itself with training - Reproduce, from a rule you wrote and trained themselves, the three canonical dopamine signatures: burst at reward (naive), burst at cue / no response at reward (trained), dip at the omission time (trained, reward withheld) - Build the intuition that "the response migrates backward in time" is not a story bolted onto TD — it falls out of the Bellman recursion for free

Task

Represent one trial as a fixed timeline of \(T=20\) discrete steps, cue (CS) always at \(t=0\), reward (US) always at \(t=T_{US}=10\). Keep a tabular value function \(V[0..T-1]\) (initialized to zero) plus one fixed, never-updated baseline value \(V_{\text{ITI}} = 0\) representing the inter-trial interval (it doesn't predict anything, so nothing should ever push it away from 0 — this is what makes the response appear to originate at the cue rather than drift backward forever).

Per trial: 1. Build \(r[t]\): zero everywhere except \(r[T_{US}] = 1\) (or \(0\) on an omission probe). 2. Compute the "response at cue" as the TD error for the transition into the trial: \(\delta_{\text{cue}} = 0 + \gamma V[0] - V_{\text{ITI}}\) (this does not update \(V_{\text{ITI}}\)). 3. Step through \(t = 0 \ldots T-1\) in order. At each \(t\): \(\delta_t = r[t] + \gamma V[t+1] - V[t]\) (using \(V[T]:=0\)), then update \(V[t] \leftarrow V[t] + \alpha\,\delta_t\) immediately (online, not batched). 4. Record \(\delta_{\text{cue}}\) and \(\delta_t\) at \(t=T_{US}\) for every trial you care to inspect.

Run \(\geq 300\) training trials with \(\gamma=0.98\), \(\alpha=0.1\). Then run one omission probe trial (do not train on it, or train on a separate copy of \(V\)) with \(r[T_{US}]=0\), and record \(\delta_{\text{cue}}\) and \(\delta_{T_{US}}\) on that probe.

Report, as printed numbers (a plot is a nice-to-have, not required): \((\delta_{\text{cue}}, \delta_{T_{US}})\) at trial 1, at roughly the halfway point, at the final trained trial, and on the omission probe.

Deliverable A runnable script (numpy or plain PyTorch tensors, no autograd needed, under ~100 lines) plus the four \((\delta_{\text{cue}}, \delta_{T_{US}})\) number-pairs, plus 3-4 sentences stating which pair corresponds to which of the three textbook signatures (naive burst-at-reward; trained burst-at-cue/silent-at-reward; trained-but-omitted dip-at-reward-time) and why \(V_{\text{ITI}}\) had to be held fixed for the cue response to show up at all.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Code runs and reproduces all three signatures within reasonable tolerance (trial 1: δ_cue ≈ 0, δ_reward ≈ 1; final trained: δ_cue clearly positive and δ_reward ≈ 0; omission probe: δ_reward clearly negative, δ_cue ≈ unchanged from final trained value); explanation correctly attributes the cue response's origin point to the transition from the fixed \(V_{\text{ITI}}=0\), not to \(V[0]\) updating itself; correctly notes the omission probe's cue response is unaffected because the agent can't know in advance a given trial will omit. Adequate Signatures qualitatively present (right signs, right rough trend) but code has a minor bug (e.g. \(V[T]\) not treated as 0, or \(V_{\text{ITI}}\) accidentally updated causing the cue response to fade); explanation gets 2 of 3 signatures right without the \(V_{\text{ITI}}\) mechanism. Not yet Missing signature (e.g. no dip at omission, or cue and reward responses never separate); \(V_{\text{ITI}}\) updated like any other state (this silently destroys the cue-response signature — the giveaway is that the "cue response" keeps growing across arbitrarily many trials instead of converging); no working code, or code that doesn't correspond to the description (batched update instead of online, wrong reward timestep, etc).

Type: guided reading · Time: 45 min

Learning goals - Read the Rescorla-Wagner rule and TD model as D&A actually present them, not as reconstructed from memory of three-factor rules - Identify the specific textual claim linking \(\delta(t)\) to Schultz's dopamine recordings - Distinguish "the chapter's model" from "you's prior mental model" at the two points where they diverge

Task Read D&A ch. 9, the sections covering the Rescorla-Wagner rule, the temporal difference (TD) model of classical conditioning, and the section relating the TD model to dopamine neuron recordings. Answer:

  1. State the Rescorla-Wagner rule and identify, in D&A's own terms, what the "error" term represents. What does the chapter say is unrealistic about applying this rule to a whole trial as a single lumped event (why did D&A need the TD model at all)?
  2. What specific change does the TD model make to how the prediction error is computed, compared to Rescorla-Wagner? (Point to the timing/bootstrapping mechanism specifically — not just "it's more realistic.")
  3. Find the passage(s) where D&A connect \(\delta(t)\) to Schultz's dopamine data. What does the chapter say the correspondence is (firing rate ↔ what, specifically), and what caveat or limitation, if any, does D&A attach to that correspondence?
  4. According to the chapter, what happens to the modelled response at the time of reward once the reward is fully predicted, and what happens if a predicted reward is omitted? Quote or closely paraphrase the specific claim (not your own derivation from Piece 1 — the point here is to check the book says the same thing your arithmetic produced).

Deliverable Four short answers (2-4 sentences each), each naming which subsection of ch. 9 it's drawn from (a page range or subsection heading is enough — this is a self-study log, not a citation exercise).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All four answers accurately reflect the chapter's content in your own words (not copied verbatim); Q2 correctly identifies the bootstrapped/successive-prediction mechanism as the specific fix, not a vague "TD is better"; Q4's answer matches (in direction and reasoning) what you independently derived in Piece 1, and you explicitly notices and states that match. Adequate Three of four answers correct; Q4 correct but you doesn't connect it back to Piece 1 even when prompted. Not yet Answers describe three-factor/eligibility-trace framing instead of what the chapter actually says (i.e., you is still describing their prior mental model rather than reading the new material); Q3 or Q4 answered from general knowledge without locating it in the chapter.

Type: written defence · Time: 60 min · 300-600 words

Learning goals - Articulate, without a textbook open, the specific ways real neuromodulation breaks the "one chemical, one direction, instant broadcast" model - Make a scoped, falsifiable design decision for the project rather than a general essay

Background you needs but that isn't in the available sources (given here directly, not as an assigned reading, because the papers that would normally carry this — Yu & Dayan 2005 on expected/unexpected uncertainty, and standard pharmacology on D1/D2 signalling — aren't in the source list): - Volume transmission (how dopamine, ACh, and NE actually reach targets outside direct synapses) diffuses over roughly tens to low hundreds of microns and acts over hundreds of milliseconds to seconds — orders of magnitude slower and more spatially constrained than a fast synaptic release event (sub-micron cleft, sub-millisecond), and very far from an instantaneous, uniform, whole-network mist. - The standard division of labour: noradrenaline (locus coeruleus) tracks unexpected uncertainty — a sudden, unsignalled change in the rules (a cue that used to mean X now unpredictably means Y) — and tends to trigger a global interrupt/gain-reset. Acetylcholine (basal forebrain) tracks expected uncertainty — known, stable ambiguity or stochasticity within a model you already trust (a cue you know is only 70% reliable) — and tunes how strongly you weight new evidence against your existing belief, without necessarily discarding that belief. - Dopamine's effect on plasticity is receptor-dependent in sign: neurons/synapses expressing D1-type receptors are typically pushed one way (associated with the direct pathway, generally facilitating potentiation) by rising dopamine, while D2-expressing neurons/synapses are typically pushed the other way — so the same concentration of the same molecule, at the same time, produces opposite plasticity effects depending on what's listening, not what's broadcasting.

Task Write 300-600 words that: 1. Answer AC2-AC4 in your own words using the background above (don't just restate it — explain why each point is a problem for "one chemical, one direction, instant broadcast," specifically). 2. State one concrete, specific way your original "misted chemical" model is factually wrong about real biology (AC5) — a mechanism, not a restatement of the lesson's goal sentence. 3. Make an explicit decision for the project: does the stress variable (a single scalar per neuron tracking persistent unresolved prediction error, gating growth of new neuron pairs) need to become more than one channel before it's used to gate growth/pruning in Steps 3-4? Justify from the biology above, not from software-engineering taste. If you decide one channel is fine for now, say specifically what it would take to prove you wrong later (what a two-channel need would look like once you see it in simulation). 4. Name one concrete thing that breaks in the current single-scalar stress design if the answer to (3) turns out to be "no, one isn't enough" — e.g. a scenario where a neuron with high stress from an unpredictable structural change and a neuron with high stress from known, stable noisy input get treated identically by the same growth trigger, when biologically they'd be handled by different systems (NE-style global rewiring interrupt vs. ACh-style local reweighting).

Deliverable 300-600 word written defence covering all four points, addressed to a reader who knows the project but hasn't just read this lesson.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong AC2-AC4 explained with the implication for the broadcast model stated explicitly, not just the fact recited; AC5 names a specific mechanism (e.g. omission dip requiring signed subtraction, or receptor-dependent sign, or volume-transmission spatial/temporal scale) rather than re-stating the lesson goal; the project decision in (3) is a real yes/no with a stated falsification condition, not "it depends" or "more research is needed"; (4) gives one concrete scenario, not a generic worry. Adequate AC2-AC4 present but treated as isolated facts without stating what they break; AC5 correct but generic; (3) states a decision but the falsification condition is vague; (4) is generic ("stress might need more nuance") rather than a specific scenario. Not yet AC5 restates the lesson's goal sentence ("real neuromodulators are more specific than a misted chemical") instead of naming a mechanism — this is the explicit failure mode the lesson spec calls out; (3) ducks the decision entirely; word count far outside 300-600.

docs.title: B2 · Cortical microcircuits and laminar structure
docs.text:
At a glance

Length — two to three sittings · about ~6 hours across 3 sittings (derivation ~1h, simulation ~2h, guided reading ~1.5h, written defence ~1.5h) Before this — the PV/SST/VIP-to-PC-quantities mapping and the Dale's principle discussion in comp_neuro_notes.md Reading — Largely absent from D&A — closest is ch. 2 Introduction to the Early Visual System and Constructing V1 Receptive Fields for the feedforward story, which is the part this lesson complicates. Primary: Bastos et al. 2012 (Neuron), Canonical microcircuits for predictive coding; Hertäg & Sprekeler 2020 (eLife), the read already flagged in comp_neuro_notes.md.

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: Name which cortical layer does what, and map Bastos et al. (2012)'s canonical microcircuit onto predictive coding: superficial layers carrying error, deep layers carrying predictions, with a feedforward/feedback asymmetry in both wiring and frequency band. Closes the gap between "PV/SST/VIP compute PC quantities" (functional, no wiring) and "those quantities live in a specific six-layer scaffold" (structural), and forces a decision on whether the column is real enough to justify a Step 5 cluster unit.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • The six layers and their canonical roles: L4 thalamic input, L2/3 cortico-cortical output, L5 subcortical output, L6 corticothalamic feedback
  • Bastos et al. 2012: superficial pyramidal cells as error units sending driving feedforward connections terminating in L4 of the target area (gamma); deep pyramidal cells as prediction units sending modulatory feedback that avoids L4 (beta/alpha)
  • Where PV, SST and VIP sit in that scaffold (Hertäg & Sprekeler): PV perisomatic inhibition gating feedforward drive, SST dendrite-targeting inhibition onto L1 apical tufts gating predictions, VIP disinhibiting SST — reconciled with the precision / prediction-mean / uncertainty mapping already known
  • Cortical columns: the evidence for (anatomical repetition, Mountcastle) and against (functional heterogeneity across areas and species) treating the column as a real functional unit
  • Not covered: dendritic computation within a pyramidal cell (B3), neuromodulatory gain control of the circuit (B1)

You should be able to answer: 1. Which numbered layer receives thalamic feedforward input, and which projects back to thalamus? 2. In Bastos et al. 2012, which layers are the error units and which the prediction units, and which frequency band is linked to each direction? 3. Trace a feedforward error signal from L2/3 of area A — which layer does it terminate in, in area B, and why does that matter for the feedforward/feedback asymmetry? 4. Where does SST inhibition land anatomically, and how does that location support SST encoding the mean of a top-down prediction rather than precision? 5. Give one piece of evidence for and one against the cortical column as a real functional unit, then say which way your evidence points.

Project tie-in: Step 5 wants cortices as dense clusters with sparse inter-cluster links. This supplies the internal layout — a superficial error sub-population, a deep prediction sub-population, feedforward links terminating on the error layer, feedback links avoiding it — making the cluster a specific circuit rather than an unstructured blob.

Done when: You sketches a six-layer canonical microcircuit with PV/SST/VIP placement and proposes a specific Step 5 cluster wiring diagram from it, without re-deriving the PC-quantity mapping.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine:

audio overview → guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written defence (Piece 4)

Pieces are numbered by type, not by sequence. The reading front-loads the concepts, the derivation makes them exact, the simulation is where they stick and get refined, and the defence is where you find out whether they did.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1 — Balancing a superficial error neuron derivation 2 (error vs. prediction units), 4 (SST location → mean, not precision) 2 — Fast error, slow prediction simulation 2 (superficial=error/deep=prediction, frequency asymmetry) 3 — Guided reading: Hertäg & Sprekeler (2020) guided reading 1 (layer targets), 2 (error/prediction split), 3 (feedforward termination + asymmetry), 4 (SST location) 4 — Step 5 cluster wiring proposal written defence 1, 3, 5 (all five criteria synthesized into the project artifact) Piece 1 — Balancing a superficial error neuronPiece 2 — Fast error, slow predictionPiece 3 — Guided reading: Hertäg & Sprekeler (2020)Piece 4 — Step 5 cluster wiring proposal

Type: derivation · Time: ~1 hour

Learning goals - Derive, with numbers, the condition under which a rate neuron receiving feedforward excitation and top-down inhibition becomes a genuine prediction-error unit (zero output when prediction matches input). - Show that a local inhibitory plasticity rule (using only pre- and post-synaptic rates available at that synapse) converges to this balance point, without a global loss. - Connect the algebra to acceptance criterion 4: because the inhibitory input in this derivation is playing the role of SST-mediated top-down inhibition, show why that specific subtraction computes the mean of the prediction rather than a precision (gain) term. - Notice the model's blind spot: a single rectified unit can only be one sign of error, motivating the "positive/negative PE neuron" pair the reading in Piece 3 will introduce.

Task

Model a single superficial-layer (L2/3) error neuron as a threshold-linear rate unit:

r_E = [ w_ff * x_ff  -  w_SST * x_pred  +  b ]_+        ([.]_+ = rectification, output ≥ 0)

x_ff is the feedforward drive relayed from L4 (in Hz), x_pred is the rate at which the deep-layer prediction unit is currently firing (in Hz, same units as x_ff by construction — assume a 1:1 SST relay so the inhibitory current SST delivers is w_SST * x_pred), b = 0, w_ff = 1.0.

  1. At baseline the prediction is correct: x_ff = x_pred = 20 Hz. Solve for the value of w_SST that makes r_E = 0 at baseline.
  2. Using that w_SST, compute r_E when x_ff jumps to 35 Hz with x_pred still at 20 Hz (prediction hasn't caught up yet). Then compute r_E when x_ff drops to 8 Hz with x_pred still at 20 Hz. State in one sentence why the second case is a problem for a single rectified unit, and what a second unit would need to look like to fix it.
  3. Now derive convergence to the balanced weight from scratch. Start from a mis-set w_SST(0) = 0.6 at the baseline input (x_ff = x_pred = 20). Apply the local homeostatic inhibitory plasticity rule Δw_SST = ε · x_SST · (r_E − θ), with x_SST = x_pred = 20, θ = 0, ε = 0.002. Hand-compute w_SST and r_E for 3 update steps. Note that this rule only ever reads x_SST (presynaptic) and r_E (postsynaptic) — no external error signal is injected — and say explicitly why that satisfies the project's "purely local learning" constraint.
  4. In 3-4 sentences: why must the inhibitory term be driven by x_pred (the deep unit's rate, i.e. its estimate of the prediction's mean) rather than, say, a term proportional to the variance of recent feedforward input, for this derivation to be consistent with SST encoding the mean and not the precision of the prediction? Contrast with what a precision-coding (PV-like) term would have to multiply instead of subtract.

Deliverable

A single typed sheet (prose + algebra, not code) with: the solved w_SST, the two mismatch values of r_E, the 3-row convergence table (w_SST(n), r_E(n)), and the two short written answers (part 2's one-sentence note, part 4's paragraph).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Correct w_SST = 1.0; correct mismatch outputs (15 Hz and 0 Hz, with the rectification-to-zero explicitly flagged as a limitation); convergence table numerically correct to 2 decimal places at every step; part 4 correctly distinguishes an additive/subtractive mean term from a multiplicative/divisive precision term and states this in terms of Dale's principle already covered. Adequate Correct w_SST and mismatch values; convergence table has at most one arithmetic slip that doesn't change the qualitative trend (monotonic convergence toward w_SST=1.0); part 4 correctly identifies mean vs. precision as additive vs. multiplicative but doesn't tie it back to SST/PV explicitly. Not yet w_SST solved incorrectly or via guessing rather than algebra; convergence table missing or non-monotonic without explanation; part 4 conflates mean and precision or skips the rectification issue in part 2 entirely.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation · Time: ~2 hours

Learning goals - Build a minimal two-population rate circuit (superficial error population, deep prediction population) and verify by simulation, not assertion, that the error population's activity is faster/noisier and the prediction population's is slower/smoother. - Verify numerically that the deep (prediction) population tracks the slow component of a synthetic stimulus while the superficial (error) population's mean collapses toward zero as the prediction converges. - Practice treating "frequency band" claims as an empirical, checkable property of time constants rather than folklore — and practice not overclaiming a match to real gamma/beta oscillations from a toy leaky integrator.

Task

Write a self-contained PyTorch or NumPy script (<100 lines, synthetic data only, no external datasets). Simulate discrete time steps of dt = 1 ms for T = 5000 steps (5 s).

  1. Synthetic stimulus s(t): a slow random-walk mean μ(t) (step ±0.02 every 200 ms) plus fast i.i.d. Gaussian jitter (σ = 1.0) added at every 1 ms step: s(t) = μ(t) + noise(t).
  2. Two populations, N = 20 units each, independent noise realizations per unit, shared dynamics:
  3. Error population E: τ_E dE/dt = -E + relu(s(t) - P), τ_E = 5 ms.
  4. Prediction population P: τ_P dP/dt = -P + η·E, τ_P = 50 ms, η = 0.5. (Note: P's update uses only E, its own local error signal — this is the same locality property as Piece 1's rule, now running as a dynamical system instead of a discrete weight update.)
  5. Discard the first 500 ms as transient. On the remainder, compute: a. The power spectral density (Welch or plain FFT-of-autocorrelation is fine) of the population-mean-of-E and population-mean-of-P traces. Report the peak/corner frequency of each. b. The mean of E over the last 1 s vs. the mean of P over the last 1 s vs. the true μ(t) over the same window. c. The Pearson correlation between P's trace and μ(t) (the slow component only, not s(t)).
  6. Write a 150-300 word comment block in the script (or a short markdown note alongside it) stating: which population's PSD peaks at higher frequency, by roughly what factor, and whether that factor is close to τ_P/τ_E; whether P tracks μ(t) and E's mean shrinks as expected; and — explicitly — that this toy model is not claiming to reproduce real cortical gamma/beta frequencies (the corner frequencies here are set by arbitrary millisecond time constants), only the qualitative claim that a fast feedforward-driven population and a slow feedback-driven population will occupy different, separable frequency ranges purely as a consequence of their time constants.

Deliverable

The script, its console output (numeric PSD peaks, means, correlation), and the written comment block.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Script runs, implements the two-population dynamics correctly with local-only updates; PSD peak of E is measurably higher than P's (within a factor of 2 of the ~10x predicted by τ_P/τ_E); P correlates with μ(t) at r > 0.6 after transient; comment block correctly states the overclaiming caveat unprompted. Adequate Script runs and dynamics are correct; frequency separation and tracking are qualitatively right but the numeric comparison to τ_P/τ_E is missing or off by a large factor without explanation; caveat about not literally reproducing gamma/beta is present but only after being asked. Not yet Populations don't actually separate by time constant (e.g. same τ used for both, or P updates from something other than E), or the script fits a curve/uses a real dataset instead of synthetic generation, or the write-up claims to have reproduced real gamma/beta oscillations.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: guided reading · Time: ~1.5 hours

Source: papers/B2_hertag_sprekeler_2020_prediction_error_neurons.pdf (open access). This is the required read before committing Step 5 to a layout. Bastos et al. 2012 (the canonical-microcircuit paper) is open access and readable in a browser at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3777738/ — PubMed Central blocks scripted downloads, not people. Read it: it is the source for the laminar and frequency-band claims, and the questions below about layers and bands are answerable from it directly rather than by inference. Douglas & Martin remains unavailable. Dayan & Abbott ch. 2 supplies the feedforward baseline this lesson complicates.

Learning goals - Extract the mechanism by which a local, biologically plausible plasticity rule turns an ordinary pyramidal neuron into a genuine prediction-error unit, without an externally supplied error signal. - Identify how the paper's dendrite-targeting vs. soma-targeting interneuron distinction maps onto the SST-vs-PV distinction already learned, and onto anatomical location (distal dendrite/apical tuft vs. perisomatic). - Practice explicitly flagging where a source is silent on a question the lesson requires an answer to (layers, frequency bands, columns), rather than inventing a citation for it.

Task — answer each question with a page/section reference from the PDF plus 2-5 sentences (page/section numbers may differ slightly by PDF version — cite whatever locator you actually have; the grader checks the content, not the exact page number):

  1. Where in the paper are "positive" and "negative" prediction-error neurons introduced, and what distinguishes them at the level of the circuit (not just the sign of their response)? Relate this to Piece 1 part 2's finding that a single rectified unit could only be a positive-error unit.
  2. Find the paper's plasticity rule for the dendrite-targeting inhibitory synapses. What two quantities does it depend on, and are they both locally available at that synapse (i.e., does it require anything like a global loss or a teacher signal)? Compare this to the rule you used by hand in Piece 1 part 3 — same shape or different?
  3. The paper distinguishes soma-targeting from dendrite-targeting inhibition functionally. Which one plays the role that, in this course's PV/SST/VIP mapping, corresponds to gating the feedforward drive, and which plays the role of delivering the top-down expectation? Does the paper's anatomical framing (soma vs. distal dendrite) match the SST→apical-tuft/L1 picture from the lesson scope, or is it silent on layers specifically? Say which.
  4. The paper does not discuss cortical layers or oscillation frequency bands. Given only what the paper does establish (dendrite-targeting inhibition conveying an expectation, arriving anatomically distal to soma-targeting inhibition), construct your own one-paragraph argument for why it would be consistent with dendrite-targeting/SST-like inhibition landing in layer 1 (where apical tufts of deep and superficial pyramidal cells both arborize) rather than, say, at the soma. Flag explicitly that this paragraph is your inference bridging the paper to the lesson's layer claim, not something the paper itself states.
  5. Skim the paper's discussion/functional-implications section. Name one stated functional benefit of having both positive and negative PE neuron types (rather than just one), and relate it in one sentence to why a Step 5 cortex cluster might want an analogous pair of error sub-populations rather than a single one.

Deliverable

Five answers, each with its locator and inline citation of which sentence/figure/equation in the paper backs the claim.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All five answered with correct, specific paper content; Q2's rule correctly identified as depending only on local pre/post quantities; Q4's layer claim is supported from Bastos et al. directly — superficial pyramidal cells encoding and broadcasting prediction errors, deep pyramidal cells encoding expectations and elaborating feedback predictions that terminate outside L4; Q5 names a real stated benefit (e.g. coding efficiency / covering both signs of mismatch with a shared dynamic range) and connects it to Step 5. Adequate Four of five correct and located; minor imprecision in describing the plasticity rule's dependencies; Q4 attempts the bridge but doesn't clearly separate "paper says" from "I'm inferring." Not yet Answers are generic paraphrase without a locator, cite content not actually in the paper, or Q4/Q3 assert the paper discusses layers/frequency bands directly (it does not — this is the specific error to watch for).

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: written defence · Time: ~1.5 hours · 300-600 words

Learning goals - Synthesize all three prior pieces plus the prerequisite PV/SST/VIP mapping into one concrete, named wiring diagram for a Step 5 cortex cluster. - Practice the discipline of stating what is not being copied from biology and why — a project decision, not a reading-comprehension answer. - Take an explicit position on the cortical-column debate (acceptance criterion 5) and let that position visibly shape the proposal (e.g., "one canonical layout per cluster" vs. "layout varies per cluster").

Task

Write the actual Step 5 cluster proposal the project currently lacks. It must include:

  1. An ASCII (or equivalent plain-text) wiring diagram of one cluster, with named sub-populations — at minimum: an input-relay population (L4-analog), a superficial error population, a deep prediction population, and inhibitory gating populations (PV-analog, SST-analog, VIP-analog) placed consistently with the prerequisite mapping and with Piece 1/3's finding about soma- vs. dendrite-targeting.
  2. Sparse inter-cluster links drawn explicitly: feedforward (error-carrying) links must terminate on the input-relay/error side of the target cluster, never on its deep/prediction population; feedback (prediction-carrying) links must terminate on the deep population and explicitly bypass the input-relay/error population. State this as a hard wiring rule, not just a diagram detail.
  3. One justification per structural choice, each citing which of the five acceptance criteria (or which piece) it answers.
  4. An explicit "not copying from cortex" list — at least three things deliberately left out or simplified relative to real cortex (candidates: six discrete anatomical layers collapsed to two functional sub-populations; literal oscillatory frequency-band routing, since the spiking implementation can route by connectivity rather than by phase/frequency; literal columnar repetition across an entire cortex — state the column position taken in acceptance criterion 5 and how it resolves in favor of a functional, not anatomical, replication of the layout per cluster; any other simplification you choose), each with one sentence on why the simplification is safe for the project's goals.
  5. One open risk: name one place where this layout might break the "purely local learning" constraint (e.g. does routing feedforward-vs-feedback by target population require any non-local bookkeeping at connection-formation/pruning time?) and how you'd check for it.

Deliverable

300-600 words total (diagram doesn't count against the word limit), structured as: diagram, wiring rule, criterion-by-criterion justification, not-copying list, open risk.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Diagram is concrete and internally consistent with Pieces 1-3 (SST/dendrite-targeting feeds deep→superficial subtraction, not soma); the feedforward/feedback termination rule is stated as an explicit, checkable wiring constraint; every listed choice is tied to a specific acceptance criterion; column position is a clear, argued stance (not "it depends") that visibly drives a specific decision (e.g., one fixed sub-population template reused per cluster, or explicitly heterogeneous templates, with a stated reason); at least 3 well-reasoned not-copying items; the open risk is specific and checkable, not generic ("local learning is hard"). Adequate Diagram present and mostly consistent but one element misplaced relative to Pieces 1-3 (e.g. PV/SST roles swapped, or feedback allowed to touch the error population); justifications present but some are generic rather than tied to a specific criterion; column stance stated but doesn't clearly change any design decision; at least 2 not-copying items. Not yet No explicit wiring rule for where feedforward vs. feedback terminate (an "unstructured blob" per the lesson's own framing of what this is supposed to fix); column debate skipped; fewer than 2 not-copying items; over word limit by more than ~50% or under 300 words.

docs.title: Verified against the source
docs.text:
These claims were checked against the text of Bastos et al. 2012 rather than recalled:

  • superficial pyramidal cells "encode and broadcast prediction errors" and provide feedforward connections
  • deep pyramidal cells "encode conditional expectations... so that they can elaborate feedback predictions", and feedback "terminates outside of L4"
  • the spectral asymmetry is the paper's own prediction: "superficial cells should express more gamma relative to beta, and deep cells should express more beta relative to gamma", with feedforward connections using higher frequencies than feedback

The grader key may be applied to these as sourced fact.
