docs.title: B3 · Dendritic computation
docs.text:
At a glance

Length — one to two sittings · about one to two sittings (~4.5 hours: 45 min derivation, 90 min simulation, 75 min guided reading, 60 min written defence) Before this — the point-neuron LIF model; E/I and Dale's principle Reading — D&A ch. 6 The Cable Equation and Multi-compartment Models — the passive grounding for why location is a weight, and the machinery for compartmental models. Not in D&A: the two-layer and apical-gating accounts — Poirazi, Brannon & Mel 2003 (Neuron); Larkum 2013 (TINS); London & Häusser 2005 for an overview.

  • B3 · Dendritic computation
    • Lesson spec
    • Coursework
    • Completion bar

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: Replace the point neuron — soma sums weighted inputs — with dendrites as active, spatially structured compartments. Why a synapse's location on the tree changes its effective weight, why a branch can spike on its own, and how apical input can gate somatic firing: a top-down prediction mechanism inside a single cell, before any network-level PC machinery.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • Passive cable properties: distal current attenuates before reaching the soma, so location is an implicit weight independent of synaptic strength
  • Active dendrites: NMDA and calcium spikes as branch-local thresholded events, distinct from the somatic Na⁺ spike
  • Poirazi & Mel's two-layer-network-in-a-neuron: branches as a hidden layer of nonlinear subunits feeding a somatic output unit, and the rough capacity gain over a linear point neuron
  • Larkum's apical-tuft mechanism: apical (feedback) and basal (feedforward) input on separate compartments, and how coincidence at the tuft gates or amplifies the somatic response
  • Not covered: which cortical layers apical and basal inputs come from (B2), spine pruning (B4)

You should be able to answer: 1. Two synapses deliver the same peak current, one proximal, one 300 μm out on a distal branch — which produces the larger somatic EPSP, and why in terms of cable properties? 2. What distinguishes an NMDA spike from the somatic Na⁺ spike — what triggers it, and does it stay local to the branch? 3. In Poirazi & Mel's model, what are the two layers, and roughly how much does capacity rise compared to a linear point neuron? 4. In Larkum's model, which compartment receives basal input and which apical, and what happens to somatic output when both arrive together vs apical alone? 5. If basal input alone produces a normal spike but apical input alone produces none, what does that predict about a neuron receiving strong bottom-up drive with no matching top-down signal?

Project tie-in: Step 4's stress mechanism currently has one lever when a neuron cannot predict its input — grow a new neuron pair. Active dendrites suggest a second: give the existing prediction neuron more internal capacity instead.

Done when: All five answered unprompted, and you can state the two-lever design tension (grow a pair vs add dendritic capacity) that B3 hands to Step 4.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine:

audio overview → guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written defence (Piece 4)

Pieces are numbered by type, not by sequence. The reading front-loads the concepts, the derivation makes them exact, the simulation is where they stick and get refined, and the defence is where you find out whether they did.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1 — Cable attenuation derivation AC1 2 — Two-layer dendrite vs. point neuron simulation AC3 (capacity gain), grounds AC2 (branch nonlinearity as the mechanism) 3 — D&A ch. 6 + active-dendrite primer guided reading AC1, AC2, AC3, AC4, AC5 4 — Step 4 design defence written defence AC3, AC4, AC5, project tie-in, "done when" clause Piece 1 — Distance as an implicit weightPiece 2 — Branches as a hidden layer: a capacity demoPiece 3 — D&A ch. 6 + active-dendrite primerPiece 4 — Written defence: growing a pair vs. adding dendritic capacity

Type: derivation · Time: 45 min

Learning goals - Compute a passive cable's length constant from membrane/axial parameters. - Apply steady-state exponential attenuation to get a numeric somatic-EPSP ratio. - State, without hand-waving, why synapse location is a weight independent of synaptic strength.

Task

A dendritic branch is modelled as a passive cylindrical cable with: - specific membrane resistance R_m = 10,000 Ω·cm² - axial resistivity R_L = 200 Ω·cm - diameter d = 2 μm

  1. Compute the length constant λ = √(R_m·d / (4·R_L)). Show units at each step (convert d to cm before plugging in).
  2. Two synapses deliver identical peak current, producing an identical local peak depolarization of 5 mV at their own injection site. Synapse P sits 20 μm from the soma; synapse D sits 300 μm from the soma. Using steady-state attenuation V(soma) = V(local)·exp(−x/λ) for a semi-infinite cable, compute the somatic EPSP for each.
  3. Compute the ratio EPSP_P / EPSP_D.
  4. In 3–5 sentences, explain why this ratio exists even though the two synapses are electrically identical at the point of injection — i.e., why "location on the dendrite" is itself a weight, separate from synaptic conductance.
  5. One sentence: is the steady-state exp(−x/λ) attenuation an over- or under-estimate of attenuation for a fast transient EPSP (as opposed to a sustained current step), and why (hint: capacitive shunting is frequency-dependent).

Deliverable

A short written page (typed or a clear photo of handwriting) showing: the λ calculation with units carried through, both attenuation factors to 4 significant figures, both somatic EPSP values in mV, the ratio, and the two short-answer explanations (Q4, Q5).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong λ correct with units shown; both EPSPs and the ratio correct to ≥3 sig figs; Q4 explanation names axial current leaking across the membrane along the path (not "signal gets weaker" vagueness); Q5 correctly says steady-state underestimates real transient attenuation. Adequate λ and EPSPs correct but units skipped or ratio rounded early causing drift beyond 3 sig figs; Q4 correct in substance but generic ("distance matters"); Q5 attempted but reasoning thin or absent. Not yet λ formula misapplied (e.g. wrong factor of 4, or d not converted to cm) causing an order-of-magnitude error; or ratio computed with additive instead of multiplicative attenuation; or Q4 conflates location-dependence with synaptic-strength-dependence.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation · Time: 90 min

Learning goals - Implement per-branch nonlinearity as a structural (block-sparse) constraint, not just "add a hidden layer." - Observe, with numbers, a task a linear point neuron cannot solve that a branched unit can. - Connect the empirical gap back to AC3's "two-layer-network-in-a-neuron" framing.

Task

Build a self-contained PyTorch (or numpy, if you implement gradients by hand) script, under ~100 lines, with:

  1. Data: N = 4000 samples, x ∈ {0,1}⁸ drawn uniformly at random. Partition the 8 inputs into 4 disjoint pairs: (x₀,x₁), (x₂,x₃), (x₄,x₅), (x₆,x₇). Label y = 1 if any pair has both bits = 1 (an OR-of-ANDs / DNF target), else y = 0. Split 80/20 train/test.
  2. Model A — point neuron: a single linear unit over all 8 inputs + sigmoid (nn.Linear(8,1) → sigmoid), trained with BCE loss.
  3. Model B — dendritic unit: 4 independent "branch" subunits, each a linear+sigmoid over only its own pair of inputs (nn.Linear(2,1) → sigmoid, applied 4 times — this is the block-sparse constraint that makes it a branch, not a fully-connected hidden layer), concatenated and fed into one somatic linear+sigmoid unit (nn.Linear(4,1) → sigmoid).
  4. Train both models for the same number of epochs with the same optimizer/learning rate. Report final train and test accuracy for both in a printed table.
  5. Add a 3–5 sentence comment/docstring explaining, in terms of AC3, which "layer" of Model B is the branches and which is the soma, and why Model A's single linear boundary structurally cannot represent an OR-of-ANDs target (a single hyperplane can't carve out this decision region) while Model B can (each branch pre-computes one AND, the soma only needs an OR over already-nonlinear branch outputs).

Deliverable

The script (.py file) plus its captured stdout showing the final accuracy table for both models on held-out test data.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Model B's first layer is genuinely block-sparse (each branch only ever sees its own 2 inputs — verified by inspecting the code, not just the docstring); test accuracy gap is clearly demonstrated (Model B ≥ 97%, Model A visibly and reproducibly lower, ideally by ≥5 points); explanation correctly identifies branch layer vs. somatic layer and gives the hyperplane argument for why Model A is structurally capped. Adequate Correct task/data and both models trained and evaluated correctly, gap is present and reported, but the explanation is vague about why (e.g. "the dendrite model has more parameters" without the linear-separability argument). Not yet Model B is actually fully-connected (4-unit hidden layer with no block-sparsity, i.e. an ordinary MLP) — this is not a dendrite model, it's just a bigger network, and it defeats the point of the exercise; or the label function is accidentally linearly separable (e.g. built from overlapping input pairs) so no capacity gap appears.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: guided reading · Time: 75 min

Learning goals - Read the passive cable equation and multi-compartment formalism precisely enough to explain each term physically. - Connect the textbook's passive machinery to the (non-textbook) active-dendrite mechanisms the project actually needs.

Task

Part A — D&A ch. 6, The Cable Equation and Multi-compartment Models. Answer:

  1. Write the passive cable equation in terms of V(x,t), λ, and τ_m. Identify, in words, which term is the capacitive current, which is the leak current, and which is the axial (longitudinal) current.
  2. State the steady-state solution to the cable equation for a semi-infinite cable with current injected at x = 0. What role does λ play in this solution, concretely?
  3. Using λ = √(r_m/r_l), explain why a thinner dendrite has a shorter length constant than a thicker one with identical membrane properties (connect to how r_l scales with 1/d² and r_m scales with 1/d).
  4. In the multi-compartment model, each compartment is a lumped RC circuit connected to its neighbors by an axial coupling conductance. Using this circuit picture, explain why adding more compartments between a synapse and the soma reduces the somatic EPSP without changing the synapse's own conductance at all.
  5. D&A's compartments are passive (linear) by default. What, mechanically, would you need to add to one compartment's differential equation to make it behave as a thresholded nonlinear subunit instead (the branch nonlinearity from Part B)?

Part B — active-dendrite primer (not in D&A; short grounding text, read before answering):

Two active nonlinearities live in real dendrites that the passive cable equation doesn't capture. An NMDA spike is a local, regenerative depolarization confined to a single branch: it is triggered when enough co-active glutamatergic synapses on that branch push local voltage past the Mg²⁺-block threshold of NMDA receptors, producing calcium/NMDA-receptor-driven current that stays largely local to the branch rather than actively propagating like the somatic Na⁺ spike (which is a single global all-or-nothing event triggered at the axon initial segment once total somatic input crosses threshold). Separately, many pyramidal neurons physically segregate inputs onto two compartments: basal dendrites (near the soma) carry feedforward, bottom-up drive, while the apical tuft (far from the soma, at the top of the cell) carries feedback/top-down input. Basal input alone can already drive a normal somatic spike. Apical input alone, arriving at the distal tuft, is too attenuated to fire the soma by itself — but if it arrives together with basal input, the resulting calcium spike at the apical trunk boosts the somatic response well above what basal input alone would produce. Apical input alone: no somatic effect. Apical + basal together: amplified somatic output.

  1. What distinguishes an NMDA spike from the somatic Na⁺ spike — what triggers each, and does the NMDA spike propagate outside its branch?
  2. In the apical-gating picture, which compartment carries basal (feedforward) input and which carries apical (feedback) input? What happens to somatic output when both arrive together, versus apical alone?
  3. If basal input alone produces a normal spike but apical input alone produces none, what does that predict about a neuron receiving strong bottom-up drive with no matching top-down signal?

Deliverable

Written answers to all 8 questions, 2–5 sentences each, Q3 and Q4 must name the specific scaling relationship or circuit element (not just "distance matters" or "more compartments = more attenuation").

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All 8 answered correctly and specifically; Q3 explicitly uses r_l ∝ 1/d² and r_m ∝ 1/d to get λ ∝ √d (thinner ⇒ smaller λ); Q6–8 correctly distinguish local/branch-confined (NMDA) from global/regenerative (Na⁺), and correctly state apical-alone gives no somatic effect. Adequate 6–7 of 8 correct; minor imprecision (e.g. Q4 says "attenuation increases" without invoking the RC/coupling-conductance picture); Q8's prediction is directionally right but not clearly connected to a "no top-down confirmation ⇒ suppressed/undistinguished response" statement. Not yet Fewer than 6 correct, or Q6 conflates NMDA spike with the somatic spike (says both are global), or Q7/Q8 swap which compartment is basal vs. apical.

Grader key hidden

Type: written defence · Time: 60 min · Length: 300–600 words

Learning goals - Turn AC3–AC5 into a concrete design rule for Step 4, not just a restatement of the biology. - Identify what the stress variable would have to measure to distinguish the two cases. - State the tradeoff (parameter/graph cost vs. representational limit) explicitly.

Task

Step 4's stress mechanism currently has exactly one response when a neuron's persistent prediction error (stress) is high: grow a new neuron pair (prediction neuron + error neuron). This lesson has introduced a second lever — give the existing prediction neuron more internal (dendritic-style) capacity instead, e.g. splitting its inputs across nonlinear branch subunits before somatic combination, without changing the graph.

Write 300–600 words arguing for one of: (a) always grow a pair, (b) always add dendritic capacity, (c) a hybrid rule. Your answer must include:

  1. A stated rule for when each lever applies — not "it depends," a concrete trigger condition.
  2. What the stress variable would have to measure to distinguish the two cases (a single scalar "unresolved error" can't tell them apart — say what additional signal or second scalar would).
  3. The cost tradeoff: what growing a pair costs (new graph edges, more parameters, potential network-wide instability) versus what adding dendritic capacity costs (per-neuron parameters only, no topology change).
  4. Confirmation that whichever lever is chosen stays consistent with the project's hard constraint that all learning is local (a per-neuron branch-split is still a local change; check that your argument doesn't smuggle in a global signal to decide between the two levers).

Deliverable

The 300–600 word written argument, as a single piece of prose (not a bulleted outline standing in for prose — bullets are fine as sub-structure but the core argument must read as an argument).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Concrete, checkable trigger rule (e.g. "if stress stays high after a branch-capacity increase, only then grow a pair" or equivalent nested-threshold logic); explicitly names a second observable/signal the stress variable lacks today (e.g. residual error after a capacity increase, or a measure of whether the error is separable across input subsets vs. genuinely unrepresentable by any recombination); cost tradeoff stated in concrete terms (edges/parameters/stability vs. per-neuron parameters); explicitly checks the rule against the locality constraint. Adequate Takes a clear position with a rule, but the rule is soft ("usually add capacity first, and grow a pair if that doesn't work" with no operational definition of "doesn't work"); cost tradeoff mentioned but generic; locality check is asserted, not demonstrated. Not yet No concrete trigger rule (settles for "both have their uses"); doesn't say what the stress variable would need to measure differently; ignores cost tradeoff or locality constraint entirely.

docs.title: B4 · Developmental pruning: how brains choose their own size
docs.text:
At a glance

Length — one sitting · about ~2.5–3 hours (one sitting) Before this — B2; homeostasis (synaptic scaling, threshold adaptation) Reading — D&A ch. 8 Unsupervised Learning — Hebbian development, synaptic competition and normalization, ocular dominance. Not in D&A: the elimination machinery and critical-period closure — Schafer et al. 2012 (Neuron) on microglia and complement; Hensch 2005 (Nat Rev Neurosci) on critical periods; Huttenlocher & Dabholkar 1997 for the density-over-development numbers.

  • B4 · Developmental pruning: how brains choose their own size
    • Lesson spec
    • Coursework
    • Completion bar

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: State, with real developmental numbers, that mammalian brains build far too many synapses and cut most back rather than growing to a target — and that elimination is an active, cell-mediated process, not passive decay. Closes the gap between Step 4's "stress triggers growth" and the fact that biological growth is front-loaded and largely undirected, while the real control lever is selective, signal-marked removal.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • Overproduction and elimination timeline: peak synaptic density age in human cortex, elimination continuing into adolescence, and the fraction gone by adulthood (~40–50%)
  • Activity-dependent competition: what correlated vs uncorrelated activity does to a synapse's survival odds, distinct from Hebbian strengthening
  • The marking signal: complement tagging (C1q/C3) flags weak or inactive synapses; microglia phagocytose the tagged ones — machinery, not weight decay
  • Critical periods: what one is operationally, ocular dominance as the example, and what closes it (inhibitory maturation, perineuronal nets)
  • Adult neurogenesis: where it demonstrably occurs and how restricted it is — a direct reality check on the project's growth mechanism
  • Not covered: the PC error signal that would drive stress (track C), synaptic scaling mechanics (already known)

You should be able to answer: 1. At what age does human cortical synapse density peak, and roughly what fraction of synapses present at peak are gone by adulthood? 2. Two synapses have identical weight but different recent activity correlation with their partners — which survives, and what is the actual tagging step between "weak" and "physically removed"? 3. Name the two cellular/molecular players in synapse elimination and say which one tags and which one eats. 4. What closes the ocular-dominance critical period, and why can the same manipulation not reopen it in an adult? 5. Name one adult mammalian region that still generates neurons — then say whether Step 4's growth should be modelled as constant background neurogenesis or as front-loaded overproduction plus pruning, and why.

Project tie-in: Directly sets Step 4 policy: the overproduction data argues for seeding excess neuron pairs early and pruning down rather than growing on demand per stress spike, and complement tagging argues for a two-stage mark-then-remove rule rather than a single near-zero-weight threshold.

Done when: You states a specific growth-rate and pruning-threshold policy for Step 4, citing the elimination fraction and the tag-then-remove principle as justification.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine:

audio overview → guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written defence (Piece 4)

Pieces are numbered by type, not by sequence. The reading front-loads the concepts, the derivation makes them exact, the simulation is where they stick and get refined, and the defence is where you find out whether they did.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1 — Overproduction/pruning rate arithmetic derivation AC1 (peak age, elimination fraction); AC5 (front-loaded growth vs constant background growth, as a policy number) 2 — Overproduce-then-prune vs grow-on-demand simulation AC5 (empirical size/performance tradeoff between the two growth models) 3 — D&A ch. 8 guided reading guided reading AC2, half (activity-correlation determines which synapse survives — the Hebbian-competition mechanism D&A actually covers) 4 — Step 4 policy defence written defence AC2 (tagging step), AC3 (complement/microglia), AC4 (critical-period closure), AC5 (neurogenesis reality check) — synthesized into the policy document

Note on sources: Schafer et al. 2012, Hensch 2005, and Huttenlocher & Dabholkar 1997 are the natural primary sources for the developmental numbers in this lesson (synapse density curves, complement/microglia tagging, critical-period closure mechanisms) but are not available in this course's papers/ set. Where the acceptance criteria require those facts, this coursework states them directly as given background in the task text below — clearly marked — rather than assigning them as a reading. The only assigned reading is D&A ch. 8, which covers the mechanism (activity-correlation-driven Hebbian competition) but not the cellular machinery (complement/microglia) or the raw developmental numbers.

Piece 1 — Overproduction/pruning rate arithmeticPiece 2 — Overproduce-then-prune vs. grow-on-demandPiece 3 — D&A ch. 8 guided readingPiece 4 — Step 4 policy defence

Type: derivation · Time: ~40 min

Learning goals - Convert developmental synapse-count data into per-unit-time growth and pruning rates. - Show quantitatively that the overproduction phase is much faster than the elimination phase. - Translate a biological rate ratio into a concrete per-epoch schedule for a stated network size.

Task

Given (background, stated directly — not from an assigned reading; these are standard, widely-replicated developmental synaptic-density figures for human cortex, order-of-magnitude accurate): - At birth (age 0): ~2,500 synapses per cortical neuron. - At peak density (age ≈ 2.5 years): ~15,000 synapses per neuron. - At adult, stable density (age ≈ 18 years): ~7,500 synapses per neuron — i.e. ~50% of the peak count has been eliminated by adulthood.

Compute, showing units at every step: 1. The growth rate during the overproduction phase (birth → peak), in synapses/neuron/year. 2. The pruning rate during the elimination phase (peak → adult), in synapses/neuron/year. 3. The ratio of (1) to (2). 4. Using that ratio: for a Step 4 network with a target steady-state size of Nss = 100 neuron pairs, choose a seed size N0 and peak size Npeak that mirror the birth:peak:adult ratios above (2,500 : 15,000 : 7,500), and split a total training budget of 200 epochs into a growth-phase epoch count and a pruning-phase epoch count in proportion to the rate ratio from (3).

Deliverable

A short worked sheet: the four numbered computations above, each showing the arithmetic (not just the answer), plus one sentence stating the final policy as N0 = _, Npeak = _, Nss = _, epochs_growth = _, epochs_prune = _.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All four values correct with units shown; the epoch split in (4) is derived from the rate ratio in (3), not guessed; states in one sentence why the two phases must differ in duration (fast bulk growth vs. slow selective removal). Adequate Rates and ratio in (1)–(3) correct; (4) uses a reasonable but not clearly rate-derived epoch split. Not yet Arithmetic errors in (1)–(3), or (4) ignores the ratio entirely (e.g., 50/50 split).

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation · Time: ~55 min

Learning goals - Implement two competing capacity-control policies on identical synthetic data and a shared training budget. - Measure the size/performance tradeoff empirically rather than assuming one policy dominates. - Connect the empirical result back to Step 4's current design (stress-triggered growth only, no scheduled overproduction phase).

Task

Write a self-contained PyTorch or numpy script (<~100 lines) with a single-hidden-layer MLP regressing a fixed synthetic target, e.g. y = sin(3x1) + 0.5*x2^2 - x1*x2 + noise over x in R^2, 500 train / 200 test points, generated with a fixed seed.

Implement two training runs on the same data and the same total epoch budget (e.g. 200 epochs):

  • Policy A — overproduce-then-prune: start with 200 hidden units. Train normally. Every 10 epochs after epoch 20, rank hidden units by |outgoing weight| · |incoming weight| (a cheap salience proxy) and permanently zero out (mask, don't un-allocate) the bottom 5% still active, down to a floor of 10 units. Record final active-unit count and test MSE.
  • Policy B — grow-on-demand: start with 10 hidden units. Track an EMA of training loss (τ ≈ 20 epochs) as a stress proxy. Whenever stress has not decreased for 15 consecutive epochs, add 10 new hidden units (initialized small/random), up to a cap of 200. Record final active-unit count and test MSE.

Print a comparison table: {policy, final_unit_count, test_MSE, epochs_to_reach_final_size}.

Deliverable

The script, its printed comparison table, and 3–5 sentences interpreting the result: which policy reached a smaller final network, which reached lower test error, and whether either policy ever removed a unit it had grown (Policy B should not — this is the flaw the lesson is pointing at).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Both policies implemented correctly and share data/budget/seed; pruning in A is irreversible and floor-respecting; growth in B is genuinely stress-gated (not just scheduled); interpretation correctly identifies that B has no removal mechanism and so cannot recover from over-growth, while A can end up smaller than B. Adequate Both policies run and produce a table; one part (e.g. stress-gating, or the floor/cap) is stubbed or approximate but the comparison is still meaningful. Not yet Only one policy implemented, or "stress" in B is not actually derived from the loss trend (e.g. it's just a fixed schedule), collapsing B into a relabeled version of A.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: guided reading · Time: ~30 min

Learning goals - Explain why unconstrained Hebbian growth is unstable and what normalization schemes fix it. - State the mechanism by which activity correlation, not weight magnitude alone, determines which synapse a competitive process keeps. - Connect D&A's ocular-dominance model to the general principle "correlated-with-partner activity protects a synapse."

Task — read D&A ch. 8, Unsupervised Learning, and answer:

  1. (§8.2–8.3, basic Hebb rule) Why does the plain Hebb rule Δw = η u v have no stable fixed point for |w| on its own — what happens to synaptic weight over repeated presentations, and why does this force some form of normalization?
  2. (§8.3, normalization schemes) D&A presents subtractive and multiplicative (Oja's rule) normalization. State the practical difference in what kind of solution each tends toward — does one tend toward a winner-take-all outcome (most weights driven to zero, one or few dominant) and the other toward a softer, shared outcome? Which behavior looks more like "a synapse either survives or gets removed" versus "all synapses shrink a little"?
  3. (§8.3, Oja's rule) Write Oja's rule and state which eigenvector of the input covariance matrix the weight vector converges to. Why does this mean a synapse driven by an input direction with low variance/correlation is disadvantaged relative to one driven by a high-variance, well-correlated input, independent of their starting weights?
  4. (§8.4, ocular dominance) In D&A's treatment, inputs from the same eye are more correlated with each other than inputs from opposite eyes. State how this correlation asymmetry, combined with the normalization/competition rule from Q2–3, produces eye-specific (segregated) territories rather than a blended input from both eyes. This is the direct analogue of "correlated activity protects a synapse" — identify exactly where in the model that protection enters (is it in the learning rule, the normalization step, or the initial conditions?).
  5. (§8.3, BCM) The BCM rule uses a sliding modification threshold rather than a fixed one. What problem with a fixed threshold does the sliding threshold solve, and why might a Step 4 pruning rule want an analogous sliding prune threshold (relative to a neuron's own recent activity) instead of one fixed weight cutoff for every neuron?

Deliverable

Five short written answers (2–5 sentences each), each ending with one explicit sentence connecting it to Step 4's stress/pruning design.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All five answers technically correct (instability, normalization contrast, Oja's eigenvector result, correlation-driven segregation, sliding-threshold rationale) and each carries a specific, non-generic Step 4 connection. Adequate Four of five technically correct; Step 4 connections present but somewhat generic ("this relates to pruning"). Not yet Confuses subtractive/multiplicative normalization outcomes, or answers Q4 without identifying where correlation enters the mechanism, or Step 4 connections are missing.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: written defence · Time: ~35 min

Learning goals - Turn Piece 1's rate arithmetic and Piece 3's mechanism into a committed, numbered policy for Step 4. - State a two-stage tag-then-remove pruning rule instead of a single instantaneous threshold. - Separate which policy numbers claim biological grounding from which are unjustified engineering choices.

Task

Background, stated directly (not an assigned reading — Schafer et al. 2012 is not available in this course's sources, but this mechanism is required by the acceptance criteria, so it is given here): - Synapse elimination in developing cortex is carried out by two distinct players: complement proteins (C1q, then C3) deposit a molecular tag on weak/inactive synapses; microglia recognize that tag and phagocytose (physically engulf and remove) the tagged synapse. Tagging and removal are separate steps with a delay between them — a synapse is not removed the instant it is tagged. - The ocular-dominance critical period closes as inhibitory (GABAergic, particularly parvalbumin-interneuron) circuitry matures and structural brakes (e.g., perineuronal nets) form around cortical neurons. The same manipulation that shifts ocular dominance in an infant (monocular deprivation) does not reopen or shift dominance in an adult, because the circuit is no longer in the low-inhibition, structurally unconstrained state that permitted large-scale rewiring — the brake, not the input, is what changed. - Robust adult neurogenesis is restricted to a small number of sites (the hippocampal dentate gyrus is the standard example; olfactory-bulb neurogenesis via the subventricular zone is well established in rodents, much more limited in adult humans). Outside these sites, the adult cortex does not generate new neurons.

Write a 300–600 word Step 4 policy document with exactly these four numbered decisions, each with a specific number and one sentence of justification:

  1. Initial over-provisioning factor — how large should the network be seeded/allowed to grow relative to its intended steady-state size, and over what fraction of total training should this growth be front-loaded?
  2. Growth-trigger rule — under what condition (and during what window of training) does the network create new neuron pairs? State whether growth is stress-gated throughout training or restricted to the front-loaded window from (1), and say why.
  3. Two-stage tag-then-remove pruning rule — the exact condition that tags a connection, the tag duration before removal is possible, and the condition (if any) that can cancel a tag before removal.
  4. Biological-grounding ledger — for each of the three numbers above, one line stating whether it is directly justified by a biological fact from this lesson (name the fact) or is an engineering choice with no biological backing (say so plainly).

Deliverable

The 300–600 word document, numbered 1–4 as above.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All four numbered decisions present with specific numbers (not "some" / "a while"); the two-stage tag/remove rule has a distinct tag condition, tag duration, and remove condition (three separate numbers, not one threshold reused); ledger in (4) correctly separates biologically-grounded claims (front-loaded overproduction ratio, tag-then-remove as two stages, growth-window restriction echoing limited adult neurogenesis) from unjustified engineering constants (exact epoch counts, exact ε/threshold values, exact tag/grace durations); word count in range. Adequate All four decisions present with numbers, but the ledger conflates one biologically-grounded item with an engineering one, or the tag-then-remove rule collapses tag and remove into a single threshold. Not yet Missing a numbered decision, no concrete numbers given, or growth described as continuous/unrestricted stress-gating throughout training with no front-loaded window (contradicts the overproduction argument this lesson exists to make).

docs.title: B5 · Hippocampal replay and consolidation
docs.text:
At a glance

Length — one to two sittings · about ~3 hours across 4 pieces (one to two sittings) Before this — A2 (attractors and network state); the Step 2b online-learning results Reading — Not in D&A. McClelland, McNaughton & O'Reilly 1995 (Psych Review) for the CLS argument; Foster & Wilson 2006 (Nature) on reverse replay; Ólafsdóttir, Bush & Barry 2018 for a current review.

  • B5 · Hippocampal replay and consolidation
    • Lesson spec
    • Track C — predictive coding
    • Coursework
    • Verified against the source
    • Completion bar

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: State why a fast one-shot store and a slow interference-free store are in tension (the CLS argument), what sharp-wave ripple replay actually looks like in data, and how both map onto catastrophic forgetting and experience replay in ML. Closes the gap between "replay sounds like a buzzword" and "replay is the specific fix for a specific interference problem the online-learning work has already hit".

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • Sharp-wave ripple replay as observed: forward and reverse place-cell sequences, ~10-20x temporal compression, in quiet wake and slow-wave sleep rather than during active behaviour
  • Systems consolidation: hippocampus as fast episodic store, neocortex as slow interleaved store, replay as the offline training signal between them
  • Complementary Learning Systems (McClelland, McNaughton & O'Reilly): the explicit argument that one network cannot be both fast-learning and interference-free, stated as a trade-off rather than an assertion
  • Catastrophic forgetting as the ML restatement of the same problem, and RL experience-replay buffers as the engineering answer - what corresponds to hippocampal replay and what does not
  • Preplay of never-experienced trajectories, and what it implies about planning versus pure rehearsal
  • Not covered: the mechanisms generating ripple oscillations (A3), the PC inference/learning schedule (C2)

You should be able to answer: 1. Roughly what compression factor does hippocampal replay run at relative to the original behavioural sequence, and in which behavioural states does it occur? 2. State the CLS argument in one sentence: why can a single network not be both a fast one-shot learner and interference-free? 3. In the Step 2b online rollout, what symptom would indicate catastrophic forgetting, and how would you tell it apart from the state-dependent output the attractor test already demonstrated? 4. What does preplay of an unvisited trajectory rule out as an explanation for replay? 5. Name one concrete difference between a hippocampal replay episode and a sample drawn from an RL experience-replay buffer - ordering, compression, or source of samples.

Project tie-in: The Step 2b online rollout updates weights live from a single correlated stream with no buffer and no replay step. This lesson supplies the basis for diagnosing whether the instability seen there is starvation for interleaved replay rather than a learning-rate or optimizer-state problem.

Done when: You states, unprompted, whether the current Step 2b setup needs a replay mechanism and sketches the cheapest version of one in a sentence or two.

docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine:

audio overview → guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written defence (Piece 4)

Pieces are numbered by type, not by sequence. The reading front-loads the concepts, the derivation makes them exact, the simulation is where they stick and get refined, and the defence is where you find out whether they did.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1 — Replay compression and interference arithmetic derivation AC1 (compression factor, behavioral states, replay counts); AC2 (why interleaving reduces interference, worked mechanistically) 2 — Catastrophic forgetting and the cheapest fix simulation AC2 (CLS trade-off, demonstrated not just asserted); AC3 (forgetting symptom vs. state-dependent output) 3 — Guided reading: Ólafsdóttir et al. 2018 guided reading AC1 (compression, behavioral states); AC2 (systems consolidation framing); AC4 (preplay); AC5 (replay vs. RL buffer) 4 — Written defense: does Step 2b need replay? written defense AC3 (diagnosing the online-rollout symptom); AC5 (replay vs. buffer, applied); Done-when criterion Piece 1 — Replay compression and interference arithmeticPiece 2 — Catastrophic forgetting and the cheapest fixPiece 3 — Guided reading: Ólafsdóttir et al. 2018Piece 4 — Written defense: does Step 2b need replay?

Type: derivation · Time: ~35 min

Learning goals - Convert a stated replay compression factor into concrete event durations and rest-period replay counts. - Separate "how much replay capacity exists" from "how replay changes interference," using the same numbers. - Derive, from a minimal delta-rule model, how fast a single-stream (blocked) update forgets a prior target, and how a small interleaving fraction slows that down — with a closed-form relationship, not a hand wave.

Task

Part A — compression and rest-period capacity. 1. A rat runs a linear-track arm in T_behavior = 6.0 s, laying down a place-cell sequence. Hippocampal SWR replay compresses this by C = 20×. Compute the replay event duration T_replay. 2. In a 10-minute (600 s) post-run rest period, SWR events occur at an average rate of one every 2 s (0.5 Hz, typical for quiet wake / early sleep shortly after behavior), each carrying one replay of that sequence. Compute how many replay events fit in the rest period, and express that as a ratio to the single live run (which happened exactly once). 3. In one sentence, state what that ratio implies about how many times a downstream (cortical) learner effectively "sees" the episode if it learns only from replay, not from the live event.

Part B — interference arithmetic with a delta rule. Model a scalar weight learning online: w_{t+1} = w_t + η(target_t − w_t), η = 0.1, w_0 = 0. 4. Phase 1 (task A only, 50 steps): target_t = w_A = 2.0 for t = 1..50. Using the closed form w_t = w_A(1 − (1−η)^t), compute w_50. 5. Phase 2, blocked condition (matches Step 2b's single correlated stream — no task-A samples at all once the switch happens): target = w_B = −3.0 for the next 50 steps. Using w_t = w_B + (w_50 − w_B)(1−η)^t (t counted from the switch): (a) compute w after 50 more steps; (b) find the number of steps t after the switch at which the task-A error |w_t − w_A| first falls to half its maximum possible value (|w_A − w_B| / 2 = 2.5, i.e. w_t = −0.5). 6. Phase 2, interleaved condition: each step draws target = w_B with probability 0.8 and target = w_A with probability 0.2 (a 20% replay ratio). Compute the expected target, the steady-state expected weight (t → ∞, where expected update = 0), and the resulting steady-state task-A error. Compare it numerically to the blocked condition's steady-state error (r = 0).

Deliverable: a half-page to one-page writeup with all 6 numeric answers and working shown, plus 2-3 sentences connecting question 6's result to why a modest interleaving fraction — not a huge buffer — already recovers most of the benefit.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All 6 numeric answers correct within rounding; the general formula in Q6 (steady-state error = (1−r)·|w_B−w_A|) is stated or clearly implied; the closing sentences correctly identify that error scales linearly (not steeply) with replay fraction r. Adequate Part A fully correct; Part B has the right method but an arithmetic slip in one of Q4-6, or the closing interpretation is present but vague. Not yet Compression arithmetic wrong (e.g. multiplying by C instead of dividing), or the delta-rule recursion is set up backwards (target and current value swapped), or Q6 treated as requiring simulation rather than the fixed-point argument.

Type: simulation · Time: ~70 min

Learning goals - Build a minimal two-task forgetting setup in plain PyTorch, using only SGD (matching Step 2b's optimizer constraint). - Observe catastrophic forgetting as a number, not a claim. - Implement the cheapest possible replay buffer and show numerically that it mitigates forgetting. - Articulate the difference between "forgetting" (weights moved by new gradients) and "state-dependent output" (same weights, different carried-forward input/state) — the distinction the Step 2b attractor test already raised.

Task

Build one self-contained script (<100 lines, numpy/PyTorch only, no downloads):

  1. Two synthetic supervised tasks over the same input distribution x ~ N(0, I_8): task A target y_A = w_A·x + 0.3·sin(v_A·x), task B target y_B = w_B·x + 0.3·sin(v_B·x), where (w_A, v_A) and (w_B, v_B) are two different fixed random vectors (seeded). Generate 2000 training samples and 500 held-out test samples per task.
  2. A small MLP: 8 → 32 (tanh) → 1. A single torch.optim.SGD instance with one fixed learning rate for the whole experiment — no Adam, no schedule (this mirrors Step 2b's "Adam state carried over blows up, SGD only" constraint).
  3. Phase 1: train on task-A batches only (batch size 32) for 300 steps. Save the model state and record task-A test MSE — this is the baseline.
  4. Phase 2, blocked: reload the phase-1 checkpoint fresh, train exclusively on task-B batches for 300 more steps with the same optimizer settings. Record task-A and task-B test MSE.
  5. Phase 2, replay: reload the same phase-1 checkpoint again. Before any task-B training, freeze a buffer of 64 task-A samples. Train on task-B batches for 300 steps, but on every step replace ~20% of the minibatch (6 of 32 examples) with examples drawn (with replacement) from that frozen buffer. Record task-A and task-B test MSE.
  6. Print a 3×2 table: {baseline, blocked, replay} × {task-A MSE, task-B MSE}.

Deliverable: the script, plus 4-6 sentences covering: (a) which condition shows forgetting and roughly by what factor; (b) whether replay recovers task-A performance and what it costs task-B performance; (c) one sentence distinguishing this forgetting (a weight change driven by new gradients) from the attractor test's state-dependence (same weights, different carried-forward state producing different settled output).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Script runs end-to-end and produces baseline < replay < blocked ordering on task-A MSE; write-up correctly attributes the ordering to interference vs. buffer-mitigated interference, and (c) draws the forgetting/state-dependence distinction precisely (weight change vs. no weight change). Adequate Ordering holds but write-up (c) is vague or conflates the two phenomena; or buffer size/interleave ratio was changed from spec without noting why, but the comparison is still fair (same checkpoint reloaded for both phase-2 branches). Not yet Blocked and replay conditions don't start from the same phase-1 checkpoint (confounds the comparison); or no held-out test set (train-set MSE only); or buffer captured after task-B training has already started; or forgetting doesn't appear at all and the script wasn't debugged against the checklist in Hint 2.

Type: guided reading · Time: ~40 min

Learning goals - Extract specific, prose-only claims about replay's temporal structure and behavioral-state dependence. - Connect the paper's systems-consolidation framing to the CLS argument already covered in this lesson. - Identify precisely what preplay evidence does and does not establish about replay's origin. - Locate causal (manipulation-based), not merely correlational, evidence for replay's function, and articulate why that distinction matters.

Task

Read papers/B5_olafsdottir_2018_replay_memory_planning.txt once in full (no figures are available in this text — all questions are answerable from prose). Answer the following in your own words, 2-5 sentences each, naming the section/paragraph each answer is drawn from:

  1. What temporal compression factor (or range) does the review report for hippocampal SWR replay relative to the original behavior, and in which behavioral states does the review say this replay predominantly occurs (relative to active locomotion)?
  2. The review situates replay within systems consolidation. In your own words, what role does it propose replay plays in moving information from hippocampus to neocortex — and how does that connect to the CLS argument (one network cannot be both a fast one-shot learner and interference-free)?
  3. The review distinguishes forward and reverse replay sequences. Summarize the functional or contextual difference it associates with each (e.g. reward-related/retrospective vs. prospective/planning).
  4. Find the review's discussion of "preplay" — replay of a trajectory the animal has not yet physically traversed. What does the existence of preplay rule out as a complete explanation of where replay content comes from, and what alternative function does it support instead?
  5. The review discusses experiments that disrupt SWRs (e.g. closed-loop stimulation timed to ripples) rather than just recording them. What behavioral/memory consequence is reported when SWRs are selectively disrupted, and why does the review treat this kind of evidence as stronger than correlational place-cell recordings alone?
  6. Find one passage connecting replay to spatial planning or decision-making (not just passive consolidation). What does it suggest about replay's function beyond rehearsing already-lived experience?
  7. (Synthesis — not from the paper's text alone.) Based on what you've read about how a replay event is structured — a compressed, temporally ordered place-cell sequence drawn from very recent experience — contrast this with how a single sample is typically drawn from a standard RL experience-replay buffer (i.i.d./uniform sampling over a large stored history). Name one concrete structural difference: ordering, compression, or source of samples.

Deliverable: numbered answers (2-5 sentences each), each citing the section/heading it was drawn from.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All 7 answered with correct content traceable to the actual text (verified by the grader against the source), each with a real section citation; Q7 names one specific, correctly-reasoned structural difference rather than a vague "they're different." Adequate 5-6 of 7 correct and cited; one answer conflates two concepts (e.g. preplay with reverse replay) or Q7 is directionally right but imprecise. Not yet Citations are missing or don't match what's actually in that section when checked; more than 2 answers wrong or fabricated (e.g. inventing a specific number not in the text).

Type: written defense · Time: ~40 min · 300-600 words

Learning goals - Convert the quantitative and CLS/replay understanding above into a scoped, falsifiable engineering proposal. - Reason about what "replay" means for a network that carries persistent activity state across timesteps, rather than resetting per sample. - Propose an experiment that can distinguish "replay helped" from "we got a good seed or learning rate."

Task

Write 300-600 words addressing, specifically for Step 2b's online rollout (single correlated stream, no buffer, no interleaving, SGD-only because Adam state carried over from training blows up):

(a) Should Step 2b add a replay mechanism, or is the instability seen in the online rollout better explained by something else (learning rate, optimizer-state carryover, etc.)? Take an explicit stance.

(b) If yes: sketch the cheapest version — buffer size (order of magnitude is fine), interleave ratio, and, critically, what gets stored given the network carries persistent activity state across timesteps. Raw (observation, target) pairs replayed later land in whatever state the network happens to be carrying at that later moment, not the state they originally occurred in — say what you'd snapshot instead (or argue explicitly why raw pairs are good enough despite this).

(c) Name one concrete experiment, using the project's existing tooling (headless_rollout / online_rollout — no code required, just describe the comparison), that would distinguish "the buffer is doing something" from "this run just had a favorable seed or learning rate."

Deliverable: one 300-600 word document.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Clear stance with reasoning tied to the CLS/interference arguments above; buffer sketch gives a concrete order-of-magnitude size and interleave ratio; explicitly engages with the persistent-state storage problem (not just "store transitions"); experiment description isolates the buffer as the causal variable (matched seeds/other hyperparameters, a repeatable probe). Adequate Stance and buffer sketch present but the persistent-state issue is only gestured at, not resolved; experiment description compares conditions but doesn't control for seed/hyperparameters, so it wouldn't actually isolate the buffer's effect. Not yet No clear stance ("it depends," no commitment); buffer sketch is generic ML boilerplate with no engagement with Step 2b's specific persistent-state constraint; no proposed experiment, or one that couldn't in principle distinguish replay's effect from noise.

docs.text:
At a glance

Length — two to three sittings — the hand derivation is the point, don't rush it · about two to three sittings (~4-6 hours total: ~75 min derivation, ~75 min simulation, ~50 min guided reading, ~50 min written defence) Before this — A2 (energy landscapes, fixed points); working familiarity with the Step 1/2 settling loop Reading — D&A ch. 10 Causal Models for Density Estimation — generative models, EM and the Helmholtz machine: the textbook grounding for "a node predicts its input and the residual is the error". PC itself is not in D&A. Primary: Bogacz 2017 (J Math Psychol), A tutorial on the free-energy framework — the best entry point; Rao & Ballard 1999 (Nat Neurosci) for the original.

  • C1 · Predictive coding as energy minimization

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: Write down the PC energy function for a small layered network, take its gradient with respect to one node's activity by hand, and explain why that gradient depends only on quantities local to the node. Closes the gap between "I have run settling loops" and "settling is gradient descent on a specific scalar function".

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • Generative-model framing: each node predicts its inputs from its neighbours' activities and the weights on those edges
  • Energy as a sum of squared prediction errors; its relation to negative-log Gaussian free energy at precision 1
  • Hand derivation: write E for a 3-node chain, take ∂E/∂x for the middle node, show which terms survive
  • The error neuron as the physical carrier of one error term in that sum
  • Settling as gradient descent on E with weights fixed, connecting to A2's fixed points as energy minima
  • Not covered: weight updates and schedule (C2), precision ≠ 1 (C3), non-layered graphs (C4)

You should be able to answer: 1. For a 3-node chain x₀ → x₁ → x₂ with prediction x̂₁ = w·x₀, write the full energy E as a sum of two error terms. 2. Given x₀ = 1, w = 2, x₁ = 1.5, compute the local error e₁ = x₁ − x̂₁. 3. Take ∂E/∂x₁ by hand for that chain and state which two terms in E contribute, and which do not. 4. Name the three quantities ∂E/∂x₁ depends on, and say why none of them require information from outside x₁'s immediate neighbours. 5. If settling is gradient descent on E, what does it mean for a node's activity to be at a fixed point, in terms of ∂E/∂x?

Project tie-in: The formal justification for the purely-local constraint — the settling loops in steps/02_pc_graphs/ and steps/02b_persistent_state/network.py are running exactly this gradient descent, and the error-neuron-as-energy-term view is what makes the neuron-pair abstraction principled rather than merely convenient.

Done when: You derives ∂E/∂x₁ for the 3-node example from scratch without being shown the formula, and identifies it as depending only on local pre/post activity and local error.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine:

audio overview → guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written defence (Piece 4)

Pieces are numbered by type, not by sequence. The reading front-loads the concepts, the derivation makes them exact, the simulation is where they stick and get refined, and the defence is where you find out whether they did.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1. The 3-node chain, by hand derivation 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (primary) 2. Settling is gradient descent simulation 4 (empirical), 5 (empirical) 3. Reading Bogacz structurally guided reading 1, 4, 5 (cross-check against a second source) 4. Why locality isn't a coding convenience written defence 4, 5 (applied to the project) Piece 1 — The 3-node chain, by handPiece 2 — Settling is gradient descentPiece 3 — Reading Bogacz structurallyPiece 4 — Why locality isn't a coding convenience

Type: derivation · Time: ~75 min

Learning goals - Write a layered network's predictive-coding energy as an explicit sum of squared prediction errors. - Differentiate that energy by hand with respect to a single node's activity. - Identify, term by term, which parts of the energy a given node's gradient touches and which it doesn't. - State precisely what "local" means for that gradient, in terms of quantities a real neuron/synapse could access.

Task

Consider the 3-node chain x₀ → x₁ → x₂. x₁ predicts... no — x₁ is predicted by x₀, and x₁ in turn predicts x₂. Concretely:

  • x₁ is predicted from x₀ by weight w: prediction x̂₁ = w·x₀
  • x₂ is predicted from x₁ by weight v: prediction x̂₂ = v·x₁
  • Fixed numbers: x₀ = 1, w = 2, v = 0.5, x₂ = 0.9. x₁ = 1.5 for the pointwise questions below.

Work through, showing every step:

  1. Define the two local prediction errors e₁ = x₁ − x̂₁ and e₂ = x₂ − x̂₂, and write the full energy E = ½e₁² + ½e₂² as an explicit function of x₀, w, x₁, v, x₂ (no numbers yet).
  2. Plug in the numbers above and compute e₁ and e₂ at x₁ = 1.5. Compute E at that point.
  3. Take ∂E/∂x₁ by hand — differentiate ½e₁² and ½e₂² separately with respect to x₁, using the chain rule, then add. State explicitly which of the two terms contribute a nonzero derivative and why (for this specific 3-node chain, check both — don't assume).
  4. Evaluate ∂E/∂x₁ numerically at x₁ = 1.5.
  5. Name the three quantities your final expression for ∂E/∂x₁ depends on. For each one, say which physical component (a specific neuron's error output, or a specific synapse's stored weight) it corresponds to, and explain why computing it never requires reading a value from any node other than x₁'s two immediate neighbours.
  6. Set ∂E/∂x₁ = 0 and solve for the value x₁* at which x₁ would stop moving under gradient descent (keep x₀, x₂, w, v fixed at the values above). State in one sentence what "fixed point" means here in terms of ∂E/∂x.

Deliverable

A written derivation (PDF, markdown, or legible photographed handwriting) covering steps 1-6 above, with every algebraic step shown — not just final answers. No formula should appear without the line before it that produced it.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All six steps correct with intermediate algebra shown; step 5's locality argument is stated in terms of physical quantities (error-neuron outputs, synaptic weights), not just "it only has x1 in it"; step 6 fixed point correctly solved and interpreted as zero net force from E. Adequate Steps 1-4 correct with correct numbers; step 5 identifies the three quantities but locality argument is vague ("these are nearby" without saying why nothing further is needed); step 6 attempted, possibly with an algebra slip that's otherwise structurally sound. Not yet E is written with a sign error, a missing factor of ½, or e1/e2 swapped; ∂E/∂x1 omits one of the two terms without justification; or step 5 lists quantities that include x0 or x2 directly rather than e1/e2/v.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation · Time: ~75 min

Learning goals - Implement settling (activity updates only, weights frozen) on the same 3-node chain and confirm it performs gradient descent on E. - Confirm empirically that the fixed point matches the hand-derived x₁*. - Structure the code so that the update for a node is architecturally incapable of reading anything non-local — demonstrating the Piece 1 locality claim in code, not just in prose.

Task

Build a self-contained script (PyTorch or plain numpy, under ~100 lines) that:

  1. Fixes x₀ = 1, x₂ = 0.9 (clamped, as in Piece 1), w = 2, v = 0.5 (fixed weights — no weight learning in this lesson).
  2. Initializes x₁ at some starting value (e.g. 0.0 or 1.5 — pick one and say so).
  3. Defines e1(x0, w, x1) and e2(x1, v, x2) and energy(x1) = 0.5*e1**2 + 0.5*e2**2 as small separate functions.
  4. Defines a local_update(e1, e2, v) function whose signature takes only e1, e2, v — not x0, x2, or w directly — and returns e1 - v*e2 (the gradient) or the resulting activity delta. This is the architectural locality check: if the function signature needed x0 or x2, that would already be a violation, independent of what the function body does with them.
  5. Runs a settling loop: at each iteration compute e1, e2, the gradient via local_update, update x1 by a small step against the gradient (x1 -= lr * grad), and record the energy at each step.
  6. Cross-checks the hand-computed gradient against autograd: build x1 as a tensor with requires_grad=True, compute energy(x1) and call .backward(), and confirm x1.grad matches your manual e1 - v*e2 at that point.
  7. After the loop, plots or prints the energy trace and confirms two things numerically: (a) energy is non-increasing at every step (with a small numerical tolerance), and (b) the final x1 is within 1e-3 of x1* = 1.96.

Deliverable

The script itself, plus a short (5-10 line) printed or written summary reporting: starting energy, final energy, final x1, number of iterations to convergence, and the autograd cross-check result.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Script runs standalone; energy trace is strictly non-increasing (or non-increasing within float tolerance) at every step; final x1 within 1e-3 of 1.96; autograd cross-check passes; local_update signature genuinely excludes x0/x2/w, and you's summary explicitly connects this to Piece 1's locality argument. Adequate Script runs and converges to the right x1, but the locality restriction is only asserted in comments/prose rather than enforced by the function signature (e.g. local_update takes the whole state and just doesn't use x0), or the monotonic-decrease check is eyeballed from a plot rather than asserted numerically. Not yet Script diverges or converges to the wrong fixed point (check for a sign error in the update direction — gradient descent needs -=, not +=, or vice versa depending on gradient sign convention); or autograd disagrees with the manual gradient and the discrepancy isn't investigated.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: guided reading (papers/C1_bogacz_2017_free_energy_tutorial.txt) · Time: ~50 min

Learning goals - Recognize the generative-model framing (predict inputs from causes) in a second source, independent of this lesson's own notation. - Map Bogacz's error/free-energy formalism onto the e1, e2, E already derived by hand. - Correctly place precision=1 as a special case of a more general treatment, without needing precision-weighted errors for this lesson.

Task — answer in your own words; equations in the source file may be mangled by text extraction, so answer at the level of argument structure, not by quoting formulas.

  1. Bogacz sets up perception as inferring a hidden cause from a noisy observation, i.e. a generative model running from causes to predictions. Find where he introduces this setup and state, in your own words, which direction the model runs (cause → prediction, or prediction → cause) and why that direction matters for calling it "generative."
  2. Locate where Bogacz shows that maximizing the posterior probability of the cause is equivalent to minimizing a sum of two squared error terms. Describe each of his two error terms in words (what each one measures), and say which one plays the role of your e1 and which plays the role of your e2 in the 3-node chain — even though his example may have different dimensionality or symbols.
  3. Bogacz's general derivation weights each error term by a precision (inverse variance). Does he ever consider the special case where both precisions equal 1? If you can find it, note where. Either way, explain in one or two sentences why your E = ½e1² + ½e2² (unweighted) is the precision=1 special case of his general expression, not a separate formula.
  4. Bogacz gives an update rule for the node representing the estimate of the hidden cause, structured as "this node's own error term minus a weight-scaled downstream error term" (or the equivalent, in whatever notation the extraction preserved). Compare its shape to your ∂E/∂x1 = e1 − v·e2 term by term, in words — which piece of his rule corresponds to e1, which to v, which to e2?
  5. Bogacz separates fast dynamics (the estimate settling to a value) from slow dynamics (weights being learned). Find where he makes this two-timescale argument and summarize, in 2-3 sentences, why "settling" — the object you implemented in Piece 2 — is the fast dynamics with weights frozen, and why weight learning being slower is what makes that separation valid rather than an arbitrary implementation choice. Do not describe the weight-update rule itself — that's C2.
  6. State in one or two sentences why "free energy" (in Bogacz's terms) at precision 1 is the same object as the E you derived by hand in Piece 1, up to the precision factor.

Deliverable

Written answers to 1-6, each a few sentences, citing roughly where in the source text (section heading or nearby distinctive phrase) each answer comes from, since page/equation numbers may not survive extraction.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All six answers correct and correctly located; the e1/e2 correspondence in Q2 and Q4 is stated explicitly and correctly (not just "sounds similar"); Q3 and Q6 correctly identify precision=1 as a special case rather than treating precision-weighting as a separate, unrelated mechanism. Adequate Most answers correct; Q4's term-by-term correspondence is present but loose (e.g. correctly identifies "own error minus something" without pinning down that the "something" is v-scaled e2); Q5 correctly identifies the two-timescale claim but doesn't connect it to your own settling-loop code. Not yet Q1 gets the generative direction backwards; Q2/Q4 fail to distinguish which of Bogacz's terms is upstream vs downstream; Q3/Q6 treat precision-weighting as something E is missing rather than as a generalization E is a special case of.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: written defence · Time: ~50 min · Length: 300-600 words

Learning goals - Argue, from the derivation (not from the codebase's existing structure), that the project's "purely local" learning-rule constraint is a mathematical consequence of what settling is, not an arbitrary implementation choice. - Use the neuron-pair / error-neuron vocabulary correctly and specifically, tied to the concrete e1/e2 example. - Correctly scope the claim: this lesson only establishes locality for activity settling, not for weight updates.

Task

Write 300-600 words defending this claim: "The settling loop already implemented in this project (network.py, the Step 1/2 settling loop, the 100-iteration CartPole settle) is not merely inspired by predictive coding — it IS gradient descent on a specific scalar energy E, and the fact that each node's update only touches local quantities is a direct consequence of E's structure as a sum of pairwise terms, not a design choice that happened to be convenient for neuromorphic hardware."

Your defence must: - Use the 3-node chain's ∂E/∂x1 = e1 − v·e2 as your concrete example, explaining what e1 and e2 physically are (outputs of specific error neurons) and what v physically is (a specific synapse's stored weight — connect this explicitly to the "virtual memristor" idea: the synapse stores v and only needs e1/e2-adjacent information to be involved in the update, nothing global). - State explicitly why a hypothetical non-local rule (e.g. one where x1's update needed x2's raw activity value directly, bypassing e2, or needed a global loss computed over the whole network) would require information x1 physically cannot have without extra wiring that predictive coding doesn't posit. - Connect this to the neuron-pair abstraction: explain why the error neuron is not a bookkeeping convenience but the physical carrier of exactly one term in the energy sum — which is what makes "prediction neuron + error neuron, reasoned about as one unit" a principled abstraction rather than a naming convention. - Explicitly scope the claim: state that this argument establishes locality for the activity-settling phase only (weights v, w held fixed); whether the weight-update rule is equally forced to be local, or is merely designed to be local, is a separate question deferred to C2. Do not claim this lesson proves weight-update locality.

Deliverable

A 300-600 word written defence meeting the four requirements above.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All four required elements present and correct; the physical-carrier argument for the error neuron is stated precisely (one specific term in the sum, not "represents error" vaguely); the scoping statement explicitly names weight-update locality as open/deferred to C2 rather than silently assuming it. Adequate Three of four elements present; the "why a non-local rule is physically impossible" argument is asserted rather than derived from the concrete e1/e2/v example; scoping to activity-settling vs weight-updates is present but underdeveloped (mentioned in passing, not explained). Not yet Defence describes locality only in terms of "it's what the code already does" without deriving the claim from E's structure; conflates activity settling with weight learning as though this lesson covers both; error neuron is described generically ("it computes error") without tying it to one specific term in the energy sum.

docs.text: C1 is complete when: (1) Piece 1's derivation is produced from scratch — you is not shown ∂E/∂x1 = e1 − v·e2 before deriving it — with correct e1 = −0.5, correct ∂E/∂x1 = −0.575 at x1=1.5, and a locality argument stated in terms of e1/v/e2 as physical quantities rather than "nearby variables"; (2) Piece 2's simulation empirically confirms monotonic energy decrease and convergence to x1* = 1.96 (±1e-3), with an update function whose signature architecturally excludes non-local inputs; (3) Piece 3's reading answers are structurally correct and don't rely on transcribing garbled equations; (4) Piece 4's defence contains all five required claims from its grader key and explicitly scopes the argument to activity settling, not weight updates.
