docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine: guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written explanation (Piece 4). Pieces are numbered by type, not sequence.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1 derivation AC1 (membrane time constant), AC2 (Nernst / K+ reversal potential) 2 simulation AC3 (gate terminating the rise), AC4 (delayed K+ → refractory period) 3 guided reading AC3, AC4, AC5 (gating-variable roles; stochastic-channel averaging) 4 written explanation AC3, AC4, AC5 — synthesis into the "done when" causal account Piece 1 — RC membrane and the Nernst equationPiece 2 — Simulation: Hodgkin–Huxley spike generatorPiece 3 — Guided readingPiece 4 — Written explanation

Type: derivation · Time: ~45–60 min

Learning goals - Derive the membrane time constant from the passive RC circuit and reason about how it scales with conductance. - Derive the Nernst equation from equal electrochemical potential, not just quote it. - Use a computed reversal potential to reason about current direction and synaptic sign (excitatory vs. inhibitory).

Task

Part A — RC circuit. A patch of membrane has specific capacitance C_m = 1 µF/cm² and leak conductance g_L = 0.3 mS/cm² (the values used in the classic Hodgkin–Huxley squid-axon model, D&A ch. 5, Single-Compartment Models). 1. Write the sub-threshold (leak-only) single-compartment membrane equation per unit area: C_m dV/dt = −g_L(V − E_L) + I_e/A. 2. Rearrange it into the standard form dV/dt = −(V − V_∞)/τ_m and read off τ_m in terms of C_m and g_L. 3. Compute τ_m in ms for the numbers above. 4. State τ_m if g_L doubles (e.g., a synaptic conductance opens on top of the leak), and in one sentence explain what that does to the neuron's ability to temporally summate two inputs a few ms apart.

Part B — Nernst equation. At equilibrium the electrochemical potential of an ion is equal on both sides of the membrane: μ = RT ln[X] + zFV is the same inside and outside. 1. Starting from μ_in = μ_out, solve algebraically for (V_out − V_in) and show it reduces to E_X = (RT/zF) ln([X]_out/[X]_in). Show the intermediate line where the ln[X] terms are separated from the zFV terms — don't skip straight to the formula. 2. Compute E_K at human body temperature (37 °C = 310.15 K) for [K+]_in = 140 mM, [K+]_out = 5 mM, using R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), F = 96485 C/mol, z = +1. 3. Given a typical resting potential V_rest ≈ −65 mV, state whether the net K+ current at rest is inward or outward, and justify it from the sign of (V_rest − E_K). 4. A hypothetical synaptic channel has reversal potential E_syn = 0 mV. In one sentence, state the general rule (in terms of E_syn vs. V_rest) for when opening a channel is depolarizing (excitatory) vs. hyperpolarizing (inhibitory), and classify this channel.

Deliverable

A written (handwritten photo or typed) derivation covering both parts, with every algebraic step shown — not just final numbers — and the one-sentence answers where asked.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Both derivations show the intermediate algebra (RC rearrangement; μ_in = μ_out separated into log and voltage terms). Both numeric answers correct to within rounding. Both one-sentence reasoning answers correctly use the sign/magnitude of a voltage difference, not just a memorized rule. Adequate Final numbers correct but one derivation jumps a step (e.g. quotes τ_m = C/g without showing the ODE rearrangement, or quotes Nernst without the equal-electrochemical-potential setup). Reasoning answers correct but stated as a rule without justifying from this specific case. Not yet Numeric answer(s) wrong, unit mismatch (e.g. mixing mS/cm² and µF/cm² without cancelling units), or the excitatory/inhibitory rule is stated backwards.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation · Time: 90–150 min

Learning goals - Implement the full conductance-based Hodgkin–Huxley model from its equations, not a library. - Demonstrate the all-or-none property empirically via a threshold search. - Identify, from simulated gating-variable traces, which gate ends the spike's rising phase and why. - Measure the refractory period directly with a paired-pulse protocol, distinguishing absolute from relative refractoriness.

Task

Implement the standard Hodgkin–Huxley squid-axon model (D&A ch. 5, The Hodgkin-Huxley Model), in Python with NumPy only, no downloads, roughly 60 lines. Use exactly these parameters and rate functions (V in mV, rates in ms⁻¹, currents in µA/cm², t in ms):

C_m  = 1.0     µF/cm²
gNa  = 120.0   mS/cm²      E_Na = 50.0  mV
gK   = 36.0    mS/cm²      E_K  = -77.0 mV
gL   = 0.3     mS/cm²      E_L  = -54.4 mV

alpha_m(V) = 0.1*(V+40) / (1 - exp(-(V+40)/10))
beta_m(V)  = 4*exp(-(V+65)/18)
alpha_h(V) = 0.07*exp(-(V+65)/20)
beta_h(V)  = 1 / (1 + exp(-(V+35)/10))
alpha_n(V) = 0.01*(V+55) / (1 - exp(-(V+55)/10))
beta_n(V)  = 0.125*exp(-(V+65)/80)

dm/dt = alpha_m(V)*(1-m) - beta_m(V)*m      (same form for h, n)

C_m dV/dt = I_ext - gNa*m^3*h*(V-E_Na) - gK*n^4*(V-E_K) - gL*(V-E_L)

Initialize V = −65 mV (resting) and initialize m, h, n at their steady-state values at that voltage (x_∞ = α_x/(α_x+β_x)) — do not start them at 0. Integrate with forward Euler, dt = 0.01 ms.

Then:

(a) Threshold and all-or-none. Deliver a 1 ms current pulse starting at t = 5 ms. Write a bisection search over pulse amplitude (µA/cm²) that finds the current at which the trace transitions from "peak V stays below 0 mV" to "peak V shoots above 0 mV". Report the threshold current and the peak V just below vs. just above it.

(b) Which gate ends the rise. Run one clearly suprathreshold pulse. Record m(t), h(t), n(t) alongside V(t) through the spike. Identify, by inspecting the traces, which of the three variables is falling (not rising) at the moment V peaks and starts to repolarize, and state what that variable physically gates.

(c) Refractory period. Deliver a first pulse (amplitude comfortably above your threshold from (a)) at t = 5 ms, then a second, separate 1 ms pulse at t = 5+delay ms, for at least 8 delay values spanning roughly 1–20 ms. For each delay, determine (by inspecting V(t) in the window around the second pulse, not just a threshold-crossing counter) whether the second pulse evokes a genuine second spike. Do this once with the second pulse at the same amplitude as the first, and once with a much larger second-pulse amplitude (e.g. ~10× threshold). Report the shortest delay at which even the very strong pulse fails to spike (absolute refractory period) and the shortest delay at which the same-amplitude pulse succeeds (an estimate of the relative refractory period).

Deliverable

One self-contained .py file (~60 lines) that prints: the bisected threshold current and the two peak-V values bracketing it; a short printed statement naming which gating variable ends the rising phase; and a table of delay → spike/no-spike outcomes for both second-pulse amplitudes, with your stated absolute and relative refractory period in ms.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Model spikes correctly (steady-state init, correct rate functions). Threshold within ~15% of the grader key. Correctly names the inactivation gate (h) as terminating the rise, referencing its own falling value near the peak. Refractory table correctly separates the very-short-delay "spike" readings (an artifact of the window overlapping the first spike's own falling phase) from genuine second-pulse recovery, and reports an absolute refractory period in the 5–10 ms range and a longer relative-refractory recovery time for the weaker pulse. Adequate Model spikes and threshold is in a plausible range, but the refractory analysis conflates the short-delay artifact with a real second spike, or reports only one of absolute/relative refractoriness. Gate identification correct but not tied to your own trace values. Not yet Model never spikes (usually a units error, missing division by C_m, or gates initialized at 0), threshold search doesn't converge, or the wrong gating variable (m or n instead of h) is named as ending the rise.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: guided reading · Time: ~45 min

Learning goals - Extract D&A's own definitions of the passive membrane equation, the gating-variable formalism, and the Hodgkin–Huxley current-balance equation. - Locate, in the text, which gate D&A assigns to opening vs. closing the Na+ conductance. - Extract D&A's account of stochastic single-channel models and what the macroscopic conductance represents.

Task

Read D&A ch. 5, sections Introduction, Electrical Properties of Neurons, Single-Compartment Models, Voltage-Dependent Conductances, The Hodgkin-Huxley Model, Modeling Channels. Answer in your own words (no verbatim copying), naming the subsection each answer comes from:

  1. In Electrical Properties of Neurons, what physical quantities do the membrane capacitance and the leak conductance each represent, and what is the resulting sub-threshold equation usually called?
  2. In Single-Compartment Models, write out the general current-balance equation D&A gives for a membrane with an arbitrary number of ionic conductances (the sum over channel types, each with its own reversal potential).
  3. In Voltage-Dependent Conductances, what is the standard differential-equation form D&A gives for a gating variable, and how are its steady-state value and time constant expressed in terms of the α/β rate functions?
  4. In The Hodgkin-Huxley Model, which three gating variables are introduced, and which ionic conductance (and power of the gate) does each belong to?
  5. Still in that section: what specifically extinguishes the inward sodium current during a spike — and is it the same gate that opened it, or a different one?
  6. In Modeling Channels, what is a single ion channel assumed to do, and what does the macroscopic conductance g(t) represent when there are N such channels?

Deliverable

Six short answers (2–5 sentences each), each tagged with the subsection it draws from.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All six answers match the expected content below, in your own words, correctly tagged to subsection. Adequate Four or five answers correct; the rest close but missing a specific detail (e.g. names m and h but not the power m³, or gives the gating ODE without the τ(V)/x_∞(V) form). Not yet Fewer than four correct, or answers copied near-verbatim rather than paraphrased, or the wrong gate is named as closing the Na+ current.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: written explanation · Time: ~45–60 min

Learning goals - Give a causal (kinetics-based) account of why an HH spike is all-or-none, without invoking "threshold" as an assumed model feature. - Give a causal account of why a refractory period necessarily follows a spike. - Ground both explanations in your own numbers from Piece 2.

Task

In 300–600 words, explain why a Hodgkin–Huxley spike is all-or-none and why a refractory period follows it, using only the kinetics of m (Na+ activation), h (Na+ inactivation), and n (K+ activation) — do not describe the neuron as having a hardcoded "threshold" that gets "reset". Cite at least two concrete numbers from your own Piece 2 run (e.g. your bisected threshold current, your spike-peak timing, or your measured refractory delays).

Deliverable

300–600 words of plain prose (not a bulleted list).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Explains all-or-none as the outcome of a positive feedback loop (depolarization → more m open → more Na+ current → more depolarization) racing against h's slower inactivation, so the response is binary rather than graded; explains the refractory period as the joint effect of h being slow to recover and n/K+ conductance still being elevated after the spike; cites ≥2 of your own Piece 2 numbers correctly; never falls back to "because it crosses threshold" as an unexplained primitive. Adequate Gets the qualitative mechanism right but leans on "threshold" language at least once without unpacking it in kinetic terms, or cites only one own-number, or omits one of the two feedback loops (positive Na+ or slow K+/h recovery). Not yet Explanation is circular (spikes because it crosses threshold; refractory because it's refractory) or doesn't reference your own simulation numbers at all.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

docs.title: Completion bar
docs.text: Done when you can state, unprompted and without reaching for "threshold-and-reset" as a primitive: (1) why a spike is all-or-none — as the outcome of Na+ activation (m) racing its own slower inactivation (h), evidenced by their own bisected threshold and the sharp sub-/supra-threshold voltage gap in Piece 2; (2) why a refractory period follows — as the joint effect of h not yet recovered and K+ activation (n) still elevated, evidenced by their own absolute (~7–8 ms) and relative (~12–13 ms) refractory measurements; and can back both claims with the derived numbers from Piece 1 (τ_m, E_K) and the guided-reading answers from Piece 3 (which gate is which, and what the deterministic conductance is an average over).

docs.text:
At a glance

Length — two to three sittings — three distinct payloads (the LIF derivation and f-I curve, the Hodgkin-Huxley loss ledger, and conductance-based synapses) rather than one continuous argument · about 3–4 hours across two to three sittings Before this — F5 Reading — D&A ch. 5 — Integrate-and-Fire Models · Synaptic Conductances · Synapses on Integrate-and-Fire Neurons

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: Derive the leaky integrate-and-fire model as a reduction of the single-compartment model from F5 and work its f-I curve with real numbers. State explicitly, with one concrete cost each, what the reduction discards. Replace current-based synaptic input with conductance-based input and show why the difference is not cosmetic.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • LIF derived from the membrane equation, with tau_m, threshold and reset as explicit parameters rather than fitted constants
  • The f-I curve derived from the subthreshold solution and evaluated at two or three real current values; the refractory period added and its effect on saturation shown numerically
  • What LIF discards relative to Hodgkin-Huxley — spike shape, adaptation, bursting — with one named phenomenon lost per omission
  • Synaptic input as a conductance rather than a current: shunting inhibition and the input-dependent effective membrane time constant, derived rather than asserted
  • AMPA, NMDA and GABA-A time courses in milliseconds and their reversal potentials, tabulated
  • Not covered: reset-mode variants and short-term plasticity (A4), wiring these units into networks (F8), learning rules on these synapses (F9)

You should be able to answer: 1. With V_rest = −65 mV, V_threshold = −50 mV, V_reset = −70 mV, tau_m = 10 ms and R = 10 megohm, solve for the interspike interval at an injected current of 2 nA. 2. Adding a 2 ms refractory period to that interval, what is the firing rate in Hz, and at what input current does the refractory period start to dominate the curve's shape? 3. Name one spiking phenomenon a real cortical neuron shows that plain LIF cannot produce, and identify which discarded mechanism is responsible. 4. Derive why a synapse modelled as a conductance times a driving force can shorten the effective membrane time constant even when it delivers no net current at rest, and name the effect. 5. Order AMPA, NMDA and GABA-A by decay time constant, with a millisecond value for each.

Feeds: F8 (networks are built from these units), F9 (plasticity acts on this synaptic machinery), A4 (which extends reset modes and short-term plasticity).

Done when: You derives the LIF f-I curve with a refractory period from the bare membrane equation, states the Hodgkin-Huxley trade-offs with a named phenomenon per loss, and explains shunting inhibition as a consequence of conductance-based input.

docs.title: Authors' exercises
docs.text:
Dayan & Abbott wrote exercise sets for every chapter and publish them free at gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~dayan/book. This lesson's are in exercises/c5.pdf (chapter 5), with any code and data under exercises/exercises/c5/. Work the integrate-and-fire and synapse ones — the biophysics ones belong to F5.

They are the authors' problems, not this course's, so they take precedence where the two overlap: if an exercise here duplicates one of theirs, do theirs. They are written for MATLAB; translating to numpy is part of the work and is not hard. The teacher agent has no answer key for these — it marks by reading your code and output, and says so rather than pretending to a key it does not have.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine: guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written explanation (Piece 4). Pieces are numbered by type, not sequence.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1 derivation 1 (ISI at 2 nA), 2 (refractory-limited rate and dominance current), 4 (shunting inhibition derived) 2 simulation 3 (LIF vs HH divergence observed), 4 (shunting made visible in a voltage trace) 3 guided reading 3 (HH loss ledger — reading side), 5 (AMPA/NMDA/GABA-A time courses and reversal potentials) 4 written explanation 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (synthesis) Piece 1 — LIF derivation, f-I curve, and shunting inhibitionPiece 2 — Simulation: LIF vs. HH f-I curves, and shunting made visiblePiece 3 — Guided reading: D&A ch. 5Piece 4 — Written explanation

Type: derivation · Time: 70–90 min

Learning goals - Derive the LIF equation as a reduction of the F5 single-compartment membrane equation, with tau_m, threshold, and reset as explicit parameters. - Solve the subthreshold LIF equation and use it to derive the interspike interval (ISI) and firing rate as functions of injected current. - Add a refractory period and find the current at which it starts to reshape the f-I curve, with a numeric criterion. - Derive, from the membrane equation with a conductance-based synaptic term, why a conductance synapse changes the effective membrane time constant even when it carries no net current at rest — and name the effect.

Task

Task A — LIF and its f-I curve. 1. Start from the single-compartment membrane equation from F5: C dV/dt = -g_L(V - E_L) + I_e(t). Divide through by g_L and define tau_m = C/g_L = R C (R = 1/g_L) to get the standard LIF form: tau_m dV/dt = -(V - V_rest) + R I_e, with V_rest = E_L. State in one sentence why this is a reduction, not a new model: what part of the F5 equation did you just delete? 2. Solve this linear ODE for constant I_e, starting from V(0) = V_reset. Show the general subthreshold solution V(t), and identify the steady-state (asymptotic) voltage V_ss = V_rest + R I_e. 3. Using parameters V_rest = -65 mV, V_threshold = -50 mV, V_reset = -70 mV, tau_m = 10 ms, R = 10 MΩ, and I_e = 2 nA: compute V_ss, then solve for the time t_isi at which V(t) first reaches V_threshold. Give t_isi in ms and the corresponding firing rate 1/t_isi in Hz. 4. Add an absolute refractory period t_ref = 2 ms (after each spike, V is clamped to V_reset for t_ref before the subthreshold equation resumes). Give the new interspike interval and firing rate. 5. Find the injected current I_e at which t_ref equals t_isi (i.e., the refractory period accounts for exactly half the total ISI at that point). Show your algebra symbolically before plugging in numbers. State in one sentence what happens to the f-I curve's shape above this current, and what value the firing rate approaches as I_e → ∞.

Task B — conductance-based synapse and shunting inhibition. 6. Extend the membrane equation with one synaptic conductance: C dV/dt = -g_L(V - E_L) - g_syn(t)(V - E_syn) + I_e. Collect terms in V and show that this is still a linear ODE in V, with an effective time constant tau_eff = C / (g_L + g_syn) and a new effective resting point. Do this algebraically — do not just state the result. 7. Now set E_syn = V_rest (an inhibitory synapse reversing right at rest, e.g. GABA-A near -65 mV) and evaluate the synaptic current -g_syn(V - E_syn) at V = V_rest. What is its numeric value, for any g_syn? Given that answer, explain how tau_eff can still be shorter than tau_m — walk through the algebra of tau_eff versus tau_m explicitly, don't just assert it changes. 8. Using C = 100 pF, g_L = 10 nS (so tau_m = 10 ms), and an inhibitory conductance g_syn = 10 nS with E_syn = V_rest: compute tau_eff numerically. Name the phenomenon this demonstrates.

Deliverable

Handwritten or typed pen-and-paper derivation for Tasks A and B, in order, showing every algebraic step (not just final formulas) and every substitution of numbers with units carried through. Final numeric answers stated on their own line, e.g. t_isi = 16.09 ms.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All 8 steps present with correct algebra and correct final numbers (within rounding); Task A step 5 shown symbolically before the numeric current is computed; Task B step 7 explicitly evaluates the driving force at rest before arguing about tau_eff, not just asserting shunting occurs. Adequate LIF reduction, subthreshold solution, and Task A criteria 1–2 numbers correct; refractory-dominance current attempted with correct method even if arithmetic slips; Task B derives tau_eff = C/(g_L+g_syn) correctly but the "zero net current, shorter tau anyway" argument is asserted rather than derived from the algebra. Not yet Formulas copied without derivation steps; numeric answers wrong or missing units; Task B treats shunting as "inhibition that also lowers V" rather than a time-constant effect.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation · Time: 60–75 min

Learning goals - Run LIF and Hodgkin-Huxley side by side on the same injected-current sweep and read off where the LIF abstraction holds and where it breaks. - Observe a concrete case of a phenomenon LIF cannot produce, as a simulation result rather than a memorized fact. - Watch shunting inhibition directly: a conductance-based inhibitory input that delivers ~zero net current at rest but still visibly shrinks and speeds up an EPSP, compared with a current-based synapse that does nothing when matched to zero current at rest.

Task

Write and run a self-contained Python script (numpy only, no downloads) with two parts.

Part A. Implement hh_rate(I): standard Hodgkin-Huxley (C=1 µF/cm², g_Na=120, g_K=36, g_L=0.3 mS/cm², E_Na=50, E_K=-77, E_L=-54.4 mV, standard alpha/beta gating kinetics) with a constant injected current density I (µA/cm²), Euler-integrated at dt=0.01 ms over 300 ms, discarding the first 100 ms as settling time, counting upward threshold crossings through V=0 mV. Implement lif_rate(I): the LIF from Piece 1 (same parameters, t_ref=2 ms), same integration and counting scheme, with I in nA. Sweep both across a current range that spans each model's rheobase up to several times over, and print firing rate vs. current for each. Identify: (a) the current near which each model's firing rate turns on from zero, and whether that onset is gradual or abrupt; (b) whether either model's rate ever drops back toward zero at high current, and if so, why (inspect the gating variables, not just the voltage, at that current).

Part B. Implement a passive (non-spiking) neuron (C=100 pF, g_L=10 nS, V_rest=-65 mV) receiving an AMPA-like excitatory conductance pulse (E_exc=0 mV, alpha-function shape, peak 5 nS, tau=2 ms, onset t=50 ms) and, in a separate condition, a concurrent inhibitory conductance step (g_inh=50 nS, E_inh=-65 mV — exactly at rest — active from t=45 to 80 ms). Run three conditions: no inhibition, conductance-based inhibition as above, and the "matched" current-based inhibition (a constant current equal to g_inh × (E_inh − V_rest), computed once at rest). Measure and report the EPSP peak (mV above rest) in each condition.

Deliverable

The script (< 100 lines), its printed output, and 4–6 sentences stating: the LIF and HH onset behavior (gradual vs. abrupt, with the currents), what happens to the HH rate at high current and which gating variable is responsible, and the three EPSP peak values from Part B with a one-line explanation of why the current-based condition differs from the conductance-based one.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Both models implemented correctly and swept over a broad enough range to see HH's rheobase and its high-current rollback; the HH rollback is diagnosed by inspecting a gating variable (not just "rate went to zero"); Part B reports three distinct, correctly computed EPSP peaks with the current-based case identified as ~equal to baseline. Adequate f-I curves computed and roughly match expected shapes; high-current HH behavior noted but not diagnosed mechanistically; Part B run with at least the no-inhibition and conductance-inhibition conditions compared correctly. Not yet Only one model implemented, or integration is unstable (NaN/blow-up) without being caught and fixed; Part B skipped or the current-based "matched" condition not computed from g_inh × (E_inh − V_rest).

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: guided reading · Time: 40–50 min

Learning goals - Locate, in the text, what the integrate-and-fire reduction is explicitly said to give up relative to conductance-based (HH-type) models. - Extract the standard synaptic conductance time courses and reversal potentials the text gives for AMPA, NMDA, and GABA-A.

Task

Read D&A ch. 5, sections Integrate-and-Fire Models, Synaptic Conductances, and Synapses on Integrate-and-Fire Neurons. Answer:

  1. What does Integrate-and-Fire Models say the model omits relative to a full conductance-based (Hodgkin-Huxley-style) description? List at least two specific omissions the text names (not your own guesses).
  2. What example phenomena does the text associate with the richer conductance-based models that a bare integrate-and-fire neuron cannot reproduce (e.g., adaptation, bursting, or others it names)?
  3. In Synaptic Conductances, what functional form does the text use for a synaptic conductance's time course (e.g., single-exponential, alpha function, or difference-of-exponentials), and what parameters does it define for it?
  4. What decay time constant(s) and reversal potential does the text give for AMPA-type synapses? For NMDA-type? For GABA-A-type? (If the text gives a range or a specific worked value, record it exactly as given, with units.)
  5. In Synapses on Integrate-and-Fire Neurons, how does the text define the total synaptic conductance driving the neuron, and how is it combined with the leak conductance in the membrane equation?

Deliverable

Five numbered answers, each 1–4 sentences, with a note of which subsection each answer came from. Direct quotes are welcome but not required; paraphrase in your own words is fine as long as the content is traceable to the named section.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All 5 answered with content specific to the named sections (not generic neuroscience knowledge); Q4 gives numeric values with units for all three synapse types; Q1–2 name concrete omitted phenomena rather than a vague "it's simplified." Adequate 4 of 5 answered correctly; Q4 has values for at least two of the three synapse types; answers are traceable to the right sections even if brief. Not yet Answers are generic (not clearly drawn from these sections), Q4 has no numeric values, or fewer than 3 questions answered.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: written explanation · Time: 30–40 min

Learning goals - Synthesize the derivation, simulation, and reading into a single coherent account of what LIF is, what it costs, and why conductance-based synapses are not a cosmetic variant of current-based ones.

Task

Write 300–600 words covering, in your own words: 1. How the LIF model is obtained from the full membrane equation, and what tau_m, threshold, and reset represent physically. 2. The f-I curve you derived and simulated: state the ISI and rate at I_e = 2 nA, the effect of adding a 2 ms refractory period, and the current at which the refractory period starts to dominate the curve's shape. 3. One named phenomenon (from your simulation observation) that plain LIF cannot produce, and the mechanism HH has that LIF discards to lose it. 4. Why a conductance-based synapse can shorten the effective membrane time constant while delivering ~zero net current at rest — the shunting inhibition argument, stated in your own words, referencing your Part B numbers. 5. The AMPA/NMDA/GABA-A ordering by decay time constant, with your recorded values.

Deliverable

A single prose document, 300–600 words, no bullet-point dumping of the five numbered points — an integrated explanation a labmate could read without also having your derivation and script in hand.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All 5 points present, correct, and integrated into connected prose (not five disconnected paragraphs answering five questions); the shunting explanation correctly separates "current at rest" (zero) from "conductance's effect on tau_eff" (nonzero); numbers from your own derivation/simulation are used, not generic textbook numbers. Adequate All 5 points present with correct content but written as a checklist rather than connected prose; minor numeric imprecision. Not yet Missing points, numbers not carried over from your own work, or the shunting explanation conflates "delivers no current" with "has no effect."

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

docs.title: A note on parameters before you start
docs.text: F5 worked in Hodgkin-Huxley's numbers — a squid giant axon at 6.3 °C, where the membrane time constant is about 3.3 ms. This lesson uses tau_m = 10 ms, which is a mammalian cortical neuron at body temperature. Neither is wrong and neither is a typo: they are different preparations, and the integrate-and-fire parameters here are chosen to match the cells the rest of the course models. If a number from F5 does not reproduce here, check the preparation before you check your arithmetic.

docs.title: Completion bar
docs.text: All four pieces at Adequate or better, with every acceptance-criterion number (ISI, refractory rate, dominance current, EPSP peaks, tau_eff, AMPA/NMDA/GABA-A ordering) reproduced correctly in at least one piece and referenced consistently across the others. F6 is done when you can, without notes, state the LIF f-I curve from the bare membrane equation, name one HH-only phenomenon LIF cannot produce and why, and explain shunting inhibition as a tau_eff effect rather than a voltage-shift effect.

docs.text:
At a glance

Length — two to three sittings — the cable equation derivation and the discretisation step are the parts that run long · about ~4-4.5 hours across 2-3 sittings Before this — F5 Reading — D&A ch. 6 — Levels of Neuron Modeling · Conductance-Based Models · The Cable Equation · Multi-compartment Models

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: Move the neuron from a point to a spatially extended structure. Derive the cable equation from current conservation along a leaky cylinder, extract the electrotonic length constant, and use it to show that a synapse's dendritic location sets how much of its current survives to the soma — making location an implicit weight.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • The levels-of-modelling spectrum from point neuron to full reconstruction: what each tracks, what it discards, and how to choose
  • Conductance-based models with ionic currents beyond the standard sodium and potassium pair
  • The cable equation derived from axial and membrane current balance, with the electrotonic length constant defined and typical values (hundreds of micrometres up to about a millimetre for dendrites)
  • Steady-state attenuation of a distal EPSP at the soma as a function of distance in units of the length constant
  • Multi-compartment discretisation into coupled ODEs, and the rule for compartment length relative to the length constant
  • Not covered: active dendritic currents, NMDA spikes and the two-layer dendritic model (B3)

You should be able to answer: 1. For a dendritic cylinder with membrane resistivity 20,000 ohm-square-centimetre, axial resistivity 200 ohm-centimetre and diameter 2 micrometres, compute the length constant in micrometres. 2. A synapse sits two length constants from the soma. What fraction of its steady-state local voltage reaches the soma? 3. Write the cable equation and identify which term is axial current flow and which is transmembrane leak. 4. Why must compartment length be chosen relative to the length constant rather than to the neuron's physical size — what breaks in the discretised ODEs otherwise? 5. Name two ionic currents a conductance-based model might add beyond sodium and potassium, and what each contributes that those two cannot.

Feeds: B3 (active dendrites, NMDA spikes and apical gating are nonlinear modifications on top of this passive framework).

Done when: Given a cylinder's resistivities and diameter, you computes the length constant, uses it to find steady-state attenuation at the soma, and explains why compartment size is chosen relative to it.

Dayan & Abbott wrote exercise sets for every chapter and publish them free at gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~dayan/book. This lesson's are in exercises/c6.pdf (chapter 6), with any code and data under exercises/exercises/c6/. Work all.

docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine: guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written explanation (Piece 4). Pieces are numbered by type, not sequence.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 1 derivation 1 (compute λ), 2 (attenuation fraction), 3 (cable equation terms) 2 simulation 1 (λ from a real cylinder), 2 (attenuation, numerically), 4 (compartment-size rule, demonstrated) 3 guided reading 3 (cable equation as presented in the text), 5 (conductance-based currents), plus the levels-of-modeling scope item 4 written explanation 4 (why compartment size tracks λ), 5 (ionic currents in context) Piece 1 — Deriving the cable equation and the length constantPiece 2 — Multi-compartment cable: attenuation curve and the discretisation rulePiece 3 — Guided reading: D&A ch. 6Piece 4 — Written explanation: location as an implicit weight

Type: derivation · Time: ~75 min

Learning goals - Derive the passive cable equation from Kirchhoff's current law on an infinitesimal cylinder segment. - Extract the electrotonic length constant λ from the balance of axial and membrane-leak resistance. - Compute λ numerically from given resistivities and diameter, carrying units through. - Apply the steady-state exponential-attenuation solution to a concrete synapse-to-soma distance.

Task

Part A — derive the cable equation. Consider a cylindrical dendrite of diameter d. Take a segment of length Δx and apply Kirchhoff's current law at its boundary: the axial current entering minus the axial current leaving must equal the membrane leak current plus the capacitive charging current, minus any current injected into the segment. Write the axial current via Ohm's law using an axial resistance per unit length r_a, and the leak/capacitive currents using a membrane resistance per unit length r_m and membrane capacitance per unit length c_m. Take Δx → 0 and show the resulting PDE.

Part B — extract λ. Set ∂V/∂t = 0 and the injected current to zero. Express r_m and r_a in terms of the specific membrane resistivity R_m (Ω·cm²), specific axial resistivity R_a (Ω·cm), and diameter d, and show that the steady-state equation reduces to ∂²V/∂x² = V/λ² with λ = √(d·R_m / (4·R_a)).

Part C — compute. Using R_m = 20,000 Ω·cm², R_a = 200 Ω·cm, d = 2 µm = 2×10⁻⁴ cm, compute λ in cm and convert to µm.

Part D — attenuation. Using the steady-state solution for a synapse on an (idealized, semi-infinite) cable, V(soma) = V(local) · e^(−x/λ), compute the fraction of a synapse's local steady-state voltage that reaches the soma when the synapse sits at x = 2λ.

Part E — label the terms. Rewrite the PDE from Part A and label which term is axial (longitudinal) current flow and which is transmembrane leak current.

Deliverable

Written pages (handwritten or typed) covering: the Kirchhoff-law setup and the Δx → 0 limit (Part A, shown explicitly, not skipped); the λ formula in terms of R_m, R_a, d (Part B); the numeric λ with units (Part C); the attenuation fraction as both an expression and a decimal (Part D); the labeled cable equation (Part E).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All five parts correct; the Δx → 0 step is shown explicitly; λ correct to ≥3 significant figures with units carried through; attenuation given as both e^(−2) and its decimal value; axial/leak terms labeled specifically (not "term 1"/"term 2") with one line each on why. Adequate Cable equation and λ formula correct; final numeric λ and attenuation fraction correct even if intermediate unit bookkeeping is sloppy; terms labeled but justification thin. Not yet A term missing or wrong sign in the PDE; λ formula missing the factor of 4, or diameter dependence inverted; numeric λ off by more than 2× or missing units; attenuation computed as a linear (not exponential) falloff, or with the wrong sign in the exponent.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation · Time: ~90 min

Learning goals - Translate the continuous cable equation into a discretized system of coupled compartment ODEs with sealed (no-flux) boundaries. - Numerically reproduce the analytic exponential attenuation law from Piece 1 when compartments are small relative to λ. - Demonstrate, by direct numerical comparison (not assertion), that violating Δx ≪ λ produces a measurably wrong attenuation curve.

Task

Work in normalized units: x̃ = x/λ, t̃ = t/τ_m (τ_m = R_m·C_m; assume the standard specific membrane capacitance C_m = 1 µF/cm², giving τ_m = 20,000 Ω·cm² × 1×10⁻⁶ F/cm² = 0.02 s = 20 ms). In these units the cable equation becomes

∂V/∂t̃ = ∂²V/∂x̃² − V + E(x̃, t̃)

with E the injected current in normalized units. Model the soma as an interior compartment, not an end compartment: extend the cable at least 6λ on either side of the soma with sealed (Neumann) boundaries at the two far ends. (If the soma sits at a sealed boundary instead, its own reflection corrupts the comparison to the semi-infinite exp(−x/λ) law — this is a deliberate design constraint, not a simplification you can skip.)

Discretize into N compartments of width h = Δx̃. For each interior compartment i:

dV_i/dt̃ = (V_{i+1} − 2V_i + V_{i-1})/h² − V_i + E_i(t̃)

with the sealed-end rule at i=0 and i=N−1 (drop the term that would come from outside the cable, i.e. reflect the missing neighbor).

Part A (well-resolved). Choose h = 0.1 (Δx = 0.1λ). Inject a constant unit current, one run at a time, at compartments 1λ, 2λ, and 3λ from the soma. Integrate forward in time with a stable step until the somatic voltage plateaus. Record the ratio V(soma)/V(local injection site) at each distance and compare against e^(−x/λ) from Piece 1.

Part B (violating the rule). Repeat with h = 1.0 (one compartment spans a full length constant) and again with h = 2.0, same physical span. Record the same ratios (where a compartment lands at that distance) and compute percent deviation from e^(−x/λ) at a fixed distance (e.g. x = 2λ) across all three values of h.

Deliverable

The script (under ~100 lines), the attenuation curves (fine vs. coarse vs. analytic, plotted or tabulated), and a short error-vs-h/λ table at a fixed distance.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Fine-resolution (h ≪ λ) curve matches analytic e^(−x/λ) to within ~1%; coarse cases show clearly increasing error as h/λ grows, reported as computed percentages; soma correctly placed as an interior compartment with the reason stated; explicit error-vs-h table included. Adequate Fine case matches within a few percent and at least one coarse case is shown to deviate, but error isn't quantified precisely or only one coarse case is tested. Not yet Soma placed at a cable endpoint (breaking the exp(−x/λ) comparison even in the fine case); no quantified comparison to the analytic curve; only one resolution tested, so criterion 4 isn't actually demonstrated; unstable integration (blown-up/NaN voltages) not diagnosed.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: guided reading · Time: ~45 min

Learning goals - Locate where each level of neuron modeling sits on the abstraction spectrum, and what it keeps versus discards. - Identify what conductance-based models add beyond the Hodgkin-Huxley Na⁺/K⁺ pair. - State the cable equation's terms and boundary conditions as the text presents them, cross-checked against Piece 1. - Extract the text's rule of thumb for multi-compartment discretisation.

Task

Read D&A ch. 6, sections Levels of Neuron Modeling, Conductance-Based Models, The Cable Equation, and Multi-compartment Models. Answer in your own words (no verbatim quoting), naming the subsection each answer draws from:

  1. List the levels of neuron modeling the chapter distinguishes, simplest to most detailed. For each, name one thing it captures and one thing it deliberately discards.
  2. The conductance-based section goes beyond the Hodgkin-Huxley Na⁺/K⁺ pair. Name at least one additional ionic current it discusses and its functional role.
  3. In the text's derivation of the cable equation, what physical assumption lets axial current be written via a simple 1-D Ohm's law (what is assumed about intracellular vs. extracellular resistance)?
  4. What boundary condition does the text use at a sealed dendritic end, and what condition applies at a branch point where two dendrites meet?
  5. What rule of thumb does the text give for compartment length relative to the electrotonic length constant, and what goes wrong if it's violated?

Deliverable

Answers to Q1-Q5, at most one paragraph each, each tagged with the subsection it was drawn from.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All five answered accurately with the correct subsection cited; levels of modeling distinguished by what state each one tracks; sealed-end and branch-point conditions stated distinctly and correctly. Adequate Correct in substance, citations vague, or one answer thin. Not yet Conflates levels of modeling; misses that conductance-based models include currents beyond Na⁺/K⁺; can't state the compartment-length rule, or states it relative to neuron size instead of λ.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: written explanation · Time: ~45 min, 300-600 words

Learning goals - Synthesize the derivation and simulation results into a coherent account of why dendritic location acts as an implicit synaptic weight. - Explain, in your own words and with their own numbers, why compartment size must track λ rather than physical neuron size. - Situate the passive-cable result within the levels-of-modeling spectrum and conductance-based extensions.

Task

In 300-600 words, explain to a reader who knows Hodgkin-Huxley point neurons but has not seen cable theory:

  1. Why a synapse's distance from the soma, measured in units of λ, determines how much of its current survives to influence somatic voltage — use your computed λ and attenuation fraction from Piece 1 as a concrete example.
  2. Why, when simulating this numerically, compartment length must be chosen relative to λ and not the neuron's physical size — reference your Piece 2 fine-vs-coarse comparison and at least one of its error numbers.
  3. How this passive-cable picture fits into the broader levels-of-modeling spectrum (Piece 3, Q1), and what a conductance-based extension (e.g. adding a calcium current, Piece 3 Q2) would let the model do that a passive cable structurally cannot.

Deliverable

300-600 words of prose covering all three points, citing specific numbers from Pieces 1 and 2 (not just symbols).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Explains attenuation as exponential decay in units of λ with a concrete number (e.g. "at 2λ, only ~13.5% of the local voltage survives to the soma"); explains the discretisation failure mechanistically (why the finite-difference second derivative needs small Δx/λ) with a concrete error number from their own simulation; correctly places the passive cable in the levels spectrum and names a specific, correct consequence of adding an active current; word count in range. Adequate Covers all three points with generally correct reasoning but vaguer mechanism (e.g. asserts the discretisation rule without explaining why) or omits concrete numbers. Not yet Treats synaptic location as a fixed/additive weight without connecting it to distance and exponential decay; says compartment size should just be "small" with no reference to λ; conflates active/passive cable properties or misstates the calcium current's role; well outside word count.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: Move from single neurons to populations described by firing rates, and show that a linear recurrent network's behaviour is fully characterised by the eigenstructure of its weight matrix. Establish selective amplification, effective time constants and stability as the load-bearing ideas that A2 and A3 each extend in a different direction.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • The firing-rate model as an approximation to a spiking population, with its assumptions stated and a regime where it breaks
  • Feedforward networks: what a weight matrix does to an input pattern
  • Linear recurrent networks by eigen-decomposition: selective amplification of eigenvector-aligned components, the effective time constant per mode, and the stability condition
  • Nonlinear saturating recurrent networks: winner-take-all and gain control as consequences of saturation
  • Excitatory-inhibitory networks: the conditions for stable, damped or oscillatory return to equilibrium
  • Stochastic networks as a bridge to energy functions and noise, introduced but not developed
  • Not covered: attractors, basins and Hopfield memory built from the energy function (A2); E-I dynamics developed into rhythms, bands and synchrony (A3)

You should be able to answer: 1. A linear recurrent network has largest real eigenvalue 0.8. Given membrane time constant tau, what is that mode's effective time constant, and what happens as the eigenvalue approaches 1? 2. State the stability condition for a linear recurrent network in terms of the eigenvalues of the recurrent weight matrix. 3. In a linearised E-I network, what condition on the eigenvalues distinguishes damped oscillatory return to equilibrium from monotonic decay? 4. For an input aligned with an eigenvector of eigenvalue lambda, give the expression for steady-state amplification compared to the feedforward-only case. 5. Name two computations saturation enables that a linear recurrent network cannot perform, and say specifically why linearity precludes each.

Feeds: A2 (energy functions and recurrent dynamics), A3 (E-I dynamics), F9 (plasticity acts on these architectures).

Done when: From a given recurrent weight matrix you computes eigenvalues and predicts which input components are amplified, how fast each mode relaxes, and whether the network is stable — without reaching for attractor or oscillation vocabulary.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine: guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written explanation (Piece 4). Pieces are numbered by type, not sequence.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 3 Guided reading Background comprehension underlying all of 1-5 (firing-rate assumptions, feedforward filtering, recurrent eigenbasis, E-I stability, stochastic bridge) 1 Derivation 1 (effective time constant), 2 (stability condition), 3 (oscillatory vs. monotonic E-I decay), 4 (steady-state amplification) 2 Simulation 1, 2, 4 (numeric verification), 5 (saturation prevents blow-up, set-up for the written argument) 4 Written explanation 5 (primary), synthesis of 1-4 Piece 1 — Eigenmode analysis of a linear recurrent networkPiece 2 — Verifying eigenmode predictions in a linear recurrent network, then breaking itPiece 3 — Guided reading: D&A chapter 7Piece 4 — Written explanation: why linearity is not enough

Type: derivation · Time: 90-120 min

Learning goals - Derive the effective time constant and steady-state gain of a single eigenmode of a linear recurrent network, from the network's defining ODE. - State and justify the stability condition for the full network in terms of the eigenvalues of the recurrent weight matrix. - Reduce a linearised excitatory-inhibitory network to a 2x2 eigenvalue problem and derive the algebraic condition that separates damped oscillatory return to equilibrium from monotonic decay.

Task

Part A — single-population eigenmode. Take the standard linear recurrent network equation from D&A §7.3: tau du/dt = -u + h + W u, where u(t) is the vector of population firing rates, h is the (constant, step) feedforward drive, and W is the recurrent weight matrix. Let e_a be an eigenvector of W with real eigenvalue lambda_a, and suppose the input is aligned with that eigenvector: h = h_a e_a, u(0) = 0.

  1. Write u(t) = c(t) e_a, substitute, and reduce the vector ODE to a scalar ODE for c(t). Solve it in closed form.
  2. Read off the effective time constant tau_eff(lambda_a) and the steady-state value c_ss.
  3. Define the amplification factor A(lambda_a) as the ratio of c_ss to the steady-state value the same input would produce with W = 0 (feedforward-only). Give A(lambda_a) as a function of lambda_a alone.
  4. Evaluate tau_eff and A at lambda_a = 0.8 with tau = 10 ms. State in words what happens to tau_eff as lambda_a -> 1^-, and why lambda_a = 1 is a singular point of your formula.
  5. Generalise: for an N-dimensional W with eigenvalues lambda_1, ..., lambda_N (assume W diagonalisable), state the condition on {lambda_a} under which every mode of the network is stable (bounded as t -> infinity for bounded h). Justify it from the sign of (1 - lambda_a) in your part-2 solution.

Part B — excitatory-inhibitory 2x2 reduction. Consider the linearised two-population E-I system from D&A §7.5, written in the same form as Part A with u = (v_E, v_I)^T and a single shared tau: tau du/dt = -u + h + W u, W = [[w_EE, -w_EI], [w_IE, -w_II]], all four w's >= 0.

  1. For W_1 = [[0.5, -1.0], [1.5, -0.5]], compute trace(W_1) and det(W_1), form the characteristic polynomial lambda^2 - trace(W_1) lambda + det(W_1) = 0, and solve for the eigenvalues. State whether they are real or complex.
  2. Repeat for W_2 = [[0.5, -1.0], [0.2, -0.5]].
  3. From your part-1 solution, the decay/growth rate of a mode is governed by (lambda_a - 1)/tau. For each of W_1 and W_2, compute the eigenvalues of (W - I) and state (i) whether the network is stable, and (ii) whether its return to equilibrium after a small perturbation is monotonic or has a damped oscillatory component. Give the general algebraic rule (in terms of trace and det of the 2x2 W, or equivalently the discriminant of the characteristic polynomial) that decides real vs. complex eigenvalues, independent of the specific numbers.
  4. For the complex case, give the angular frequency of the decaying oscillation (omega, in rad/ms) and the decay time constant, using tau = 10 ms.

Deliverable

A written derivation (LaTeX, Markdown with math, or clearly legible scanned handwriting) covering all 9 steps, with every intermediate line of algebra shown — not just final formulas. Final numeric answers for steps 4, 6, 7, 9 must be stated explicitly, not left as unevaluated expressions.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All 9 steps correct and shown in full. Correctly identifies 1 - lambda_a as the mode's decay rate and derives A(lambda_a) = 1/(1 - lambda_a) from first principles (not by pattern-matching to a remembered formula). Correctly states the general stability condition as max_a Re(lambda_a) < 1 (not just "lambda < 1" for a single real eigenvalue). Correctly derives and states the trace/det (or discriminant) rule for real vs. complex eigenvalues of a general 2x2 matrix, then applies it to both W_1 and W_2. Adequate Steps 1-4 and 6-8 correct with correct final numbers, but the general N-dimensional stability condition (step 5) is stated loosely (e.g. "eigenvalues less than 1" without addressing complex eigenvalues via their real part), or the general trace/det rule in step 8 is not stated explicitly (only the two worked numeric cases are done). Not yet Arithmetic errors in the closed-form solution, effective time constant, or eigenvalue computations; amplification factor derived by guessing rather than substitution; oscillatory vs. monotonic distinction not tied to real vs. complex eigenvalues.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation · Time: 75-100 min

Learning goals - Build a linear recurrent network whose weight matrix has a known, controlled eigenstructure, and recover that eigenstructure numerically. - Verify the effective-time-constant and steady-state-amplification formulas from Piece 1 against direct numerical integration, per eigenmode. - Observe the stability boundary directly (an eigenvalue crossing 1 produces unbounded growth) and observe that a saturating nonlinearity restores boundedness without restoring linearity's clean per-mode formulas.

Task

Construct a 3-neuron linear recurrent network with weight matrix W = 0.8 (e1 e1^T) + 0.3 (e2 e2^T) + (-0.5) (e3 e3^T), using the fixed orthonormal vectors e1 = (1,1,1)/sqrt(3), e2 = (1,-1,0)/sqrt(2), e3 = (1,1,-2)/sqrt(6). (These three vectors are mutually orthogonal and unit-norm; you may verify this by hand before coding.) This construction guarantees W is symmetric with exact eigenvalues 0.8, 0.3, -0.5 and eigenvectors e1, e2, e3.

Simulate tau du/dt = -u + h + Wu by explicit Euler integration with tau = 10 ms, dt = 0.1 ms, for at least 300 ms, starting from u(0) = 0.

Part 1: For each eigenvector e_a in turn, drive the network with h = 1.0 * e_a (a step input aligned with that eigenvector, held constant). Project u(t) onto e_a at every time step. Record the simulated steady-state value and the simulated time to reach 63.2% of that steady-state value (the empirical effective time constant). Compare both against the analytic tau_eff(lambda_a) and steady-state amplification formulas from Piece 1.

Part 2: Rebuild W with the first eigenvalue changed from 0.8 to 1.2 (keep 0.3 and -0.5). Drive with h = 1.0 * e1 as before and simulate for 200 ms. Confirm the projection onto e1 grows rather than saturates, and compare its growth to the analytic solution from Piece 1's step-1 formula evaluated at lambda_a = 1.2 (same closed form, now with 1 - lambda_a < 0).

Part 3: Keep the unstable W from Part 2 (lambda_1 = 1.2). Add a saturating nonlinearity: replace the recurrent drive Wu with an elementwise cap, f(x) = r_max * tanh(x / r_max) with r_max = 5.0, applied to the vector Wu before it enters the ODE. Simulate for 400 ms with the same h = 1.0 * e1. Confirm the projection onto e1 now approaches a finite steady value instead of diverging.

Write this as under ~100 lines of self-contained Python using only numpy (no downloads, no external data). Print a small table for Part 1 (lambda, predicted tau_eff, predicted steady-state, simulated steady-state, simulated tau_eff) and the key checkpoint values for Parts 2 and 3.

Deliverable

The .py script, plus its printed output, plus 3-5 sentences per part stating whether the numerical result matched the analytic prediction from Piece 1 (and by how much, if not exact).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong W constructed correctly (numpy's eigendecomposition recovers 0.8, 0.3, -0.5 and eigenvectors matching e1, e2, e3 up to sign); Part 1 table matches analytic predictions to within a few percent for all three modes; Part 2 shows clear unbounded growth matched against the analytic exponential; Part 3 shows convergence to a finite value and you correctly identifies that the saturating network no longer obeys the simple 1/(1-lambda) amplification law because superposition (linearity) has been broken. Adequate Part 1 and Part 2 done correctly with correct qualitative conclusions, but Part 3 only shows "it doesn't blow up" without engaging the amplification-formula-breaks-down point, or the effective-time-constant measurement method (63.2% threshold) is applied inconsistently across modes. Not yet W's eigenvalues/eigenvectors not verified against the target values before use; input not actually aligned with an eigenvector (so the projection mixes modes and the comparison to Piece 1 is invalid); Part 2's instability not connected back to the sign of (1 - lambda_a); Part 3 nonlinearity applied in a way that makes it a different network (e.g. saturating u instead of the recurrent drive) without noting the difference.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: guided reading · Time: 45-60 min

Learning goals - Extract the firing-rate model's defining assumptions and the regime in which the text says it breaks down. - Extract the functional description of what a feedforward weight matrix does to an input pattern, and what a linear recurrent network's eigenbasis represents. - Extract the conditions the text gives for E-I stability and the qualitative behaviours (nonlinear saturation, stochastic units) that the chapter previews without fully developing.

Task

Read D&A chapter 7, sections Introduction, Firing-Rate Models, Feedforward Networks, Recurrent Networks, Excitatory-Inhibitory Networks, and Stochastic Networks, in that order. Answer the following, citing the section (not a page number) each answer comes from:

  1. (Firing-Rate Models) What quantity does a firing-rate model track instead of individual spikes, and what averaging assumption (over time, over a population, or both) justifies replacing the spiking description with it? Name one experimental or coding scenario the text raises where this averaging assumption fails.
  2. (Firing-Rate Models) What is the general functional form the text gives for how a firing rate depends on the summed synaptic input (linear vs. rectified vs. saturating), and which of these does the chapter use for most of the subsequent feedforward/recurrent analysis?
  3. (Feedforward Networks) In a purely feedforward network, what mathematical operation does the weight matrix perform on an input pattern? Give the example the text uses (e.g. a specific receptive-field or filtering construction) of a feedforward weight matrix computing something interpretable.
  4. (Recurrent Networks) Why does the text diagonalise/eigendecompose the recurrent weight matrix rather than working with the original coordinates? What does it mean, physically, for an eigenvector of W to be "selectively amplified"?
  5. (Recurrent Networks) What does the text call the network's behaviour as the largest eigenvalue approaches its stability boundary, and what does it say happens to the network's response time and gain there?
  6. (Excitatory-Inhibitory Networks) What are the two population variables in the E-I model, and what sign convention does the text use for excitatory vs. inhibitory weights in the recurrent matrix?
  7. (Excitatory-Inhibitory Networks) What condition(s) does the text give on the linearised system for the equilibrium to be stable, and does it separate oscillatory from non-oscillatory decay explicitly, or only implicitly through the eigenvalues?
  8. (Stochastic Networks) What update rule does the text give for a stochastic binary unit (what determines the probability it turns on), and what quantity does the text introduce that plays a role analogous to potential energy in this stochastic dynamics? (Answer only what the text states about this quantity's definition — do not attempt to characterize its long-run behaviour or interpret what it predicts about the network's fixed points.)
  9. (Synthesis, Feedforward vs. Recurrent Networks vs. the saturating-nonlinearity remarks in the chapter) The chapter notes that some population computations require nonlinearity. Find and quote (in your own words) one such computation the text mentions that a purely linear network cannot perform, and what property of linear systems the text says is responsible.

Deliverable

Written answers to all 9 questions, 1-4 sentences each, each tagged with its source section.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All 9 answered accurately and tied to the correct section; question 8 correctly reports only the definition given in the text without speculating about long-run/equilibrium behaviour of that quantity; question 9 identifies a genuine nonlinearity-requiring computation with the correct linearity-based reason. Adequate 7-8 of 9 correct; minor imprecision in the E-I stability condition (question 7) or in distinguishing the firing-rate model's averaging assumption from its saturation assumption (question 2). Not yet Answers not traceable to the named sections, or question 8 drifts into describing what the energy-like quantity implies about network fixed points / stable configurations.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: written explanation · Time: 45-60 min

Learning goals - Explain, in prose, why a linear recurrent network's entire behaviour (amplification, relaxation speed, stability) reduces to its eigenstructure. - Name and justify, using the linearity properties (superposition, homogeneity), two computations a saturating nonlinear network can do that a linear one structurally cannot.

Task

Write 300-600 words, aimed at a reader who has done Piece 1 and Piece 2 but not read D&A directly, explaining: (a) why decomposing a linear recurrent network into eigenmodes lets you predict its entire time course and stability from a list of numbers (the eigenvalues) rather than simulating the full system; (b) what "selective amplification" and "effective time constant" mean physically, using your lambda = 0.8 numbers from Piece 1 as a worked reference; (c) name two specific computations (e.g. winner-take-all selection between competing inputs, and gain control/normalization that keeps output bounded regardless of input strength) that require a saturating nonlinearity, and for each, state precisely which linear-system property (superposition or homogeneity/scale-invariance) is violated by the computation, and why that property being violated is exactly why a linear network cannot do it.

You may briefly note (1-2 sentences, no more) that the chapter also introduces stochastic units with an energy-like quantity as a preview of a different kind of network description — but do not develop what that quantity implies about network behaviour; that is out of scope for this lesson.

Deliverable

A 300-600 word written explanation, prose (not bullet points except perhaps for the two named computations in part (c)).

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong Part (a) correctly explains that eigenvectors are invariant directions so the coupled system decouples into independent scalar equations, each fully characterised by its own eigenvalue; part (b) is numerically concrete using the lambda=0.8, tau=10ms, tau_eff=50ms, amplification=5 example; part (c) names two distinct computations, each correctly tied to superposition or homogeneity being violated, with the mechanism explained rather than just asserted. Word count within range. No attractor/energy-landscape/oscillation-as-memory language, no rhythm/synchrony language. Adequate (a) and (b) correct but part (c) only asserts "nonlinearity is needed" without identifying which specific linear property (superposition vs. homogeneity) fails for each computation. Not yet Eigenvalues/eigenvectors treated as a computational shortcut without explaining why they decouple the system; numeric example from Piece 1 not used or used incorrectly; only one computation named in part (c), or the stochastic-network aside expands into attractor/memory territory.

Grader key hidden

docs.title: Lesson spec
docs.text:
Goal: Establish synaptic weights as variables changing under local activity-dependent rules rather than fixed parameters. Derive the basic Hebbian rule's instability and the normalisation fixes, then show that running such a rule on a population is doing statistics — Oja's rule extracts the principal component of the input covariance. Contrast with supervised rules that need an external teacher.

Scope — what the lesson covers
  • LTP and LTD as bidirectional weight change; STDP's timing window as the biological grounding for rate-based rules
  • The basic Hebbian rule, its unbounded growth, and subtractive versus multiplicative normalisation as two fixes producing two different weight distributions
  • Covariance and BCM rules, with BCM's sliding threshold as its stability mechanism
  • Oja's rule converging on the principal eigenvector of the input covariance; ocular dominance and receptive-field formation as what this computes developmentally
  • The delta rule and the perceptron as the supervised contrast case
  • Not covered: reward-based three-factor rules (F10)

You should be able to answer: 1. A presynaptic spike leads the postsynaptic spike by 10 ms — is the synapse strengthened or weakened, and roughly what is the half-width in milliseconds of the STDP window it falls inside? 2. For an unnormalised Hebbian rule, what happens to the weight magnitude as time goes to infinity, and why does that make the rule implausible on its own? 3. Subtractive and multiplicative normalisation both bound total weight — which drives individual weights to saturate at their bounds, and which leaves a smoother distribution? 4. For Oja's rule, what vector does the weight converge to, expressed in terms of the input covariance matrix? 5. Write the delta-rule update for a linear unit with target d and output y, and name the one input it needs that Hebbian, covariance and BCM rules do not.

Feeds: the Bridge checkpoint, A4 (short-term plasticity and eligibility traces), B4 (developmental pruning builds on the competition material), F10 (reward-based learning as the third regime).

Done when: For any rule in this lesson you states its update equation, what it converges to or diverges toward, and whether it needs a teacher signal — without consulting the chapter.

Dayan & Abbott wrote exercise sets for every chapter and publish them free at gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/~dayan/book. This lesson's are in exercises/c8.pdf (chapter 8), with any code and data under exercises/exercises/c8/. Work all.

They are the authors' problems, not this course's, so they take precedence where the two overlap: if an exercise here duplicates one of theirs, do theirs. They are written for MATLAB; translating to numpy is part of the work and is not hard. The teacher agent has no answer key for these — it marks by reading your code and output, and says so rather than pretending to a key it does not have.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text:
Consume, then apply, then refine: guided reading (Piece 3) → derivation (Piece 1) → simulation (Piece 2) → written explanation (Piece 4). Pieces are numbered by type, not sequence.

Coverage map Piece Type Lesson acceptance criteria addressed 3 guided reading 1 (STDP window), 3 (subtractive vs. multiplicative), 5 (delta rule's teacher signal) 1 derivation 2 (unbounded Hebbian growth), 4 (Oja fixed point = top eigenvector) 2 simulation 2 (Hebbian divergence, numerically), 3 (saturation vs. smooth distribution), 4 (Oja converges to top eigenvector) 4 written explanation 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (synthesis across all five) Piece 1 — Hebbian instability and the Oja fixed pointPiece 2 — Oja vs. Hebb vs. two normalizations, on synthetic covariance-known dataPiece 3 — Guided reading: D&A ch. 8Piece 4 — Written explanation: from LTP/LTD to two kinds of learning

Type: derivation · Time: 60-75 min

Learning goals - Solve the linear ODE for an unconstrained rate-based Hebbian synapse and show the weight has no finite steady state. - Derive the general fixed-point condition for Oja's rule and show it reduces to the eigenvector equation of the input covariance. - Linearize Oja's dynamics around two candidate fixed points and use the sign of the resulting rates to determine which is stable. - State, in one paragraph, why Oja's rule finds specifically the top eigenvector and not any eigenvector.

Task

Part (a) — the instability. A linear unit has output \(y = wx\) driven by a presynaptic input with constant variance \(\sigma_x^2 = 4\). It follows the basic (rate-based) Hebb rule \(\dot w = \eta \langle yx \rangle = \eta \sigma_x^2 w\), with \(\eta = 0.1\). (i) Solve this ODE for \(w(t)\) given \(w(0) = 0.01\). (ii) Evaluate \(w(t)\) at \(t=5\) and \(t=20\) (time in whatever units make \(\eta\) dimensionless-per-unit-time). (iii) State the limit as \(t \to \infty\), and explain in one or two sentences why this is biologically impossible for a real synapse (tie it to LTP saturation).

Part (b) — the fixed point. Now a linear unit has a 2-D input with covariance matrix \(C = \mathrm{diag}(3, 1)\) (so \(e_1=(1,0)\) and \(e_2=(0,1)\) are already its eigenvectors, with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1=3\), \(\lambda_2=1\)). Oja's rule is \(\dot w = \eta\left(Cw - (w^\top C w)\,w\right)\). (i) Show algebraically that setting \(\dot w = 0\) requires \(Cw^* = (w^{*\top}Cw^*)\,w^*\), and that for any unit-norm \(w^*\) this is exactly the eigenvector equation \(Cw^* = \lambda w^*\) with \(\lambda = w^{*\top}Cw^*\). (ii) Take \(\eta = 0.05\). Linearize around \(w^* = (1,0)\): write \(w = (1+\delta_1, \delta_2)\), substitute into \(\dot w\), drop terms of order \(\delta^2\) and higher, and derive the two first-order rates \(\dot\delta_1 = a\,\delta_1\) and \(\dot\delta_2 = b\,\delta_2\). (iii) Repeat the same linearization around \(w^* = (0,1)\), writing \(w=(\delta_1, 1+\delta_2)\), and derive the corresponding rates \(c\,\delta_1\) and \(d\,\delta_2\). (iv) Using the four signed rates from (ii)-(iii), classify each fixed point (stable node vs. saddle) and state the general rule connecting the sign of the transverse rate to \((\lambda_i - \lambda_1)\).

Deliverable

A written derivation (typed or scanned handwriting) covering (a)(i)-(iii) and (b)(i)-(iv), showing every algebraic step — not just final expressions — plus the four numeric rates from (b) and a one-paragraph statement of the general result: "Among unit vectors, Oja's rule's only asymptotically stable fixed point is the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue of \(C\)."

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All sub-parts solved correctly with shown algebra; both fixed points correctly classified with correct signed rates; closing paragraph correctly generalizes beyond the diagonal example (states the result in terms of \(\lambda_i - \lambda_1\), not just "it worked for this matrix"). Adequate Part (a) fully correct. Part (b)(i) correct. At least one of the two linearizations in (b)(ii)/(b)(iii) correct with correct sign; final classification of at least \(w^*=(1,0)\) as stable is correct, even if the saddle argument is thin. Not yet Part (a) has a sign or algebra error changing the qualitative conclusion (e.g. concludes decay instead of growth), or part (b) never reaches a signed rate — only asserts "eigenvectors are fixed points" without doing the linearization.

Grader key hidden

The marking criteria for this piece are in the teacher build.

Type: simulation · Time: 90-120 min

Learning goals - Verify, numerically, that Oja's rule converges onto the principal eigenvector of a known input covariance — computed independently by hand. - Watch plain unnormalized Hebbian learning diverge on the same data and characterize the divergence quantitatively. - Reproduce the qualitative difference between subtractive and multiplicative normalization: saturation-prone vs. smooth weight distributions.

Task

Write one self-contained Python script (numpy only, no downloads, under 100 lines) with three parts. Exact parameters below are mandatory — do not substitute your own, since results are checked numerically.

Part A — Oja's rule finds the eigenvector. 1. By hand, before writing any code: for \(C = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), compute both eigenvalues and the eigenvector belonging to the larger eigenvalue, normalized to unit length. Show the characteristic polynomial and the null-space computation — don't just quote a numerical eigensolver. 2. Generate data: rng = np.random.RandomState(0), Z = rng.randn(5000, 2), Cholesky-factor \(C\) by hand as \(L=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt2 & 0\\ 1/\sqrt2 & \sqrt{0.5}\end{pmatrix}\) (verify \(LL^\top=C\) yourself), then X = Z @ L.T. 3. Implement Oja's rule as an online update over all 5000 rows in order: \(y = w\cdot x\), \(w \leftarrow w + \eta(yx - y^2w)\), with \(\eta=0.01\), \(w_0=(1,0)\). 4. Report the final \(w\), \(\|w\|\), and the cosine similarity between final \(w\) and your hand-computed eigenvector from step 1.

Part B — plain Hebbian diverges. 5. On the same X from Part A (same order), run the unnormalized rule \(w \leftarrow w + \eta\,y\,x\), \(\eta=0.01\), \(w_0=(0.05, 0)\). 6. Record \(\|w\|\) after steps 100, 500, 1000, and 5000 (0-indexed: "after step \(k\)" = after processing \(k\) rows). Report the final normalized direction \(w/\|w\|\) and compare it, in one sentence, to Part A's converged direction.

Part C — subtractive vs. multiplicative normalization. 7. Build 10 synapses' worth of input: rng2 = np.random.RandomState(1), gains = np.linspace(0.7, 1.3, 10), base = rng2.randn(8000), Xc = gains[None,:]*base[:,None] + 0.3*rng2.randn(8000,10), then shift so the minimum entry is exactly \(0.1\): Xc = Xc - Xc.min() + 0.1. 8. Implement subtractive normalization: each step, \(y=w\cdot x\), \(\Delta w_i = \eta\,y\,(x_i - \bar x)\) (mean-subtracted, so \(\sum_i \Delta w_i = 0\) before clipping), then clip every \(w_i\) to \([0, 2]\), then re-distribute any excess/deficit from clipping among the not-yet-saturated units so that \(\sum_i w_i = 10\) exactly is restored each step. \(\eta = 0.01\), \(w_0 = (1,1,\dots,1)\). 9. Implement multiplicative normalization: each step, \(w \leftarrow w + \eta\,y\,x\), then rescale \(w \leftarrow w\cdot(10/\sum_i w_i)\). Same \(\eta\) and \(w_0\). 10. Report, for each rule: the final weight vector, how many entries are at or within \(10^{-3}\) of a bound (0 or 2), and the standard deviation across the 10 weights.

Deliverable

The script itself, plus a short (5-10 sentence) results note reporting: the cosine similarity number from Part A and how many degrees off-axis that implies; the four \(\|w\|\) values from Part B and the qualitative growth shape; and the saturation-count / std-dev pair for each rule in Part C, with a one-line statement of which normalization scheme is the "winner-take-all" one.

Rubric — how this is marked Band Criteria Strong All three parts implemented exactly to spec (correct RNG calls, correct constants); Part A cosine similarity ≥ 0.99 reported and correctly matched against an independently-derived hand eigenvector (not copied from code output); Part B values match expected order of magnitude at steps 100/500/1000, correctly identified as exponential blow-up; Part C correctly shows more saturated entries and higher std for subtractive than multiplicative, with the right qualitative read on which is "smoother." Adequate All three parts run and produce a result in the right qualitative direction (Oja converges, Hebb diverges, subtractive is more saturated/spread than multiplicative), but one part has a parameter deviation (wrong seed, wrong \(\eta\), wrong \(w_0\)) that you didn't catch, or the hand-eigenvector check in Part A is missing/wrong even though the code result is fine. Not yet Any part is missing, or Oja's rule fails to converge (cosine similarity well below 0.99, e.g. from an update-rule sign error), or the Part C rules are not actually distinguishable in the reported output (same std, same saturation), indicating the two update rules were implemented identically.
